manufacturerCadDirectory.scope: File listings and source links; not verified product or symbol counts

scope: Independently authored explanations and original educational illustrations, supported by public references. Not a standards database replica or engineering approval.
thirdPartyMaterials: Referenced by link only; no rights to third-party material are granted.

entries.name: Current transformer
entries.summary: A current-measurement transformer used with metering and protection equipment.
description: A current transformer produces a secondary current related to the current in its primary conductor. A drawing uses the CT representation to show where current is measured and which metering or protection circuit receives that measurement. It does not, by itself, specify the CT ratio, accuracy class, burden or secondary connection.

On a single line diagram, the CT is placed at the measurement location. A schematic expands the secondary wiring, terminals and connected devices. Multi-core and multi-secondary CT arrangements require additional information; one generic preview cannot describe every configuration.
readingNotes: Follow the primary conductor through the CT and then identify the secondary circuit separately.
Polarity marks and terminal labels belong to the selected device and its documented connections.
drawingChecklist: Identify the metering or protection purpose.
Reference the ratio, class and burden in the equipment documentation.
Cross-reference secondary terminals and any test facility.
entries.distinction: A CT measures current. A VT measures voltage. Their secondary circuits and isolation/testing arrangements are different.

facts.label: Exact standard graphic
facts.value: Consult the applicable standard and drawing legend

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HXF1CT, VXF1CT (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public CT symbol categories and secondary-winding variants.
Manufacturer examples of current and voltage transformers.
Manufacturer reference for CT test-terminal arrangements.

entries.name: Voltage transformer
entries.summary: A transformer providing a voltage signal for metering or protection.
description: A voltage transformer provides a secondary voltage related to the voltage on its primary winding. VT and PT, for potential transformer, are common terms encountered in power drawings. Its representation identifies a measurement function; winding connections, fuses, earthing and secondary circuits need their own documented detail.

A single line diagram places the VT at the system connection being measured. The associated schematic shows how that voltage reaches a meter, relay or control system. A power transformer can look similar in a simplified drawing, so the label and context matter.
readingNotes: Check the measured voltage connection and the number of windings or secondaries shown.
Read polarity, ratio and secondary earthing from the specified device documentation.
drawingChecklist: Identify the measured bus or feeder.
Record the specified ratio and accuracy information.
Cross-reference primary and secondary protection and terminals.
entries.distinction: A VT supplies a voltage measurement; a power transformer supplies a power circuit. A shared transformer-like outline does not make their functions interchangeable.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HXF1PT, VXF1PT (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public potential- and voltage-transformer categories.
Manufacturer instrument-transformer information.

entries.name: Circuit breaker
entries.summary: A switching device that can interrupt a circuit, with specified fault-interruption capability.
description: A circuit-breaker representation identifies a device capable of interrupting its circuit under the operating conditions for which it is rated. The drawing should connect that device to its equipment identification, protection arrangement and control information. The graphical mark alone does not establish the current rating, breaking capacity or trip settings.

Breaker representations vary between drawing conventions and may include qualifiers for operating mechanism or protection. An SLD gives system position and major connections. A control schematic expands the close, trip, indication and auxiliary-contact circuits.
readingNotes: Read device state according to the drawing legend, rather than assuming every open-looking mark means equipment is currently open.
Keep the equipment tag, graphical symbol and ANSI device-function number 52 distinct.
drawingChecklist: Reference the voltage, current and breaking-capacity data.
Identify poles and the applicable protection arrangement.
Link the control circuit and auxiliary contacts.
entries.distinction: A disconnector provides isolation; it is not automatically a fault-interrupting circuit breaker. Check published device capabilities.

facts.label: Device specification
facts.value: Voltage, current, interruption and trip information

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HCB1, VCB1 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public breaker categories and qualifying features.
Manufacturer explanation of circuit-breaker characteristics.
Public reference for device-function number 52.

entries.name: Disconnector
entries.summary: A switching device providing an electrical isolation function.
description: A disconnector, often called an isolator, provides an isolation function in an electrical circuit. Its representation should be read with the drawing legend and the selected device specification. Do not infer load-breaking or fault-interruption capability simply because a drawing contains a switch-like mark.

In a switchgear SLD the disconnector may appear next to a breaker, earthing switch or bus section. Control drawings can also show position indications and interlocking. The main-circuit representation and the auxiliary indications describe different parts of the equipment.
readingNotes: Identify which circuit segment is isolated by the device.
Distinguish the main switching function from its auxiliary position contacts.
drawingChecklist: Link the selected device and its isolation capability.
Reference the position indication and interlock documentation.
Show associated earthing arrangements where applicable.
entries.distinction: A load-break switch has a specified load-switching capability. A disconnector designation alone does not establish that capability.

facts.label: Related device number
facts.value: 89: line switch, where the convention applies

references.relevance: Manufacturer explanation of disconnector and load-breaking functions.
Public secondary-distribution switchgear context.

entries.name: Load-break switch
entries.summary: A switch with a specified capability to make and break normal load current.
description: A load-break switch operates a loaded circuit under the normal conditions covered by its rating. It should not be confused with a circuit breaker, whose specified duties can include interrupting fault current. Some products combine switching and isolation, and some are used with fuses for a protection arrangement.

The SLD shows where the switch connects the circuit. Its schedule or manufacturer reference establishes the duty and capabilities. The device name, qualifiers and associated protective equipment explain more than the generic mark alone.
readingNotes: Look for a separately identified fuse or breaker in the protection path.
Check whether isolation is an additional specified function of the chosen product.
drawingChecklist: Reference the load-switching capability.
Identify any associated protection device.
Record the product type and operating arrangement.
entries.distinction: Fault-making, load-breaking and fault-breaking are different capabilities. Avoid using a single switch label as a substitute for the equipment specification.

facts.label: Protection
facts.value: May rely on separate protective devices

references.relevance: Public explanation of load-break switches and their relationship to protection.

entries.name: Earthing switch
entries.summary: A switch used to connect an identified circuit section to earth.
description: An earthing-switch representation identifies a switching connection between an electrical circuit section and earth. This is a switching device, not merely an earth-reference mark. On an SLD, its location helps explain which part of the switchgear or circuit is connected to earth when the device operates.

Switchgear documentation can include earthing-switch position indications and interlocks with other devices. Those relationships need to be shown or referenced separately. The generic concept here does not establish operating sequence, duty, interlock logic or permission to operate equipment.
readingNotes: Identify the circuit section and earth connection on either side of the switching element.
Follow interlock and position references in the equipment documentation.
drawingChecklist: Identify the associated panel or circuit.
Reference the specified device duty.
Cross-reference interlocks and position indication.
entries.distinction: A protective-earth mark identifies a connection or function. An earthing switch identifies equipment that makes a switching connection.

references.relevance: Public earthing-switch control and indication functions.
Manufacturer switchgear equipment context.

entries.name: Fuse
entries.summary: An overcurrent protective element that interrupts a circuit by melting its fuse link.
description: A fuse representation identifies a protective fuse link in a circuit. Its rating and operating characteristics are additional information: a generic fuse mark does not specify utilization category, current, voltage, breaking capacity or coordination with other protective equipment.

Fuses appear in main power circuits, transformer circuits and control supplies. Some assemblies add indication or auxiliary contacts. A drawing should distinguish the protective link from the holder, disconnect mechanism and any indication function.
readingNotes: Follow the protected circuit and identify how many fuse links are represented.
Treat associated indication contacts as separate schematic elements.
drawingChecklist: Reference the fuse type and rating.
Identify the holder or fuse-switch assembly when relevant.
Keep auxiliary indication and replacement information linked.
entries.distinction: A fuse and a fused disconnector may share protective components, but the assembly also includes a switching or isolation function.

facts.label: Selection data
facts.value: Type, voltage, current and breaking capacity

facts.label: Assembly details
facts.value: Holder and switching functions are separate

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HFU1, VFU1 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public fuse, auxiliary-contact and indication categories.
Manufacturer explanation of fuse categories.

entries.name: Busbar
entries.summary: A common conductive connection distributing power to connected circuits.
description: A busbar connects multiple power circuits to a common electrical node. In an SLD it is commonly represented as a line with feeder connections. The representation describes connectivity; physical conductor dimensions, enclosure, phase arrangement and current-carrying capabilities are separate equipment information.

Bus sections and bus couplers describe how those electrical nodes can be connected or separated. Keep bus labels consistent between the system drawing, switchboard schedule and equipment documentation. A drawing line is not a scale representation of a physical busbar.
readingNotes: Identify each feeder connected to the same bus section.
Use device positions to determine which sections are shown as connected in the stated drawing condition.
drawingChecklist: Name each bus or bus section.
Reference ratings and fault-duty information.
Cross-reference any coupler or section device.
entries.distinction: A busbar is an electrical connection. Busbar trunking is a physical distribution system with model-specific enclosures and fittings.

references.relevance: Public bus-tap and power-distribution drawing categories.
Manufacturer example of a physical busbar distribution system.

entries.name: Normally open contact
entries.summary: A contact shown open in the normal state defined for its device.
description: A normally open contact is open in the normal state defined for the device. Operating its relay, pushbutton or other parent device may close the contact. The meaning of normal must be established from the drawing convention and equipment documentation; it is not necessarily the current live condition of the installation.

A schematic usually identifies the parent device and the relevant terminals. Several contact representations can belong to one relay or contactor. Cross-references connect those representations to their coil or parent equipment.
readingNotes: Read the parent device identifier before interpreting the contact function.
Check the terminal identifiers and the state convention in the drawing legend.
drawingChecklist: Identify the parent coil or actuator.
Use the documented terminal designation.
Cross-reference other contacts belonging to the same device.
entries.distinction: Normally open describes the stated normal condition. A position indication or operating snapshot may use a different state convention.

facts.label: Normal state
facts.value: Open, as defined for the parent device

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HCR21, VCR21 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public normally open relay contact categories.

entries.name: Normally closed contact
entries.summary: A contact shown closed in the normal state defined for its device.
description: A normally closed contact is closed in the normal state specified for its device. Actuating the parent device may open it. The drawing must establish that state convention and associate the contact with the appropriate equipment and terminal designations.

NC contacts occur in relay logic, indication and control circuits. The contact representation alone does not establish safety behaviour, failure response or suitability for a safety function. Those properties depend on the complete device and system design.
readingNotes: Follow the parent-device reference and the relevant circuit path.
Check whether the drawing describes a de-energised, unactuated or explicitly stated operating state.
drawingChecklist: Reference the parent device.
Document the contact terminals.
Explain any state convention that differs from the general legend.
entries.distinction: An NC mark does not prove a circuit is fail-safe or establish positive-opening characteristics. Consult the selected device and complete control design.

facts.label: Normal state
facts.value: Closed, as defined for the parent device

facts.label: Safety characteristics
facts.value: Not established by the generic symbol

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HCR22, VCR22 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public normally closed relay contact categories.

entries.name: Changeover contact
entries.summary: A contact arrangement switching a common connection between two contact paths.
description: A changeover contact connects a common terminal to one of two alternative contact paths according to its operating state. Form C and SPDT are terms commonly encountered for this arrangement. The actual terminal numbering and transfer behaviour come from the selected device.

The schematic should make the common terminal and normal state clear. A mirrored or differently oriented drawing can retain the same logical arrangement, but terminal associations must not be inferred from appearance alone.
readingNotes: Locate the common terminal and determine the path shown in the defined normal state.
Use device data to identify transfer timing and any special overlap behaviour.
drawingChecklist: Identify the common terminal.
Link both switched paths to the parent device.
Keep terminal identifiers consistent with wiring documentation.
entries.distinction: Two unrelated NO/NC contacts are not automatically one changeover contact. Confirm whether they share a common connection and operating mechanism.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HCR23R, VCR23R (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public Form C relay contact variants.

entries.name: Relay coil
entries.summary: The operating element associated with a relay and its separately drawn contacts.
description: A relay coil represents an operating element that changes the state of associated contacts when the device operates. Coil and contact representations are often drawn in different locations to make the circuit easier to read. Their shared identifier and cross-references establish the relationship.

The coil representation does not determine whether its supply is AC or DC, its voltage, polarity, suppression or operating duty. Those details belong to the device specification and schematic annotations. Latching and other special operating modes need explicit identification.
readingNotes: Find the device tag and follow references to its contacts.
Read supply and polarity information from the specified coil, not from an unqualified rectangle.
drawingChecklist: Reference coil supply requirements.
Identify suppression or polarity features if fitted.
Cross-reference all associated contacts.
entries.distinction: A relay coil is not a contactor power pole. Similar operating-element marks can represent equipment with different switching duties.

facts.label: Variants
facts.value: Latching, polarized and other device types

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HCR1, VCR1 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public relay-coil, latching and polarized variants.

entries.name: Contactor
entries.summary: An electrically operated switching device commonly used for repeated switching duties.
description: A contactor uses an operating mechanism to switch its main contacts and may include auxiliary contacts for control or indication. On a power drawing it represents the main switching path; on a schematic its coil and contacts may be distributed and connected by identifiers.

Its ability to switch a particular load depends on the selected device and utilization category. Overload or short-circuit protection can be provided by other devices in the arrangement. Do not treat the generic contactor representation as a complete protective device.
readingNotes: Distinguish main power poles from auxiliary control contacts.
Use the common equipment identifier to connect the power and control drawings.
drawingChecklist: Reference the load duty and contactor specification.
Show the coil supply and associated contacts.
Identify separate protective equipment where applicable.
entries.distinction: A contactor and circuit breaker have different duties. Adding an overload relay does not make every contactor assembly equivalent to a circuit breaker.

facts.label: Tag example
facts.value: KM is a convention, not a universal requirement

references.relevance: Manufacturer description of contactors and associated protection.
Public operating-coil and contact representations.

entries.name: Normally open pushbutton
entries.summary: A pushbutton contact normally shown open before actuation.
description: A normally open pushbutton combines an operator-actuated mechanism with a contact shown open in its defined normal state. Momentary and maintained or latching operation are separate characteristics that must be described explicitly.

Control schematics should identify both the contact function and the operator-facing purpose. A start label is a circuit-specific use, not an intrinsic property of every NO pushbutton. Multiple contact blocks can belong to a single actuator.
readingNotes: Read the actuator description and contact-block association.
Check whether the operating mode is momentary, maintained or latching.
drawingChecklist: Identify the actuator and contact terminals.
State the intended operating mode.
Link additional contact blocks to the same operator device.
entries.distinction: A NO contact symbol by itself does not identify the pushbutton actuator or its mechanical operating mode.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HPB11, VPB11 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public NO pushbutton and operating-mode variants.

entries.name: Normally closed pushbutton
entries.summary: A pushbutton contact normally shown closed before actuation.
description: A normally closed pushbutton has a contact closed in its specified normal state. Actuation changes that contact state according to the selected operator and contact block. Momentary, maintained, latching and positive-opening characteristics must be identified from device documentation.

A stop circuit is a common use, but the generic representation does not establish emergency-stop suitability or the required control-system behaviour. Operator labels, device specifications and the complete circuit remain necessary.
readingNotes: Identify the contact block and its parent operator.
Read mechanical and contact characteristics from the manufacturer information.
drawingChecklist: Show terminal designations.
State the mechanical operating mode.
Reference the complete circuit purpose and device selection.
entries.distinction: An ordinary NC pushbutton and an emergency-stop device are not interchangeable solely because both drawings show a closed contact.

facts.label: Safety function
facts.value: Requires complete device and circuit assessment

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HPB12, VPB12 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public NC pushbutton and actuator variants.

entries.name: Emergency-stop operator
entries.summary: An identified emergency-stop operator and its documented contact arrangement.
description: An emergency-stop operator is identified by its intended function and the properties of the selected device. A schematic may show its contact blocks, actuator and reset or latching features. The drawing must connect those features to the operator description and the complete control-system design.

This educational preview identifies the concept without specifying a safety circuit. A mushroom actuator, NC contact or stop label alone does not establish the required safety performance. Use the applicable standards, risk assessment and manufacturer information for the actual implementation.
readingNotes: Read the operator identification together with all associated contact blocks.
Do not infer safety performance from the actuator shape or a single contact mark.
drawingChecklist: Identify the operator and documented reset mode.
Reference contact and mechanical characteristics.
Link the complete control-system documentation.
entries.distinction: Emergency stop is a system function. A generic mushroom pushbutton depiction does not certify an emergency-stop implementation.

references.relevance: Public mushroom-head, latching and positive-break contact categories.

entries.name: Selector switch
entries.summary: An operator switch selecting between documented control positions.
description: A selector switch provides a choice between operating positions such as local and remote or manual and automatic. Its contacts may be shown separately from the operator symbol. The contact truth table or switching schedule defines which contacts operate in each position.

Maintained positions and spring-return positions behave differently. Labels, detents and return direction should be made explicit. A contact mark alone cannot describe the full switching sequence of a multi-position selector.
readingNotes: Read the position labels and any contact schedule together.
Identify maintained positions and returning positions from documented operator data.
drawingChecklist: Name each position.
Reference the associated contact blocks and terminals.
Show the return behaviour and switching schedule.
entries.distinction: A changeover contact describes connections; a selector switch also includes an operator and its position behaviour.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HSS112, VSS112 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public selector-switch positions and contact variants.

entries.name: Indicator lamp
entries.summary: A visual indicator associated with a documented control or equipment condition.
description: An indicator lamp shows an operating condition defined by its circuit and label. The generic representation identifies an indicating element; it does not define what illumination means, the supply voltage or whether the device is continuously lit or flashing.

A schematic should explain the condition driving the indication. The front-panel description should match the electrical label, so a reviewer can follow the indication from operator interface to contact, relay or controller output.
readingNotes: Read the text describing the indicated condition.
Follow the circuit supplying the lamp and identify any flashing or test function.
drawingChecklist: Record the indication label.
Reference the supply and device type.
Align schematic identification with the panel layout.
entries.distinction: An indication mark does not establish that equipment is safe, isolated or de-energised. Its meaning comes from the full circuit and operating documentation.

facts.label: Meaning
facts.value: Defined by label and control circuit

references.relevance: Public pilot-light and indication categories.
Public lighting and indication drawing categories.

entries.name: Terminal connection
entries.summary: An identified electrical connection point linking schematic and wiring information.
description: A terminal representation identifies a connection point for conductors. The terminal number and strip or assembly identifier link the schematic to physical wiring documentation. A wire number and terminal number identify different things and should not be substituted for one another.

Terminal assemblies can include links, disconnect facilities, fuses or test access. Those properties require additional identification. A generic round terminal representation does not establish the construction or rating of a selected terminal block.
readingNotes: Read the strip identifier and terminal identifier together.
Check whether the representation denotes a simple connection or an additional device function.
drawingChecklist: Match the terminal schedule.
Keep wire and terminal numbers distinct.
Reference links, test facilities and device data where applicable.
entries.distinction: An electrical junction and a physical terminal are different concepts. A connection dot alone does not necessarily identify a terminal block.

facts.label: Identification
facts.value: Strip or assembly plus terminal number

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HT0002, VT0002 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public terminal-number and wire-number variants.
Manufacturer example of terminals with added disconnect functions.

entries.name: CT test terminal
entries.summary: A current-transformer terminal arrangement providing documented test and shorting facilities.
description: A CT test-terminal arrangement connects current-transformer secondary wiring to measurement or protection equipment and provides the test or short-circuit facilities specified for the selected assembly. Its representation must be read with the manufacturer circuit and operating documentation.

Test-disconnect terminals are not all interchangeable. CT applications require the correct shorting behaviour and accessory arrangement. This reference explains what to identify in a drawing, not a procedure for disconnecting or working on a live CT circuit.
readingNotes: Identify each CT secondary path and the associated test or shorting connections.
Do not infer the operation of a test plug or link from a generic terminal mark.
drawingChecklist: Reference the exact terminal assembly.
Identify shorting links and test accessories.
Cross-reference the CT and connected measurement device.
entries.distinction: A generic disconnect terminal is not automatically suitable for a CT secondary circuit. Use an arrangement specified for the CT application.

facts.label: Application
facts.value: CT secondary measuring and test circuit

facts.label: Operating procedure
facts.value: Follow manufacturer and authorised work instructions

references.relevance: Manufacturer CT measuring, testing and leading-short-circuit terminal arrangements.
Contrast with generic disconnect-terminal products.

entries.name: Power transformer
entries.summary: Equipment transferring electrical power between winding circuits.
description: A power-transformer representation identifies equipment transferring electrical power between winding circuits. The generic mark can show the relationship between windings, but voltage levels, winding connections, vector group, rating and earthing information require additional annotations and equipment references.

Two-winding, three-winding and autotransformer arrangements describe different configurations. The SLD should identify the intended configuration clearly and link it to the transformer schedule and any associated protection or GA drawings.
readingNotes: Read the winding count and electrical connections before interpreting the rating labels.
Use the equipment reference to distinguish a power transformer from an instrument transformer.
drawingChecklist: Document the specified rating and winding connections.
Reference earthing and protection arrangements.
Link the equipment schedule and physical drawing.
entries.distinction: A transformer used for voltage measurement is a VT or PT. Its function and secondary circuit differ from those of a power transformer.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HXF1T2, VXF1T2 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public transformer types and winding variants.
Official directory for model-specific equipment CAD.

entries.name: Generator
entries.summary: An electrical generating source represented in a power-system drawing.
description: A generator representation identifies an electrical source in a power system. Its electrical connections and associated switching describe how it supplies the system. The equipment documentation establishes machine type, rating, voltage, earthing and operating capabilities.

Generator systems can also include transfer controls, synchronising, protection and paralleling equipment. These functions should be identified separately rather than compressed into a single generic generator mark. A GA drawing provides the physical package and interface information.
readingNotes: Follow the generator connection through the associated switching and protection.
Identify whether the drawing describes standby transfer, parallel operation or another documented system arrangement.
drawingChecklist: Reference the generator equipment schedule.
Cross-reference switching, control and protection.
Link the package GA and installation interfaces.
entries.distinction: A generator symbol identifies an electrical source. It does not establish permission to parallel with another source or define the transfer sequence.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HPW1G7, VPW1G7 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public generator types and representations.
Manufacturer generator switchgear and controls context.

entries.name: Three-phase motor
entries.summary: An electrical motor load connected to its switching and protective equipment.
description: A motor representation identifies an electrical machine operating as a load in the stated system arrangement. Connection count, motor type and additional winding or rotor detail can change the representation. Its nameplate and equipment schedule provide the selected machine data.

The SLD places the motor and its feeder equipment. A schematic shows the controller, coil supply, protection interfaces and auxiliary functions. A simple circle and motor label do not establish a complete motor-starting or protective arrangement.
readingNotes: Follow the feeder back to its switching and protective devices.
Read the documented motor connection and starting arrangement.
drawingChecklist: Reference motor rating and connection data.
Identify the starter or control arrangement.
Cross-reference auxiliary and protection circuits.
entries.distinction: A contactor switches the motor circuit. Motor protection and short-circuit interruption may be provided by additional specified equipment.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HMO13, VMO13 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public three-phase motor variants.
Manufacturer description of contactor and protective roles.

entries.name: PLC input / output
entries.summary: A controller interface point connecting field signals to an identified module channel.
description: A PLC input or output point connects a field signal with a controller module and channel. Input and output, digital and analogue, and one-wire or multi-wire arrangements are distinct characteristics. The module specification establishes electrical behaviour and terminal information.

A schematic should connect channel identification to the I/O schedule and field device. Shared supplies, commons and isolation boundaries require their own documentation. A generic controller box is not a pinout or wiring instruction for a particular module.
readingNotes: Identify module, channel and signal direction.
Use the selected module documentation to interpret supply, common and terminal requirements.
drawingChecklist: Match the I/O schedule.
Identify signal type and channel reference.
Link module terminals and field-device documentation.
entries.distinction: An input point, output point and communications connection are different interfaces. A generic box cannot establish their electrical compatibility.

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: PLCIOI1T, PLCIOO1T (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public input/output point and wiring-count categories.

entries.name: Capacitor
entries.summary: A capacitive component or bank identified with its circuit function and ratings.
description: A capacitor representation identifies a capacitive component or arrangement in a circuit. Polarised, non-polarised, adjustable and other variants need the appropriate representation and annotations. In power drawings a capacitor bank is a system assembly, rather than merely a scaled-up generic component mark.

Ratings, discharge arrangements, switching and associated reactors or protection depend on the application and selected equipment. A symbol is an identification aid; it does not provide those design values.
readingNotes: Identify whether the drawing denotes a component or a bank assembly.
Read polarity or adjustable features only where the selected variant documents them.
drawingChecklist: Reference the component or bank rating.
Identify any switching and associated protective equipment.
Link the equipment documentation for discharge or reactor arrangements.
entries.distinction: A capacitor-bank representation does not identify every component of the assembled bank or establish its switching duty.

facts.label: Polarity
facts.value: Must be explicitly represented where relevant

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HCA1, VCA1 (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public capacitor categories and variants.

entries.name: Resistor
entries.summary: A resistive component with its value and purpose documented separately.
description: A resistor representation identifies a resistive component in a circuit. Different drawing conventions can use different basic outlines, while additional qualifiers distinguish variable resistors, shunts or heating elements. The value, rating and purpose are separate annotations.

In power-system controls, a resistive component may belong to measurement, suppression or another specific circuit. A neutral-earthing resistor is a specialised system component and should not be identified only with an unqualified generic resistor mark.
readingNotes: Read the component value and application label alongside the mark.
Check whether a qualifier identifies a variable device, heater, shunt or another variant.
drawingChecklist: Reference resistance and rating information.
Identify the circuit purpose.
Distinguish specialised assemblies from a generic component.
entries.distinction: IEC-style rectangular and other conventional resistor depictions can describe the same component concept, but qualifiers and documentation still matter.

facts.label: Variants
facts.value: Fixed, variable, shunt and other applications

facts.label: Public Autodesk reference names
facts.value: HRE1B, VRE1B (vendor identifiers, not IEC symbol IDs)

references.relevance: Public fixed, variable, shunt and heater categories.
Historical graphic-symbol reference; vendor conventions may differ.

entries.name: Protective earth
entries.summary: An identified connection serving the protective earthing function.
description: Protective-earth identification indicates a connection serving the protective earthing function. It should be distinguished from functional earthing, signal references and other grounding conventions. The drawing context and applicable documentation establish the meaning of each connection.

A protective-earth mark does not specify conductor size, bonding arrangement or installation compliance. Those requirements are documented in the electrical design, equipment information and applicable installation rules. Equipment-marking symbols and diagram symbols can belong to different standards.
readingNotes: Read the connection label and its intended function.
Keep diagram references distinct from markings physically applied to equipment.
drawingChecklist: Identify the protective connection.
Reference bonding and conductor information separately.
Avoid ambiguous earth or signal-reference labels.
entries.distinction: Protective earth, functional earth and a signal common are different functions even when a drawing uses visually related marks.

facts.label: Equipment markings
facts.value: May reference a different symbol standard

references.relevance: Official diagram-symbol reference and related symbol standards.
Public electrical drawing-category reference.

entries.name: Battery
entries.summary: An electrochemical electrical source or storage element represented in a circuit.
description: A battery representation identifies an electrochemical source or energy-storage element. The generic depiction can suggest cells or polarity, but it does not determine the number of cells, chemistry, voltage, energy capacity or protective equipment in the selected system.

A battery energy storage system adds controls, power conversion and other equipment around its storage element. System drawings should distinguish the DC battery circuit from AC conversion, switching and protection. The physical battery cabinet is a separate GA object.
readingNotes: Identify whether the drawing denotes a cell, battery bank or complete storage system.
Read DC polarity and the conversion interface from the documented arrangement.
drawingChecklist: Reference voltage and storage equipment data.
Separate DC storage and AC interfaces.
Cross-reference protective and isolation equipment.
entries.distinction: A battery is a storage element. A BESS includes additional equipment and controls; the terms do not identify identical scope.

entries.name: Flexible conductor
entries.summary: A wavy conductor line showing a connection that must flex, such as a lead to moving equipment or a vibration break.
description: The flexible conductor mark replaces a straight run of conductor with a wave or loop to show that the connection is intended to bend in service. Typical uses are leads to hinged doors, pendant control stations, crane festoons, motor terminal boxes on resilient mounts and short links that absorb thermal movement between busbars and equipment.

On a schematic the wave says nothing about the cable construction. Stranding class, insulation type, bending radius and the number of operating cycles must come from the cable schedule or equipment specification. A drafter should not use the wave simply to make a long wire look tidy, because a reader will assume a moving or vibrating part exists at that point.

Check the cable schedule for a flexible stranding class and any drag-chain or festoon rating.
drawingChecklist: Identify the moving part the flexible section serves.
Reference a cable type suited to repeated flexing.
Show strain relief or termination details where the lead leaves the moving part.
entries.distinction: A flexible conductor bends in service; a twisted-pair mark shows conductors twisted together for noise rejection and implies nothing about movement.

entries.name: Screened conductor
entries.summary: A single conductor enclosed by a drawn screen outline, showing that the core has a conductive shield around it.
description: A screened conductor symbol adds an outline around one conductor to show a conductive screen, braid or foil surrounding the core. It is used for analogue instrument signals, encoder and thermocouple extension wiring and other circuits where capacitively coupled interference must be kept off the signal.

The outline alone does not show where or whether the screen is earthed. Earthing at one end, both ends or through a capacitor is a design decision that should be drawn explicitly with an earth or bonding symbol at the screen tail. The symbol also does not distinguish foil, braid or combined screens, which belong in the cable schedule.

Check whether a cable marker applies to the screened core and any others in the same cable.
drawingChecklist: Show the screen termination point explicitly.
Record the screen type in the cable schedule.
Keep screen drain terminals numbered on the terminal plan.
entries.distinction: A screened conductor has a conductive shield; a cable-core grouping outline only shows that several cores share one sheath and implies no shielding.

entries.name: Screened conductor with earthed screen

description: This form combines the screen outline with an explicit earth connection on the screen tail. Instrument drawings commonly earth the screen at the control end only, while drive motor cables are often earthed at both ends through 360 degree glands.

When the earth mark appears at only one end of the cable, the other end of the screen is normally cut back and insulated. A reader should not infer that both ends are bonded unless both are drawn. entries.name: Optical fibre cable

description: The optical fibre cable representation marks a link that carries light signals. entries.name: Conductors within one cable

description: On multi-line schematics each core is drawn as a separate line, which hides the fact that several of them share one sheath. The outline implies no screen and no particular core count beyond the lines it crosses. Spare cores are often not drawn, so the cable may have more cores than the outline encloses. Cores from one cable may also be split across several sheets, each with its own grouping mark and the same cable tag.

entries.name: Conductor count by numeral
entries.summary: A single oblique stroke across a line with a number beside it, stating how many conductors the single line represents.
description: Where a single line stands for several conductors, the count can be shown by one oblique stroke plus a numeral rather than by repeating strokes. This is the practical form for larger counts, such as a 12 core control cable or a 4 conductor feeder, where drawing many strokes would be cluttered.

The numeral counts conductors, not circuits or phases. A value of 4 might be three phases and neutral, or four control cores, and the drawing must say which. It also does not state conductor size. On plan drawings the count is often combined with a size, for example 4 x 16 mm2, which belongs in the annotation rather than the stroke.
readingNotes: Confirm what conductors are included in the count, for example phases, neutral and PE.
Read the size annotation separately from the count.
drawingChecklist: Place the numeral next to the stroke, not on another line.
Say what the conductors are where it is not obvious.
Keep conductor size in the cable annotation.
entries.distinction: A numeral count gives any number of conductors on one stroke; the three-phase conductor group uses three strokes specifically for three conductors.

entries.name: Neutral conductor mark
entries.summary: A mark on a single-line conductor group identifying which conductor is the neutral, often drawn as a small circle on a stroke.
description: When a single line represents a group of conductors, one of them can be identified as the neutral with a distinct mark on its stroke, together with the letter N where clarity requires. This lets a single-line diagram tell a three-phase three-wire feeder from a three-phase four-wire feeder without expanding to multi-line form.

The mark identifies the neutral but does not say whether the neutral is fully rated, reduced or oversized for harmonic loading. It also does not show where the neutral is earthed. System earthing is a separate decision shown at the source, for example a star point to earth connection or a neutral earthing resistor.
readingNotes: Check whether the feeder carries a neutral before assuming four-wire loads are supported.
Look at the source to see how the neutral is earthed.
drawingChecklist: Mark the neutral on each four-wire feeder.
State neutral sizing where it differs from phase conductors.
Show neutral switching or links where the scheme requires them.
entries.distinction: A neutral mark identifies the N conductor; a PEN mark identifies a combined neutral and protective conductor with different switching rules.

entries.name: Protective conductor mark
entries.summary: A mark on one stroke of a conductor group identifying the protective earth conductor carried with the circuit.
description: This mark identifies the protective conductor within a group of conductors drawn as one line. It shows that the circuit carries its own PE conductor to the load, which is how the fault return path for automatic disconnection is provided in TN systems. The letters PE are often written beside the mark.

The mark does not tell you whether the PE is a separate core, the cable armour or a parallel earth continuity conductor. Each option affects earth fault loop impedance differently, so the cable schedule must say which is used. The mark is also distinct from the protective earth terminal symbol, which shows a connection point rather than a conductor in a run.
readingNotes: Confirm what physically forms the PE: a core, armour or separate conductor.
Check that the PE size meets the protective conductor sizing rule used.
drawingChecklist: Mark the PE on every circuit that carries one.
Identify whether armour is used as the PE.
Show PE terminations at both ends.
entries.distinction: The PE conductor mark identifies a conductor in a run; the protective earth symbol identifies a connection point to the earthing system.

entries.name: PEN conductor mark
entries.summary: A mark identifying a combined protective and neutral conductor, as used in TN-C sections of a supply.
description: The PEN mark identifies one conductor that performs both the protective and neutral functions. It appears in TN-C and TN-C-S arrangements, typically between the supply transformer and the main switchboard, where the PEN is later separated into N and PE at a defined point.

A PEN conductor must not be switched or isolated on its own, and once separated into N and PE the two must not be rejoined downstream. A drawing that shows a PEN mark should therefore also show the separation point clearly. The mark says nothing about minimum conductor size, which local wiring rules set for PEN conductors.
readingNotes: Find the point where the PEN is split into N and PE.
Check that no switching device opens the PEN conductor alone.
drawingChecklist: Show the PEN to N and PE separation point.
Avoid single-pole switching of the PEN.
Confirm PEN sizing against the applicable wiring rules.
entries.distinction: A PEN conductor combines N and PE functions; a neutral mark shows a conductor that has no protective role.

entries.summary: A single-line notation such as 3/N/PE showing a three-phase circuit carrying both a neutral and a separate protective conductor.
description: Single-line diagrams often state the conductor complement of a circuit with a short notation beside the line, for example 3/N/PE 400/230 V 50 Hz. This tells the reader at a glance that the circuit has three phases, a neutral and a separate protective conductor, which is the normal TN-S final distribution arrangement.

The notation is a statement about which conductors exist, not their sizes. It also does not confirm that the downstream equipment uses the neutral. Changes in the notation along a feeder, for example from 3/PEN to 3/N/PE, mark the point where a PEN conductor has been split.

Read voltage and frequency that may follow the conductor notation.

entries.name: Interchange of conductors
entries.summary: A crossing mark showing that two or more conductors swap position, such as a phase transposition or deliberate phase swap.
description: The interchange form shows conductors crossing over so that their positions change along the run. On transmission lines it represents transposition, used to balance phase impedances. On motor and generator circuits it may show a deliberate swap of two phases to reverse rotation or to correct phase sequence.

The symbol must be read with the phase labels on both sides, because the purpose differs. An unlabelled crossing may be mistaken for a drafting artefact. Where the interchange changes phase sequence, any synchronising or phase-sequence-sensitive equipment downstream must be checked.
readingNotes: Read phase labels either side of the interchange.
Check whether rotation or phase sequence downstream depends on it.
drawingChecklist: Label phases on both sides of the interchange.
State the reason for the swap where it changes rotation.
Check synchronising and metering connections downstream.
entries.distinction: Interchanged conductors change position or phase; an unconnected crossing just passes over another conductor with no change.

entries.name: Conductor branching from a group
entries.summary: One conductor drawn leaving a single-line conductor group at an angle, showing where it splits from the bundle.
description: When conductors are drawn as a single line or bundle, a breakout shows the point where one conductor leaves the group to go elsewhere. The leaving conductor is normally drawn at an angle or with a short curve and carries its own identifier, so that the group line beyond the breakout has one less conductor.

The breakout is a drawing convention, not a physical joint. No splice or terminal exists at the point unless a separate symbol is placed there. Readers should track the conductor count on each side of the breakout and confirm the identifiers match on both.

Do not read the breakout as a splice.

Add a splice symbol only where a physical joint exists.
entries.distinction: A breakout is a drawing convention for a conductor leaving a bundle; a wire splice is a physical joint.

entries.name: T-connection without junction dot
entries.summary: A conductor meeting another at a right angle and stopping there, which IEC practice reads as a connection even without a dot.
description: In IEC drawing practice a conductor that runs into another and ends there forms a T-connection, and the connection is understood whether or not a dot is drawn. Many drafting standards still recommend the dot for clarity, but undotted tees are common on legacy and vendor drawings.

The convention depends on the drawing family. On some ANSI-style drawings an undotted tee may be ambiguous, which is why a dot is preferred there. Readers should check the drawing legend. A T-connection only shows electrical continuity; it does not tell you where the physical joint is, which may be at a terminal some distance away.

Find the physical terminal or joint that realises the tee.

Prefer a dot where drawings may be read under other conventions.
Avoid four-way crossings that rely on dots alone.

entries.name: Double junction of conductors
entries.summary: Four conductors joined using two offset T-junctions rather than one crossing dot, to avoid confusion with a crossing.
description: A four-way connection drawn as a cross with a single dot can be misread if the dot is lost in printing or scanning. The double junction draws the same connection as two T-junctions offset a short distance along the line, each with its own dot, so that the connection survives poor reproduction.

Electrically the double junction is the same node as a dotted cross. It does not represent two separate joints. Drafters use it to make the intent robust, and readers should not count it as an additional connection point or a different wire number unless the drawing shows one.

Confirm wire numbers are the same on all four branches.

Keep the offset small enough to read as one node.
Number all four branches consistently.
entries.distinction: A double junction is one node drawn as two offset tees; an unconnected crossing has no node at all.

entries.name: Single-core cable sealing end
entries.summary: The termination at the end of a single-core cable where it is sealed and connected to an overhead line or equipment.
description: A sealing end terminates a cable by controlling the electric stress at the screen cut-back, sealing out moisture and providing a connection to the conductor. The single-core form appears at each phase of medium and high voltage single-core cable circuits, typically at the cable to overhead line transition or at outdoor switchyard equipment.

The symbol does not show whether the termination is indoor or outdoor, heat-shrink, cold-shrink or porcelain, nor how the cable screen is bonded. Screen bonding at sealing ends, for example solid bonding or single-point bonding with sheath voltage limiters, must be drawn separately.
readingNotes: Check the screen bonding arrangement at each sealing end.
Look for surge arresters fitted beside outdoor sealing ends.
drawingChecklist: State termination type and voltage class.
Show screen bonding at the termination.
Identify the equipment or line the sealing end connects to.
entries.distinction: A sealing end terminates a cable; a straight-through joint connects two cable lengths together.

entries.summary: A joint connecting two lengths of the same cable in line, drawn as a mark on the cable route.
description: The straight-through joint connects two cable lengths end to end, restoring insulation, screen and sheath continuity. The symbol does not show whether screens are cross-bonded at the joint, which is common on high voltage single-core circuits. Cross-bonding links and sheath voltage limiters are separate items on the bonding diagram. It also does not distinguish a joint made between identical cables from one between different types, which is a transition joint.

entries.name: Separable cable connector
entries.summary: A plug-in screened termination that connects a medium voltage cable to an equipment bushing and can be separated.
description: Separable connectors, such as elbow and T-body connectors, terminate a medium voltage cable onto a bushing so that the cable can be disconnected without cutting it. They appear on ring main units, pad-mounted transformers and switchgear with standardised bushing interfaces, and the T-body form often allows a second cable or a surge arrester to be stacked behind it.

The drawing symbol identifies the plug-in interface but not the interface type, current rating or whether the connector is load-break or dead-break. Those details determine whether it may be operated under load and must be given in text. A dead-break connector must never be separated while energised.

entries.name: Sealed cable end
entries.summary: A cable end that is sealed and capped but not connected, such as a spare circuit or a cable laid for future use.
description: A sealed cable end shows a cable that terminates without connection, typically capped with a heat-shrink or cold-shrink end cap. It appears on network diagrams for spare circuits, cables laid ahead of future equipment, and cables isolated and left in the ground after a fault or diversion.

A capped cable may still be connected at its other end and therefore energised. The symbol does not tell you its state, so the reader must check the switching position at the source end before treating it as dead. Drawings should also note whether the cable is earthed for safety.

Look for notes that the capped cable is earthed or isolated.

entries.name: Feeder busway
entries.summary: A busway run used purely to carry power between two points, drawn as a distinct trunking line without tap-off points.
description: Feeder busway carries high current between a transformer and switchboard, or between switchboards, in an enclosed busbar trunking rather than parallel cables. Single-line diagrams draw it as a distinct line style or double line with its rating, so that it is not mistaken for cable.

The symbol does not show the busway impedance, which is often lower than equivalent cables and affects fault level downstream. It also does not show the conductor arrangement, such as whether a full neutral or separate earth bar is included. Expansion units, fire barriers and flanged ends are physical details on the busway layout drawing.
readingNotes: Read the busway rating and conductor arrangement.
Use busway impedance, not cable data, for fault calculations.
drawingChecklist: State current rating and conductor configuration.
Reference the busway layout drawing.
Include busway impedance in fault studies.

entries.name: Plug-in busway
entries.summary: Busway with tap-off outlets along its length, drawn with outlet marks where plug-in units can be connected.
description: Plug-in busway distributes power along its route through outlets into which tap-off units can be inserted. It is common in rising mains in multi-storey buildings, factory floors and data halls, where loads change and new feeders are added without rewiring.

description: This symbol shows a tap-off unit plugged into the busway, with the outgoing circuit leaving through a fuse or circuit breaker in the unit. On single-line diagrams it replaces the board-and-feeder pattern used for switchboards, since the busway itself acts as the distribution bus.

The connection symbol does not show the tap-off unit rating unless annotated. Tap-off units may be fused or contain a breaker, and they usually have an interlock preventing insertion or removal under load. The protective device inside the unit should be drawn with its own symbol and rating.

description: An end feed unit is the cable or transformer connection box at the start of a busway run. On single-line diagrams it shows where the supply enters the busway and is often annotated with the incoming cable details. Centre feed units, used to reduce voltage drop on long runs, are a related variant.

The symbol does not show whether the feed unit includes isolation. Many end feed units are simple cable boxes, so isolation for maintenance must be at the upstream switchboard. Check cable entry and gland plate sizes on the layout, because large parallel cable sets need substantial space.

entries.name: Power distribution block
entries.summary: A terminal assembly that splits one incoming conductor into several outgoing conductors on a common bar.
description: A power distribution block takes one large incoming conductor and distributes it to several smaller outgoing conductors on a shared conducting bar, saving space compared with stacking lugs on one terminal. It is used in control panels to distribute supply to several circuit breakers or loads.

The symbol shows the shared node and terminal count but not the short-circuit current rating, which varies widely between products and must suit the available fault current. Outgoing conductors connected to a distribution block usually need upstream protection sized for the smallest outgoing conductor unless tap rules allow otherwise.

entries.name: Multi-pole plug and socket

description: The multi-pole form draws each contact of a connector as a pin and socket pair, grouped together and tied by a common outline or mechanical link to show they belong to one connector body. It is used for machine harness connectors, removable control modules and multi-pin field connectors on instruments.

The multi-line form shows every pin, which makes it suitable for wiring diagrams where pin numbers matter. It does not show keying, coding or the connector series, which prevent mismating and must be stated in text. Unused pins are often omitted, so the pin count drawn may be less than the connector size.

entries.name: Inline cable coupler
entries.summary: A connector joining two cables without either half being mounted on equipment, such as an extension lead coupling.
description: An inline coupler joins two free cables, with neither half fixed to a panel or device. Typical uses are extension leads, portable equipment feeds and sensor cables with a disconnect point partway along the run. Drawings show both halves floating on the cable line, sometimes with a note that the coupling is located in a particular area.

Because the coupler is free, its location is not fixed by the equipment, so the drawing should state where it is. The symbol does not show ingress protection, latching or whether the coupling may be separated under load. For power couplers, the live side should be the socket half so exposed pins are not energised.

Look for a location note for the coupler.
drawingChecklist: Show which half is on the supply side.

entries.name: Connector with protective earth contact
entries.summary: A plug and socket in which one contact is the protective earth, usually making first and breaking last.
description: This form identifies a connector where one contact carries the protective conductor. The earth contact is normally longer so it makes before and breaks after the live contacts, keeping the connected equipment earthed whenever it could be energised. The earth pin is drawn with a protective earth mark or PE label.

The symbol does not prove the first-make, last-break feature exists in the selected product, so the connector type must be checked. Where a connector carries power and signals, the earth pin also often serves as the reference for screens, which should be drawn explicitly.

entries.name: Neutral link, closed
entries.summary: A removable link in the neutral conductor shown in its closed position, allowing the neutral to be opened for testing.
description: A neutral link is a bolted or plug-in link in the neutral conductor, often mounted in a fuse carrier style holder alongside phase fuses. It allows the neutral of a circuit to be disconnected for insulation testing or fault finding without disturbing other circuits on the neutral bar. The closed form shows its normal service state.

The symbol is not a switch and the link should not be opened under load. It does not provide overcurrent protection; the fuse-like holder can mislead readers into treating it as a neutral fuse. Rules on whether the neutral may be separately disconnected differ between earthing schemes.
readingNotes: Do not read the holder as a fuse.
Confirm the link is opened only with the circuit isolated.
drawingChecklist: Label the link with its circuit number.
Show it in its normal closed state.
Check scheme rules for neutral disconnection.
entries.distinction: A closed neutral link is a removable connection; a neutral fuse would be a protective device and is generally not permitted.

entries.name: Neutral link, open
entries.summary: A neutral link drawn removed or open, showing the neutral conductor disconnected at that point.
description: The open neutral link shows the link withdrawn so that the neutral is disconnected. Drawings use it where a circuit is normally run with the neutral open, for example to isolate a spare or to segregate a neutral during a changeover, and on test procedures that show the link removed.

An open neutral on a live four-wire circuit can cause severe overvoltage on single-phase loads, so an open link in normal service needs a clear reason on the drawing. The symbol says nothing about the phase conductors, which may still be energised.

Check that phases are also isolated before working.

entries.name: Neutral-to-earth link
entries.summary: The single link bonding the neutral bar to the earth bar at the point where a TN-C-S supply splits into N and PE.
description: The neutral-to-earth link connects the neutral and earth bars at one point, normally the main switchboard. In Australian and New Zealand practice it is the MEN link, and in other TN-C-S schemes it is the point where the incoming PEN is split. This illustration is an independent explanation rather than the IEEE graphic. A jumper can be a plug-in bridge, a wire link or a screwed strap, and the symbol does not distinguish them. Jumpers that must be removed for testing should be identified as such.
readingNotes: Check whether the jumper is removed during testing.
Identify the physical jumper type.
drawingChecklist: Show every jumper on the terminal plan.
Mark test-removable jumpers.
Keep the jumper current within terminal rating.
entries.distinction: A terminal jumper ties adjacent terminals; a wire splice joins conductors without terminals.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE main bonding jumper symbol
entries.summary: US-practice bonding jumper between the grounded neutral and the equipment grounding system at the service.
description: In North American practice the main bonding jumper connects the grounded conductor, the neutral, to the equipment grounding conductor and enclosure at the service equipment. Its function corresponds to the neutral-to-earth link in TN-C-S systems. Single-line diagrams show it at the service disconnect, and separately derived systems have a corresponding system bonding jumper.

This illustration is an independent explanation and not an IEEE graphic. Only one bond should exist per service or separately derived system. Sizing rules come from the applicable electrical code, and the drawing should state the conductor or strap size.
readingNotes: Locate the bond at the service or derived system source only.
Check for unwanted downstream neutral to ground bonds.
drawingChecklist: Show the jumper at the service equipment.
State jumper size.
Show system bonding jumpers on separately derived systems.
entries.distinction: A main bonding jumper bonds neutral and ground at the service; an equipment bonding jumper bonds metal parts together.

entries.name: Flexible bonding strap
entries.summary: A flexible braid or strap bonding a movable or vibrating metal part, such as a panel door, to the earthing system.
description: A bonding strap connects metal parts that cannot be bonded with rigid conductors, such as hinged doors carrying equipment, gland plates, cable tray across expansion joints and equipment on anti-vibration mounts. Braided straps also provide low impedance at high frequency, which helps with EMC bonding in drive panels.

The symbol does not state cross-sectional area or length, both of which affect protective and high-frequency performance. A long thin strap may satisfy continuity tests but give poor EMC performance. Painted surfaces under strap lugs must be cleaned for a reliable connection.
readingNotes: Check strap size against the protective conductor rule.
Look for EMC bonding requirements in drive panels.
drawingChecklist: State strap cross-section and length.
Show both bonding points.
Specify paint removal at lugs.
entries.distinction: A bonding strap is a flexible protective or EMC bond; a flexible conductor is a circuit conductor that must flex in service.

entries.name: Frame or chassis connection
entries.summary: A connection to the metal frame or chassis of equipment, which may or may not itself be connected to earth.
description: The frame or chassis connection shows that a circuit point is connected to the metal structure of a device, drawn as a line ending in a comb or hatched mark. It is common on electronics, vehicle and machine wiring, where the chassis is used as a common reference or return.

A chassis connection is not automatically an earth connection. Equipment on a vehicle or isolated supply may have a chassis that is not connected to earth at all. Where the chassis is also protectively earthed, the protective earth symbol should be shown separately so the safety function is clear.

Look for a separate protective earth connection on the frame.
drawingChecklist: Show whether the chassis is earthed.
Separate chassis returns from protective earthing.
Identify the chassis bonding point.
entries.distinction: A chassis connection ties to the equipment frame; a protective earth connection ties to the installation earthing system.

entries.name: Noiseless earth
entries.summary: An earth connection specifically designated as low-noise, used for sensitive measurement and electronics references.
description: The noiseless or clean earth symbol identifies a connection to an earth that is kept free of noise from power circuits, usually an instrument earth bar connected to the main earthing system at a single point. It is drawn as an earth symbol enclosed in a circle or with a distinguishing mark.

A noiseless earth is not a separate earth electrode. Separate electrodes not bonded to the main earth create dangerous potential differences during faults. The symbol identifies the bar and its single-point connection, which the earthing diagram should show.
readingNotes: Find the single point where the clean earth joins the main earth.
Reject any isolated clean earth electrode.
drawingChecklist: Show the clean earth bar and its bond.
Keep power returns off the clean earth.
Label which circuits use it.
entries.distinction: A noiseless earth is a dedicated low-noise bar bonded to the main earth; a functional earth is any earth used for operation rather than safety.

entries.name: Earth electrode
entries.summary: A conductor in contact with the ground, such as a driven rod, providing the installation's connection to earth.
description: The earth electrode symbol marks a rod, plate, tape or foundation electrode that makes contact with the general mass of the earth. It appears on earthing diagrams and site layouts, often numbered so that individual electrodes can be tested and recorded.

The symbol does not tell you the electrode resistance, length, material or depth. Those come from the earthing design and test records. Multiple electrodes drawn together are only effective if spaced appropriately; electrodes too close together share the same soil and add less than expected.
readingNotes: Read electrode numbering for test records.
Check spacing between multiple electrodes.
drawingChecklist: Number each electrode.
State type, length and material.
Show the test link location.
entries.distinction: An earth electrode is the physical contact with soil; an earth connection symbol is any connection to the earthing system.

entries.name: Earth grid conductor
entries.summary: A buried horizontal earthing conductor forming part of a substation or plant earth grid, drawn on layout plans.
description: Earth grid conductors are bare horizontal conductors buried under substations and plant areas to control step and touch voltages during faults. Layout drawings show them as a distinct line style, with crossings, connections to equipment and rods marked along them.

The symbol does not show conductor size, burial depth or jointing method, which come from the earthing design. A line drawn on a plan may also not indicate whether crossings are bonded; connection marks at each crossing are needed. Above-ground risers to equipment are usually shown separately.

Look for risers to each equipment item.
drawingChecklist: State conductor size and burial depth.
Mark bonded crossings.
Show risers to equipment.
entries.distinction: An earth grid conductor is a buried horizontal conductor; an earth electrode is a rod or plate in the soil.

entries.name: Earth electrode with inspection pit
entries.summary: An earth electrode drawn inside a pit outline, showing that its top and connection are accessible for inspection and testing.
description: Many earthing designs place the top of each rod in an inspection pit so the connection can be examined and the electrode disconnected for testing. Layout drawings show the electrode inside a small square or circle representing the pit, often with an electrode number.

The symbol does not tell you whether the pit includes a test link or whether the connection is welded or clamped. A pit is also a trip and traffic hazard, so its location should be coordinated with civil drawings. The pit cover rating matters where vehicles pass.

entries.name: Lightning protection down-conductor
entries.summary: The conductor carrying lightning current from air terminations on a structure down to the earth termination system.
description: Down-conductors run from the air termination network on the roof to the earth electrodes, carrying lightning current by the shortest practical path. Installation guidance describes them as part of the building protection system together with the capture device and earth leads. Elevations and roof plans show them as a distinct line style.

The symbol does not tell you material, cross-section or separation distance from internal services. Insufficient separation can cause side flashes into wiring. Structural steel or reinforcing used as natural down-conductors may not be drawn explicitly, so check the lightning protection design notes.
readingNotes: Check separation from internal wiring and services.
Identify whether structural steel is used as a down path.
drawingChecklist: Show each down-conductor route.
State material and size.
Show test joint and earth termination at the base.
entries.distinction: A down-conductor carries lightning current to earth; a protective earth conductor carries fault current from the electrical installation.

entries.name: Lightning air termination
entries.summary: A rod or mesh conductor on top of a structure intended to intercept lightning strikes before they hit the structure.
description: The air termination is the capture device of a lightning protection system. It can be a vertical rod, a stretched wire or a roof mesh. Roof plans mark rods at their positions, and the protected zone around them is set by the design method used.

The symbol does not show height, protective angle or the design method. Rooftop equipment such as solar arrays and air conditioning plant within the protected zone may still need bonding or separation, which should appear on the lightning protection layout.

Read rod heights from the layout notes.
drawingChecklist: Show every air termination position.
State rod height or mesh size.
Link to the down-conductor routes.
entries.distinction: An air termination captures the strike; a surge arrester limits overvoltage on electrical conductors.

entries.name: Lightning protection test joint
entries.summary: A disconnectable joint near the base of a down-conductor that allows the earth termination to be tested separately.
description: Each down-conductor usually has a test joint at a convenient height above ground. Opening it separates the above-ground lightning conductor from the earth electrode, so electrode resistance and conductor continuity can be measured. Elevations show it as a small box or clamp mark on the down-conductor.

The test joint is not an isolating device for electrical work; it is only opened for inspection with no storm risk. The symbol does not specify clamp type or whether it is housed in a box. Missing or painted-over test joints are a common inspection finding.
readingNotes: Locate the test joint on each down-conductor.
Confirm it is reachable for inspection.
drawingChecklist: Show a test joint on every down-conductor.
State mounting height.
Number joints to match inspection records.
entries.distinction: A lightning test joint separates the down-conductor from its electrode; an earth test link separates the installation MET from its electrode.

entries.name: Main earthing terminal
entries.summary: The terminal or bar where protective conductors, bonding conductors and the earthing conductor of an installation meet.
description: The main earthing terminal is the hub of an installation's earthing. Installation guidance describes it as the point that provides the main equipotential connection, with the earthing conductor to the electrode, main bonding conductors to metallic services and protective conductors to circuits all landed on it. Earthing schematics draw it as a bar with labelled connections.

The symbol shows the hub but not the size of each conductor, which must be scheduled. It also does not show the removable test link, which should be drawn on the electrode connection. In larger sites, sub-main earth bars are separate items connected back to the MET.

Look for the test link on the electrode conductor.

Show earthing conductor and test link.
Schedule bonding conductor sizes.

entries.name: Direct neutral earthing connection
entries.summary: A transformer or generator star point connected straight to earth with no intentional impedance, as in a solidly earthed system.
description: This representation shows a star point connected directly to an earth symbol. It marks a solidly earthed system, which gives high earth fault current and allows ordinary overcurrent devices to clear earth faults quickly. It is standard on most low voltage distribution systems and common on transmission networks.

The symbol does not tell you whether there are several earthing points on the network or the earth electrode arrangement. It also excludes resistance, reactance and resonant earthing, which are shown with impedance symbols between the star point and earth. Earth fault protection settings depend heavily on this choice.
readingNotes: Confirm there is no earthing impedance between star point and earth.
Check earth fault protection is suited to high fault current.
drawingChecklist: Show the star point and earth connection.
State the earthing conductor size.
Record the earthing arrangement in the system notes.
entries.distinction: A direct neutral earthing connection has no impedance; resistance earthing inserts a resistor to limit fault current.
