entries.name: Cable screen cross-bonding
entries.summary: Screens of three single-core cables transposed at joints so that induced sheath voltages cancel over a major section.
description: On long high voltage single-core circuits, the cable screens are cut at joints and reconnected in rotation so that each screen runs alongside each phase for one third of the section. This cancels most of the induced sheath voltage and circulating current. Bonding diagrams show the screen connections crossing at each joint, with link boxes and sheath voltage limiters.

The symbol shows the topology, not the link box arrangement or sheath voltage limiter rating. Errors in cross-bonding connections cause large circulating currents and overheating, so phase-to-screen allocation at each joint should be read carefully against the cable drawings.
readingNotes: Check screen rotation order at each joint.
Locate link boxes and sheath voltage limiters.
drawingChecklist: Show screen rotation at each joint.
Identify link boxes.
Show solid bonding at section ends.
entries.distinction: Cross-bonding transposes screens between phases; conductor interchange transposes the phase conductors themselves.

entries.name: Double spark gap
entries.summary: A spark gap form with two gaps sharing a common electrode, used to protect two conductors against a common earth.
description: The double spark gap places two gaps in one element, typically from each of two line conductors to a common centre electrode that is earthed. It protects a pair of conductors, such as a telecom pair, with a single component so that both lines are diverted together.

The symbol does not state breakdown voltages or whether both gaps are matched. If one gap breaks down before the other, a transverse voltage can appear across the protected pair. Check the product data where balanced breakdown matters.
readingNotes: Identify the common electrode connection to earth.
Check breakdown matching between the two gaps.
drawingChecklist: Show both line connections and the common earth.
State breakdown voltage.
Keep the earth lead short.
entries.distinction: A double spark gap protects two conductors to a common electrode; a single spark gap protects one path.

entries.name: Symmetric gas discharge tube
entries.summary: A protective gas discharge tube drawn with identical electrodes either side, listed as a distinct symmetric form.
description: The publisher's IEC-oriented library lists a symmetric protective gas discharge tube separately from the standard form. The symmetric drawing presents both electrodes identically, emphasising that the device behaves the same for either polarity of surge, as is typical for AC and signal line protection.

The symbol is a drawing variant and does not establish electrical ratings. Breakdown voltage, impulse current and follow current behaviour come from the product data. Readers should not infer three-terminal construction from this form; three-electrode tubes need their own representation.
readingNotes: Read ratings from the product data, not the symbol.
Check whether a three-electrode tube is intended instead.
drawingChecklist: State sparkover voltage and impulse rating.
Show the earth or return side.
Keep the form consistent with the legend.
entries.distinction: The symmetric form draws identical electrodes; the standard gas discharge tube form may show the electrodes differently.

entries.name: Socket outlet with protective earth contact
entries.summary: Installation plan mark for a socket outlet that includes a protective earth contact for Class I appliances.
description: On an installation plan this mark places a socket outlet whose contact set includes a protective earth pin or earthing clip. The basic half-circle outlet form is completed by a straight bar across the top of the curve, which tells the reader that the outlet connects the protective conductor of the final circuit to the plug.

Most general-purpose outlets in Australian, British and European buildings are earthed, so many project legends use this form as the default outlet. Where a legend shows both earthed and unearthed outlets, the bar is the only visual difference and should be checked carefully at shaver points, double-insulated equipment locations and extra-low-voltage outlets.
The mark does not state the plug pattern, current rating, mounting height or circuit number. Those come from the legend, outlet schedule and circuit labels written beside the symbol.
readingNotes: Look for the bar above the half circle; without it the outlet may be unearthed or simply drawn in a simplified style.
Read the circuit tag next to the symbol to find which final subcircuit and protective device feeds it.
drawingChecklist: Confirm the plug standard and current rating in the outlet schedule.
Tag each outlet with its distribution board and circuit number.
State mounting height or reference a typical mounting detail.
entries.distinction: A plain socket-outlet mark shows an outlet position only; the earth bar adds the protective contact. The protective earth terminal symbol itself is a schematic conductor mark, not an outlet.

facts.value: Outlet position on a floor plan

entries.name: Switched socket outlet
entries.summary: Plan mark for a socket outlet with its own integral switch that controls the supply to the plug.
description: A switched socket outlet combines the outlet and a single-pole or double-pole switch in one accessory plate. On the plan the outlet half circle carries a short switch stroke with a tick, borrowed from the light-switch form, showing that the user can interrupt supply at the outlet without removing the plug.

Switched outlets are the norm in Australian and British domestic work and common in kitchens, offices and plant rooms elsewhere. The symbol helps the electrician choose the correct accessory and helps the estimator count switched against unswitched outlets, which differ in cost and in the depth of box required.

The mark does not say whether the switch breaks one pole or both, and it does not make the outlet suitable for isolation of fixed equipment. Pole count and any isolation duty should be stated in the specification.
readingNotes: The switch stroke is attached to the outlet, not drawn as a separate switch symbol nearby.
Count switched and unswitched outlets separately when taking off quantities.
drawingChecklist: Specify single-pole or double-pole switching.
Identify outlets that must be unswitched, such as refrigerator or server outlets.
Keep circuit tags and earthing information on the symbol.
entries.distinction: A socket outlet with interlocked switch prevents plug insertion or withdrawal while energised; a plain switched outlet only lets the user switch the supply.

entries.name: Socket outlet with interlocked switch
entries.summary: Plan mark for an outlet whose switch is mechanically interlocked so a plug cannot be inserted or withdrawn while live.
description: Interlocked socket outlets are used for industrial plugs, welding outlets, portable plant supplies and higher-current three-phase outlets. The interlock forces the user to switch off before the plug can be removed or inserted, which prevents drawing an arc at the pins. The plan mark adds a switch stroke and a small interlock bar to the outlet form.

On industrial layouts the symbol is often paired with a current rating and pole count written beside it, for example 32 A 5-pin. The estimator should expect a heavier enclosure, sometimes with an integral fuse or circuit breaker, and the installer should expect a surface-mounted accessory rather than a flush plate.
The interlock mark does not confirm the presence of overcurrent or residual-current protection inside the unit. Check the schedule for combination units that include a breaker or RCD.
readingNotes: Check the rating text: interlocked outlets are usually specified by current, poles and IP rating together.
Do not confuse the interlock bar with the protective earth bar on a domestic outlet.
drawingChecklist: State current rating, pole count and plug standard.
State whether overcurrent or residual-current protection is integral.
Note IP rating and mounting surface.
entries.distinction: A simple switched outlet allows the plug to be withdrawn while energised; the interlocked form mechanically prevents it.

facts.label: Typical location
facts.value: Workshops, plant rooms and outdoor plant supply points

facts.label: Added information
facts.value: Plug cannot move while the switch is on

entries.name: Three-phase socket outlet
entries.summary: Installation plan mark for a polyphase socket outlet, shown with three conductor strokes on the outlet lead.
description: A three-phase socket outlet supplies portable or semi-fixed three-phase equipment such as compressors, welders, kilns and site distribution boards. Plan symbols typically show the outlet form with three short oblique strokes, the same convention used on single-line diagrams to indicate three conductors.

Because three-phase outlets differ in pin arrangement (with or without neutral), current rating and phase rotation, the symbol is nearly always accompanied by text such as 20 A 5P or 32 A 4P. The electrician needs this to choose the accessory and to confirm phase rotation at commissioning.

The strokes indicate phase conductors only. They do not show whether neutral and protective earth are included, and they do not replace the circuit schedule entry for cable size and protective device.
readingNotes: Count the strokes and read the pole annotation; a 4-pin and a 5-pin outlet look the same without the label.
Check whether an isolator or interlocked switch is shown in the same position.
drawingChecklist: Write current rating and pin count beside the symbol.
State whether a neutral is required.
Record phase rotation verification in the commissioning checklist.
entries.distinction: A single-phase earthed outlet has no conductor strokes; the three strokes mark the polyphase supply.

entries.name: Weatherproof socket outlet
entries.summary: Plan mark for an outdoor or wet-area socket outlet with a protective enclosure, usually tagged with its IP rating.
description: Weatherproof outlets are placed on external walls, in wash-down areas, car parks and roof plant. The plan symbol uses the normal outlet form with an IP or WP tag, and some legends add a small enclosure line around the outlet to show the hinged cover.

The tag matters to the installer because it decides the accessory family, gland type and whether the cover must keep its rating with a plug inserted. Outdoor outlets also usually require residual-current protection, so the reader should look for the RCD indication or the circuit schedule note.
The symbol does not state the actual IP code unless the number is written. WP alone is a project shorthand; the specification should fix the numeric rating.
readingNotes: Look for an IP number, not just WP or EXT text.
Check whether the outlet is also shown as residual-current protected.
drawingChecklist: State the IP code required with a plug inserted where relevant.
Confirm residual-current protection for the circuit.
Show mounting height above finished ground.
entries.distinction: An interior outlet and a weatherproof outlet can share the same base form; only the enclosure tag or outline distinguishes them.

entries.name: Shaver supply unit
entries.summary: Plan mark for a socket outlet fed through a safety isolating transformer, typically a bathroom shaver point.
description: A shaver supply unit contains a small isolating transformer so that the outlet is not referenced to earth. IEC-style plan symbols show the outlet half circle with two linked circles on the lead, the same pair of circles used for a transformer in diagrams, to show that the outlet is fed through isolation.

This is the only general outlet permitted in some bathroom zones, so the symbol tells the installer which accessory to buy and tells the inspector why an outlet appears close to a basin. The low power rating means it is for shavers and toothbrushes, not hair dryers or heaters.
The symbol does not show the transformer rating or the dual-voltage selector that many units include. A plain outlet drawn in a bathroom is not the same and may breach zone requirements.
readingNotes: The two linked circles are the key difference from an ordinary outlet.
Check the location against the bathroom zone drawing.
drawingChecklist: Confirm the unit is a shaver supply unit, not a general outlet.
Show its zone position relative to bath or shower.
Tag circuit and any residual-current protection.
entries.distinction: A general outlet in a bathroom position is not isolated from earth; the shaver supply unit is.

entries.name: Multiple socket outlet
aliases: double or triple outlet plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a group of socket outlets on one plate, shown by a gang number or stacked outlet strokes.
description: A multiple socket outlet groups two, three or four outlets in one accessory or box. IEC-style plans usually draw a single outlet form with the number of outlets written beside it, or with short parallel strokes on the outlet, instead of drawing each outlet separately.

The number is important for take-off and for load estimates. A desk position shown as a 3-gang outlet with data outlets beside it is a common office pattern; the reader should count the gang number, not the symbol, when scheduling accessories.

The library already lists a duplex receptacle form from a schematic CAD family. This plan mark is the architectural counting form; it does not say whether each outlet is separately switched or whether they share one circuit.
readingNotes: Read the gang number; the symbol may look identical to a single outlet without it.
Check whether switches are integral to each gang.
drawingChecklist: Write the gang number on or beside the symbol.
State switching per gang if relevant.
Tag the circuit.

entries.name: RCD-protected socket outlet
entries.summary: Plan mark for a socket outlet with residual-current protection built into the accessory itself.
description: Some outlets include a residual-current device in the accessory so that protection is provided at the point of use. Plans show this by tagging the outlet with RCD or a small residual-current mark, letting the electrician select a protected accessory instead of relying on the distribution board.

This approach is used for single outdoor outlets, refurbishment work where the board cannot take additional RCDs, and outlets used for portable tools. The plan symbol should be read with the board schedule so the designer can avoid double protection or check discrimination between the outlet RCD and an upstream device.
The mark does not state the RCD type, rated residual current or test arrangement. A plain outlet on an RCD-protected circuit is protected at the board and is drawn without this tag.
readingNotes: Distinguish outlet-integral protection from protection at the board.
Look for the RCD type in the specification, not on the plan.
drawingChecklist: State rated residual operating current and RCD type.
Check discrimination with upstream residual-current devices.
Show the test button accessibility if mounted high.
entries.distinction: An outlet on a circuit protected by a residual-current circuit breaker is drawn plainly; this form puts the RCD in the outlet.

entries.name: Fused connection unit plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a fused connection unit that feeds fixed equipment through a cartridge fuse instead of a plug.
description: A fused connection unit, often called a fused spur, connects a fixed appliance such as a towel rail, extractor fan or boiler directly to a final circuit through a small cartridge fuse. Plans commonly draw a small square with an S-shaped fuse mark or the letters FCU at the wall line, sometimes with a switch stroke for the switched type.

The symbol is common in British-style layouts on ring final circuits, where fixed loads must be fused down from the circuit rating. The reader should check the fuse rating and whether a flex outlet is fitted on the front or the cable leaves from the back of the box.
It is not a socket outlet: no plug is involved. It also does not provide isolation suitable for mechanical maintenance unless the specification says so.
readingNotes: Read the fuse rating written beside the symbol, often 3 A or 13 A.
Check whether the switched or unswitched version is required.
drawingChecklist: State fuse rating and switched or unswitched type.
Name the fixed appliance it serves.
Show the flex outlet or rear cable entry.
entries.distinction: A switched socket outlet accepts a plug; a fused connection unit is wired to fixed equipment.

facts.value: Towel rails, extract fans, boilers, hand dryers

entries.name: Flex outlet plate
entries.summary: Plan mark for a cord or flex outlet where fixed equipment is connected directly at a wall plate.
description: A flex outlet plate terminates fixed wiring at a wall plate from which a flexible cord leaves to an appliance, such as a wall heater, hand dryer or kitchen extract hood. Plans usually show a small outlet mark with a short tail or arrow indicating the cord exit, tagged with the equipment it serves.

The symbol helps coordinate electrical and architectural trades: the appliance supplier sees where the cord must reach and the electrician knows not to install a socket. It also flags that switching or fusing must be provided elsewhere, usually by an adjacent fused connection unit or isolator.
The mark does not show any protective device. The circuit schedule or an adjacent symbol must provide switching and protection.
readingNotes: Look for an adjacent fused connection unit or isolator that controls this plate.
Read the equipment tag to confirm what the cord serves.
drawingChecklist: Tag the equipment served.
Show the controlling switch or fuse location.
Give mounting height relative to the appliance.
entries.distinction: A fused connection unit includes a fuse and often a switch; a flex outlet plate only provides the cord termination.

entries.name: Cooker control unit
entries.summary: Plan mark for the double-pole control switch and outlet serving a fixed cooking appliance.
description: A cooker control unit is a high-current double-pole switch, sometimes with an auxiliary socket outlet, that controls and isolates a fixed cooker or hob. Plan legends usually draw a switch box with the letters CCU or a cooker mark, placed within reach of the appliance but not above the hob.

The symbol tells the electrician to run a dedicated radial circuit sized for the appliance, often 32 A or larger, and to install a separate cooker connection plate behind the appliance. Two symbols are often shown together: the control unit on the splashback and the connection outlet low behind the cooker. It does not show the cable size or the diversity used in the design. Those belong in the circuit schedule.
readingNotes: Look for a paired connection plate behind the appliance position.
Check whether the unit includes an auxiliary outlet.
drawingChecklist: State switch rating and auxiliary outlet requirement.
Show the connection plate position.
Tag the dedicated circuit.

entries.name: Floor box outlet
entries.summary: Plan mark for a flush floor box containing power and often data outlets in open-plan floors.
description: A floor box houses socket outlets and frequently data outlets below a hinged lid flush with the finished floor. Plans draw a square around the outlet mark, sometimes with a diagonal or the letters FB, and list the box contents in a schedule because each box can hold several accessory types.

Floor boxes are used in open offices, meeting rooms and lobbies where furniture is away from walls. They require coordination with the floor finish, raised-floor tiles or screed thickness, so the symbol is often cross-referenced to an architectural floor setting-out plan.
The square does not tell you how many outlets the box contains. Read the floor box schedule for power, data and AV contents and the circuit allocation of each power outlet.

Expect a schedule listing box contents.
drawingChecklist: Reference the floor box schedule entry.
Coordinate setting out with the floor plan grid.
Tag power circuits and data outlet numbers.

entries.name: ANSI single receptacle outlet plan symbol
entries.summary: US-style plan symbol for a single convenience receptacle: a circle with one line through it on the wall.
description: In US architectural electrical plans a single receptacle is commonly drawn as a small circle on the wall line with a single line through it. The form is quick to draw and visually lighter than the IEC half circle, and it is placed with the circle against the wall where the device box is installed.

Single receptacles are typically dedicated outlets for an appliance such as a refrigerator or a piece of equipment that must not share the outlet. Mounting height, NEMA configuration and circuit number are written beside the symbol or in a note.
The symbol does not tell you the NEMA configuration or whether the outlet is tamper-resistant. The receptacle schedule and code notes provide those details.
readingNotes: Compare the line count: one line through the circle for a single receptacle, two for a duplex.
Look for subscript letters that modify the type, such as WP or GFCI.
drawingChecklist: State NEMA configuration and rating.
Tag panel and circuit number.
Note tamper-resistant or dedicated use where required.

entries.name: ANSI duplex receptacle outlet plan symbol
entries.summary: US-style plan symbol for the standard duplex receptacle: a wall-mounted circle crossed by two parallel lines.
description: The duplex receptacle is the default convenience outlet in US buildings and is drawn as a circle against the wall with two parallel lines through it. Designers use the symbol to show spacing along walls, counter receptacles and circuit groupings. Circuit numbers are written beside the symbol with home-run arrows back to the panel, and mounting heights other than standard are noted with a subscript.
The symbol does not show whether one half is switch-controlled, whether the receptacle is GFCI or AFCI protected, or its NEMA configuration. Those are added by letters or notes.

Follow the home-run arrow and circuit number to the panel schedule.

entries.name: ANSI GFCI duplex receptacle plan symbol
entries.summary: US plan symbol for a duplex receptacle with built-in ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection, tagged GFCI.
description: A GFCI receptacle includes a ground-fault circuit interrupter that trips on a small residual current, protecting people in kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoors. The plan uses the duplex receptacle form with GFCI or GFI written beside it.

A GFCI receptacle can also protect downstream receptacles wired from its load terminals. Plans sometimes show this by tagging only the first device and noting protected outlets, so the installer must read notes to wire the line and load terminals correctly.

The tag says protection is at the receptacle. It does not say whether a GFCI breaker in the panel would be acceptable instead, and it does not show which downstream outlets are protected unless noted.
readingNotes: Check notes for downstream receptacles protected from the load side.
Do not confuse GFCI with AFCI, which addresses arcing faults.
drawingChecklist: Identify the protecting device for every protected outlet.
Tag weatherproof covers where outdoors.
Keep test button accessible.
entries.distinction: An IEC RCD-protected outlet performs a similar function under a different convention and tag.

entries.name: ANSI weatherproof receptacle plan symbol
entries.summary: US plan symbol for an outdoor or damp-location receptacle, drawn as a duplex receptacle with a WP subscript.
description: Outdoor receptacles in US practice are drawn with the duplex receptacle form plus WP. The tag tells the installer to fit a weatherproof cover, and for many outdoor locations an in-use cover that stays weatherproof while a cord is plugged in.

WP receptacles are typically also GFCI protected, so plans often carry both tags or a general note. Mounting height above grade and proximity to pools or fountains are common notes next to the symbol. WP does not specify the enclosure rating or whether an in-use cover is required. The specification must state these.
readingNotes: Read WP and GFCI tags together.
Check for an in-use cover requirement.
drawingChecklist: Specify cover type.
Confirm ground-fault protection.
State height above grade.
entries.distinction: The IEC weatherproof outlet uses an IP tag; the US form uses WP on the duplex receptacle symbol.

entries.name: ANSI special-purpose outlet plan symbol
entries.summary: US plan symbol for a special-purpose outlet or connection serving a specific appliance, keyed to a schedule.
description: Special-purpose outlets are drawn as a circle or triangle with a letter or number keyed to a schedule rather than with receptacle lines. They mark connections for ranges, dryers, water heaters, equipment and other loads with unusual voltage, current or configuration.

The key tells the reader to look up the schedule for voltage, phase, NEMA configuration or hard-wired connection. Without the schedule the symbol is incomplete, which is why it is usually paired with a detailed equipment connection table. The form does not say whether the connection is a receptacle or a hard-wired junction box. The schedule decides.
readingNotes: Always read the key letter against the schedule.
Check voltage and phase, which often differ from convenience outlets.
drawingChecklist: Key the symbol to the equipment connection schedule.
State hard-wired or receptacle connection.
Tag panel and circuit.
entries.distinction: A duplex receptacle is a general convenience outlet; a special-purpose outlet is keyed to one appliance.

entries.name: One-way light switch plan mark
entries.summary: Installation plan mark for a single-pole one-way switch that turns a lighting circuit on and off from one place.
description: The one-way switch is drawn on IEC-style plans as a small circle at the switch position with a short stroke ending in one tick. A dashed or curved switching line usually runs from the symbol to the luminaires it controls, telling the electrician which lights are switched together.

Gang count is shown by repeating the switch or by writing a number beside it, so a two-gang plate controlling two lighting groups appears as two strokes or a 2. Mounting height is normally covered by a general note rather than on each symbol.
The symbol shows a switching function and position only. It does not show the rating, the plate finish or whether the switch is single-pole or double-pole beyond the single tick convention.
readingNotes: Follow the switching line to the luminaires; the symbol alone does not say what it controls.
Count ticks: one tick for single-pole one-way, two ticks for double-pole.
drawingChecklist: Draw switching links to every controlled luminaire.
Indicate gang count where switches share a plate.
Reference mounting height in the general notes.
entries.distinction: A two-way switch has a second stroke so it can be paired with another switch; the one-way form controls from one point only.

entries.name: Two-pole one-way switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a one-way switch that breaks both line and neutral, drawn with two ticks on the stroke.
description: A two-pole one-way switch opens both poles of a single-phase circuit. The IEC plan convention adds a second tick to the one-way switch stroke, giving the reader an immediate visual cue that the switch interrupts both conductors.

Two-pole switches are specified for outdoor lighting, appliances where both poles must be broken, and some heating loads. They are also used where a switch is expected to provide functional disconnection of a fixed appliance without a separate isolator.
Two ticks do not mean the switch meets isolation requirements for maintenance. Where isolation is needed, the designer should show an isolator mark or state the isolating rating.
readingNotes: Count the ticks carefully when the drawing is reduced in size.
Check whether a separate isolator is also shown for the same load.
drawingChecklist: State whether isolation duty is intended.
Tag the controlled load.
Confirm current rating for heating or appliance loads.
entries.distinction: The single-tick one-way switch breaks one pole only; the two-tick form breaks both.

entries.name: Two-way light switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a two-way switch used in pairs so one lighting group can be switched from two places.
description: Two-way switches are installed in pairs at either end of a corridor or staircase so either switch changes the state of the lights. The IEC-style plan form draws the switch circle with strokes in two opposite directions, each with a tick, showing the changeover action.

On a plan the pair is linked by a switching line to the luminaire group. The electrician reads the pair to run strappers between the two switches; where an intermediate switch is shown between them, a third location can also control the lights.
The symbol does not show the wiring method, which can be conventional strappers or a converted arrangement. It also does not tell you the gang count unless written.
readingNotes: Expect two-way switches in pairs; a single two-way switch usually signals a drafting error or a spare.
Look for an intermediate switch between the pair on long runs.
drawingChecklist: Show both switch positions and the controlled luminaires.
Mark any intermediate switches.
Note gang count where plates are shared.
entries.distinction: In US terminology this is a three-way switch; the US four-way switch corresponds to the IEC intermediate switch.

entries.name: Intermediate light switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for an intermediate switch inserted between two two-way switches to add a third control point.
description: An intermediate switch reverses the connection of the two strapping conductors between a pair of two-way switches, so any number of intermediate switches can be added along a corridor. The plan form uses crossing strokes through the switch circle to suggest the crossover action.

On long corridors, open-plan stairs and large rooms with several doors, plans show two two-way switches at the ends and intermediate switches at the middle doors. Reading the switching lines confirms which group each set controls.
The symbol does not give contact arrangement detail or rating. Its presence also implies four-core or two-strapper wiring, which the installer must plan for.
readingNotes: Confirm the run has two-way switches at each end.
Count control points to check the number of intermediates.
drawingChecklist: Show the two end switches and every intermediate.
Link all to the controlled luminaires.
Allow for strapper wiring in the cable schedule.
entries.distinction: A two-way switch has a changeover contact; an intermediate switch crosses two strappers and is useless without two-way switches either side.

entries.name: Dimmer switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a switch that varies lamp brightness, drawn as a switch with an added variability arrow.
description: A dimmer varies the power delivered to luminaires using phase-cut electronics or a control signal. IEC-style plans typically draw the switch mark with an oblique arrow or a small adjustment mark to show continuous variation, and the switching line links it to the dimmed group.

Dimmer compatibility with LED drivers is a frequent site problem, so the symbol is usually backed by a schedule stating the dimming method: leading edge, trailing edge, 0-10 V or DALI. The reader should check that every luminaire on the dimmed group is dimmable by that method.
The plan mark does not state the dimming technology or minimum load. A rotary or push dimmer looks the same on the plan.
readingNotes: Check the dimming method in the schedule.
Confirm every luminaire in the group is compatible.
drawingChecklist: State dimming method and rated load.
Link to the dimmed luminaire group.
Note minimum load for LED circuits.
entries.distinction: A one-way switch has no variability mark; the dimmer adds continuous control of light output.

entries.name: Ceiling pull-cord switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a ceiling-mounted switch operated by a hanging cord, common in bathrooms and accessible toilets.
description: A ceiling pull-cord switch is a one-way or two-pole switch fixed to the ceiling and operated by a cord. The plan mark adds a short line with a small arrow or cord end to the switch symbol, telling the reader that the device sits at ceiling level and is operated from below.

These switches are used in bathrooms where a wall switch would be in a restricted zone, and in accessible toilets where the cord forms part of an assistance call system. The plan should distinguish a light-switching pull cord from an emergency assistance pull cord, which is a different device.
The plan mark does not give the cord length or ceiling fixing detail. Those come from the specification and accessibility requirements.
readingNotes: Check whether the cord switches lights, a fan or an assistance call.
Note that this is a building plan mark; schematic pull-cord switches in machine controls are a different device.
drawingChecklist: State switch rating and pole count.
Distinguish from assistance-call pull cords.
Give cord length or end height.
entries.distinction: The schematic pull-cord switch in control circuits is a machine emergency device; this plan mark is a building lighting accessory.

entries.name: Time-delay push switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a push switch that turns lights on for a set period, commonly used in stairwells and common corridors.
description: A time-delay push switch, often wired to a staircase timer, turns lighting on when pressed and lets it switch off after a set interval. Plans draw a push-button mark at each push position with a small clock or t tag, and show the timer location in the board where one is used.

Several push switches may be wired in parallel to one timer, so the switching line links them all to a common luminaire group. The electrician reads the plan to run a separate push conductor rather than switched-line wiring.
The plan symbol does not set the delay period or state whether the timer is in the switch or at the board. The specification should give both.
readingNotes: Look for the associated timer in the board schedule.
Expect several pushes wired in parallel on one landing group.
drawingChecklist: State delay time and adjustment range.
Show the timer location.
Link all pushes to the controlled group.
entries.distinction: A momentary bell push is not connected to lighting; a time-delay push switch starts a lighting timer.

entries.name: Push button plan mark
entries.summary: Installation plan mark for a momentary push button, such as a door bell push or call button, shown as a small circle with a dot.
description: On installation plans a momentary push button is drawn as a small circle, often with a smaller concentric circle or dot inside, at the wall position. It is used for door bell pushes, assistance call pushes, door release buttons and timer pushes, with a tag clarifying which.

The symbol is usually linked to the device it operates: a bell or chime, an intercom door release or a timer. Reading the link is important because the same push mark serves very different systems on a mixed plan. It does not show whether the push is illuminated, weatherproof or extra-low voltage. Those are scheduled.
readingNotes: Identify which system the push belongs to from its tag or link.
Check whether it is outdoors and needs a weatherproof rating.
drawingChecklist: Tag the system served.
State illumination or weatherproofing.
Show the link to the operated device.
entries.distinction: A schematic push button shows contacts; the plan mark shows the position of the accessory only.

entries.name: Switch with pilot light plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a switch with an integral pilot lamp that shows when the controlled load is on.
description: A switch with pilot light is used where the controlled load cannot be seen from the switch position, such as an external light, a water heater or a loft. The plan form adds a small lamp mark, a crossed circle, to the switch symbol.

The pilot lamp needs a neutral at the switch in many accessory designs, so the symbol tells the electrician to bring a neutral to the switch box. It may also signal a double-pole switch for appliance control.
The lamp mark does not tell you whether it lights when the load is on or when the switch is off as a locator. The specification decides.
readingNotes: Check whether the lamp indicates load on or acts as a locator.
Confirm a neutral is available at the switch.
drawingChecklist: State lamp function.
State pole count.
Tag the remote load.
entries.distinction: A plain one-way switch has no lamp; this form adds visual confirmation of the load state.

entries.name: Lighting presence detector plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a ceiling or wall sensor that switches lighting automatically according to occupancy.
description: Lighting presence detectors switch or dim luminaires according to occupancy, usually by passive infrared or microwave sensing. Plans show a small circle or square with a detection mark, often with the coverage radius drawn so designers can check the area is covered.

The plan should also show whether the detector operates in presence mode (automatic on and off) or absence mode (manual on, automatic off) and whether it includes a daylight sensor. These settings strongly affect energy performance and are often stated in a lighting control schedule.
This lighting sensor is distinct from an intruder alarm motion detector even when the sensing principle is the same. The two belong to different systems with different wiring and standards.
readingNotes: Check the coverage pattern against the room geometry.
Confirm whether the sensor controls a switching relay, a DALI group or a local load directly.
drawingChecklist: State presence or absence mode.
Show coverage radius.
Link the controlled luminaire groups.
entries.distinction: An intruder motion detector reports to an alarm panel; a lighting presence detector controls luminaires.

entries.name: Photoelectric light switch plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a light-sensitive switch that turns external or perimeter lighting on at dusk and off at dawn.
description: A photoelectric switch, or photocell, measures ambient light and operates a lighting circuit at a set lux threshold. Plans draw a small switch or box with inward arrows to indicate light received, placed where the cell can see the sky without seeing the luminaires it controls.
Photocells are often combined with time switches so that lighting comes on at dusk but goes off at a fixed time. The plan and schedule should show both devices and their logic.
The mark does not give the threshold, time delay or contactor rating. Large lighting loads are usually switched by a contactor operated by the cell.
readingNotes: Check the cell location for a clear view of daylight.
Look for a contactor or time switch in the same control scheme.
drawingChecklist: State lux setting range.
Show associated contactor or time switch.
Orient the cell away from controlled luminaires.
entries.distinction: A light-dependent resistor is a component; a photoelectric switch is a complete lighting control device on the plan.

entries.name: ANSI single-pole switch plan symbol
entries.summary: US-style plan symbol for a single-pole wall switch: the letter S at the switch position with a switch leg to the lights.
description: US architectural electrical plans mark a single-pole wall switch with the letter S beside the wall, usually with a short line to the wall. A curved dashed switch leg runs to the controlled lighting outlets, and lowercase letters can tie a switch to specific fixtures.

Subscripts modify the S: S3 for three-way, S4 for four-way, SD for dimmer, SK for key-operated and so on. The plain S therefore means a basic single-pole switch. The S does not say rating, colour or device style, which are specified separately.
readingNotes: Check for subscripts that change the type.
Follow switch legs or lowercase letters to the controlled fixtures.
drawingChecklist: Draw switch legs or letter keys to fixtures.
Use subscripts for special types.
State mounting height in general notes.
entries.distinction: The IEC one-way switch is drawn as a circle with a stroke; the US form is the letter S.

entries.name: ANSI three-way switch plan symbol
entries.summary: US plan symbol S3 for a three-way switch, used in pairs to control lights from two locations.
description: The US three-way switch is drawn as S with subscript 3. Two S3 symbols appear on the plan at different entries, connected by switch legs to the same lighting group, and the installer runs travellers between them.

Despite the name, a three-way switch has a single changeover contact. The name refers to its three terminals. The equivalent IEC term is a two-way switch. The symbol does not show traveller routing or box fill; the installer plans this from the pair.

Look for S4 symbols between them on long runs.
drawingChecklist: Show both S3 locations.
Link to the same fixtures.
Allow for travellers in conduit fill.
entries.distinction: S4 is a four-way intermediate device; S3 is the changeover switch used at the ends.

entries.name: ANSI four-way switch plan symbol

description: A junction box mark shows where cables are joined in an enclosure, commonly in ceiling voids for lighting circuits or above ceilings for equipment connections. Plans draw a small circle or square with a dot, sometimes labelled JB, at the location.

entries.name: Local isolator plan mark
entries.summary: Plan mark for a local isolating switch placed beside fixed equipment for safe maintenance.
description: Local isolators are placed within sight of motors, air-conditioning units, pumps and fans so maintenance staff can isolate and lock the supply. Plans draw a small switch box with an isolation mark or the letters ISO beside the equipment it serves, sometimes with a lock indication.

The mark tells the installer to provide a device rated for isolation and, where required, lockable in the off position. Pole count follows the supply: three-pole or four-pole for three-phase plant. It does not specify utilisation category or whether the device can switch motor load. Those are in the schedule.

Confirm pole count and locking provision.

The symbol does not state airflow rate or duct size, which are mechanical design items.

description: A maintained emergency luminaire operates as a normal light and continues on battery when the normal supply fails. Plans usually draw the luminaire mark with an emergency indicator, such as a filled segment or a letter E, plus an M or maintained tag.

The tag does not give the duration. Emergency duration (for example 1 h or 3 h) should appear in the schedule or legend.

entries.name: Fixed-temperature heat detector plan symbol
entries.summary: Fire alarm plan symbol for a fixed-temperature heat detector that alarms at a set temperature.
description: Fixed-temperature heat detectors alarm when the surrounding air reaches a set point, commonly around 57 to 90 degrees Celsius depending on class. Plans draw the detector box with a temperature mark or the letter H, often with a class tag.

They are used where smoke detectors would false alarm, such as kitchens, plant rooms, car parks and dusty areas. The detection is slower than smoke, so coverage spacing is tighter and the reason for choosing heat should be clear. The symbol does not give the operating temperature or class. Dish positions need line of sight to the satellite arc or the far end, and wind loading on the mount. The plan symbol therefore sits on site or roof plans with orientation notes. The symbol does not show the dish size or pointing angles, which come from the link design.

Check mount and earthing.
drawingChecklist: State dish size.
State pointing direction.
Show feeder and LNB or radio unit.
entries.distinction: The general antenna symbol has no reflector; the dish symbol shows the parabolic reflector.

entries.name: Fibre-optic link symbol
entries.summary: Symbol for an optical fibre link between devices, a line with a fibre mark, often with media converters at each end.
description: Fibre-optic links are drawn as a line carrying a fibre indication, such as a small loop, a wavy section or the tag FO, between the devices they connect. Network diagrams also show the fibre count and type, such as 12-core single-mode.

Electrical drawings use fibre links for substation communications, between buildings and through areas with electrical noise or earth potential rise, because fibre gives galvanic isolation. The symbol is often terminated in a media converter or switch fibre port. The symbol does not specify connectors, loss budget or route. The fibre schedule and test results cover these.
readingNotes: Read core count and fibre type.
Find the termination at each end.
drawingChecklist: State fibre type and cores.
Show terminations.
Reference loss test results.
entries.distinction: A copper data cable has no isolation benefit; the fibre link isolates the two ends electrically.

entries.name: Media converter symbol
entries.summary: Network symbol for a media converter linking copper Ethernet to optical fibre, drawn as a box with electrical and optical ports.
description: A media converter changes the physical medium of an Ethernet link from copper twisted pair to optical fibre, without routing or switching. Diagrams draw a box with a copper port on one side and a fibre port, often marked with a light arrow, on the other.

On electrical and control drawings, media converters appear where a device with copper Ethernet must reach a remote location or cross an area with earth potential differences. Their power supply and mounting in the panel are shown on the schematic. The symbol does not show the fibre type or wavelength. The fibre port must match the cable.

Check power supply.
drawingChecklist: State fibre type and connector.
Show power supply.
Label link ends.
entries.distinction: A network switch forwards traffic between many ports; a media converter only changes the medium on one link.

The drawing should tag managed or unmanaged, port count and any PoE capability, since PoE switches power cameras and access points. Ring or redundancy protocols are noted where the network is resilient. The symbol does not show VLANs, IP addressing or configuration. Those belong in the network design documents.

On electrical drawings the router appears in communication cabinets with its supply, antenna connection for cellular types and its WAN and LAN ports. Remote access to protection or SCADA equipment often passes through it. The symbol does not show routing tables, VPN configuration or firewall rules.

entries.name: IEC AND gate (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Rectangular IEC-style AND element marked with an ampersand; the output is active only when every input is active.
description: The IEC rectangular AND element is a plain box with the ampersand written near the top centre. Inputs enter on the left and the single output leaves on the right, so the function is identified by the qualifier rather than by the outline shape. All inputs must stand at their internal 1 state for the output to take its internal 1 state.

Rectangular gates are common on European interlock, burner-management and protection logic sheets because the same box can carry negation circles, polarity indicators and dependency labels without changing shape. A drafter can stack several & boxes in one column and the function remains readable even when the elements are abutted.

The qualifier says nothing about logic family, supply voltage, propagation delay or whether the function is realised in hardware, relay contacts or PLC code. Those details come from the device schedule or the software reference attached to the sheet.
readingNotes: Read the & qualifier first; the box outline is identical for most IEC combinative elements.
Check for negation circles or polarity triangles on inputs before writing the truth table.
drawingChecklist: Show the & qualifier clearly inside the outline.
Number each input when more than two are used.
Reference the implementing device, PLC block or relay logic on the sheet.
entries.distinction: The ≥1 OR element uses the same box; only the qualifier differs, so a misread character changes the whole function.

entries.name: IEC OR gate (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC rectangular OR element labelled ≥1, meaning at least one active input is needed to activate the output.
description: The ≥1 qualifier inside a rectangular outline identifies an OR function. The notation literally reads as at least one input active, which is why the same family of symbols uses ≥m for threshold functions in other contexts. Inputs are drawn on the left and the output on the right unless an arrow indicates otherwise.

On trip logic and permissive diagrams the ≥1 box often collects several fault signals into a single trip command. Because every input is equal, the drawing should label each incoming signal with its source tag so that a reader can trace which condition caused the output during testing.
The symbol does not state whether the inputs are latched, filtered or time-delayed. Any such behaviour must be shown by separate elements or by labels; the OR box itself is purely combinative.
readingNotes: Trace each input back to its source tag; the box does not identify which input fired.
A circle at the output turns the element into a NOR function.
drawingChecklist: Write ≥1 legibly; do not abbreviate to 1, which is the buffer qualifier.
Label each input signal with its source.
Show negation at inputs or output explicitly.
entries.distinction: A box marked 1 alone is a buffer or single-input element; ≥1 is required for the OR function.

entries.name: IEC NAND gate (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC AND box with a negation circle or polarity triangle at its output, giving the NAND function.
description: In the IEC rectangular system there is no separate NAND qualifier. The element is an & box whose output carries a logic negation circle, or in data-book practice a polarity triangle marking the output as active-low. The output therefore stands at its external 0 state only when all inputs are active.

When reading device data books that use polarity indicators instead of circles, the triangle at the output means the internal 1 state produces a low level. A drawing should be consistent: mixing circles and triangles on the same sheet invites misreading because circles depend on the declared logic convention.
The symbol does not show output drive type. Open-collector, three-state or totem-pole outputs need their own qualifier inside the outline next to the output line.
readingNotes: Look for the circle or triangle at the output edge; it is easy to miss on a reduced print.
Confirm whether the sheet uses positive logic, negative logic or polarity indicators.
drawingChecklist: Draw the negation mark touching the outline at the output.
State the logic convention in the sheet notes.
Add an output-type qualifier where the output is not a standard push-pull stage.
entries.distinction: An & box with a negated input rather than a negated output is a different function (an inhibit-type AND), not a NAND.

entries.name: IEC NOR gate (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC ≥1 element with a negated output; the output is active only when none of the inputs are active.
description: The IEC NOR element is drawn as the ≥1 OR box with a negation circle at the output. Its output is at the external 1 state only when every input is inactive, which makes it a natural way to show an all-healthy or all-clear permissive on a logic sheet.

Interlock diagrams sometimes use the NOR element to produce a ready signal from a list of blocking conditions. The reader should check whether the blocking inputs are themselves negated, because a double negation can turn the function back into an AND of healthy signals.

As with all combinative IEC elements, the drawing says nothing about the response time or the electrical output stage. A NOR used in a safety function must also be traced to its implementing device to confirm the safety rating.
readingNotes: Count negations along the path; NOR with negated inputs is an AND of the uncomplemented signals.
Confirm which external level corresponds to the active state.
drawingChecklist: Place the negation mark at the output edge.
Label each blocking input.
Reference the implementing hardware or program block.
entries.distinction: A ≥1 element without the output circle is a plain OR; the circle is the only difference.

facts.value: Output active when all inputs inactive

entries.name: IEC exclusive-OR gate (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Rectangular element marked =1: the output is active when one and only one input is active.
description: The =1 qualifier defines an exclusive-OR in the strict IEC sense: exactly one input must be active for the output to be active. For a two-input element this matches the familiar XOR truth table. For more than two inputs it is not the same as a cascaded parity function, which IEC writes as 2k+1.

On control drawings the =1 element appears in discrepancy checks, such as comparing a commanded position with a feedback contact, and in change-detection logic. The drafter should keep the element at two inputs unless the one-and-only-one meaning is truly intended.
The qualifier does not indicate timing tolerance. Discrepancy logic normally needs a delay element after the =1 box so that the alarm ignores normal transit time; that delay is a separate symbol.
readingNotes: For three or more inputs, read =1 as exactly one active, not odd parity.
Look for a following delay element in discrepancy logic.
drawingChecklist: Use =1 only where exactly-one behaviour is intended.
Use 2k+1 instead when odd parity is meant.
Show any discrepancy delay as its own element.
entries.distinction: The 2k+1 odd-parity element gives the same result for two inputs but a different result for three or more.

facts.label: Multi-input caution
facts.value: Not equivalent to odd parity above two inputs

entries.name: IEC exclusive-NOR gate (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC =1 box with a negated output, giving the two-input equivalence or exclusive-NOR function.
description: An IEC exclusive-NOR is commonly drawn as the =1 element with a negation circle at its output. For two inputs, the output is active when both inputs are in the same state, which is why the function is also called equivalence. Some drawings instead use the = logic-identity qualifier, which gives the same two-input result.

Equivalence checks appear where two redundant channels must agree, for example dual-channel position switches or duplicated sensor inputs. The drawing should make clear whether disagreement produces an alarm, a trip, or only a log entry, because the gate itself only produces the comparison.
The symbol does not tell you how long a disagreement may persist before action. That tolerance is a separate timing element or a setting in the implementing device.
readingNotes: Check whether the sheet uses =1 with negation or the = identity qualifier; both mean equivalence for two inputs.
Trace the output to see what action follows a mismatch.
drawingChecklist: Choose one convention for equivalence and use it consistently.
Limit to two inputs unless the identity function is intended.
Show the mismatch timing element separately.
entries.distinction: The = identity element extends to many inputs as all-the-same; a negated =1 with three inputs means not exactly one active.

entries.name: IEC NOT element (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Single-input IEC box marked 1 with a negation at the output, inverting the logic state.
description: The IEC inverter is a single-input element carrying the qualifier 1, meaning the one input must be active, together with a negation at the output. The result is that the output is active when the input is inactive. Data books often replace the circle with a polarity triangle to show an active-low output.

Because negation can be drawn directly on any input or output, a standalone NOT box is often only used where an inverter really exists as a component or as a separate program instruction. On purely functional logic sheets drafters usually fold the inversion into the next element as a negated input.
The symbol gives no information about input thresholds. A Schmitt-trigger inverter adds the hysteresis qualifier; without it, slow or noisy inputs may not be handled cleanly.
readingNotes: Check whether the inversion is a real component or only a notation choice.
Look for a hysteresis mark if the input comes from a slow signal.
drawingChecklist: Mark the box with 1 and negate the output.
Avoid stacking inverters when a negated input would do.
Reference the device when the inverter is a discrete part.
entries.distinction: A box marked 1 without output negation is a non-inverting buffer.

entries.name: IEC buffer element (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Non-inverting IEC element marked 1, passing the input state to the output unchanged.
description: A rectangular element with the qualifier 1 and no negation simply repeats its input. It is used to show isolation between logic stages, a fan-out point, or an interface where a physical buffer device exists. When the buffer has greater than normal drive capability, an amplifier triangle pointing in the signal direction is added inside the outline.

On logic diagrams for control panels the buffer often marks where a signal leaves one card or module and enters another. Tagging the buffer with the module reference helps fault finding because it identifies the boundary at which the signal can be measured.
A plain 1 element says nothing about output type or enable. Three-state, open-collector and Schmitt variants each require an additional qualifier.
readingNotes: A buffer may exist only to show a module boundary; check the module tag.
Look for drive, three-state or open-circuit qualifiers next to the output.
drawingChecklist: Mark the element with 1.
Add the output qualifier where the output is not a normal push-pull stage.
Identify the physical device or module when one exists.
entries.distinction: The same box with output negation is an inverter; the amplifier triangle inside marks increased drive capability.

entries.name: IEC three-state buffer (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC buffer whose output carries the three-state triangle and is controlled by an EN input.
description: The three-state buffer is drawn as a 1 element with a small downward triangle inside the outline next to the output, and an EN input. When EN is at its internal 1 state the output follows the input; at its internal 0 state the output goes to its external high-impedance state while the internal logic state is retained.

These elements appear where several drivers share a bus, such as data lines between controller cards. The drawing should make clear which signal drives each EN input and how the design prevents two drivers being enabled together, since the symbol itself does not show arbitration.

A negated EN input means the enable is active low, which is how many devices are supplied. Read the input marking carefully; reversing the enable sense would put a buffer on the bus at the wrong time.
readingNotes: Find the EN input and check its polarity.
Identify all other drivers on the same bus.
drawingChecklist: Place the three-state triangle next to the output.
Label the EN input and its source.
Show bus contention protection or a note on enable sequencing.
entries.distinction: An open-circuit output uses a diamond qualifier and has no high-impedance logic state of its own; the three-state triangle is different.

entries.name: IEC Schmitt-trigger buffer (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Rectangular buffer carrying the hysteresis mark, meaning its input switches at two different thresholds.
description: A Schmitt-trigger buffer is an IEC 1 element with the hysteresis qualifier drawn inside the box. The qualifier states that the input has two thresholds, one for a rising signal and one for a falling signal, so the output does not chatter when the input passes slowly through the switching region.

In control panels this element usually sits at the boundary between field wiring and logic, where a slow or noisy contact or sensor signal needs squaring up. Drawings sometimes place the hysteresis mark at the input line rather than at the centre; both indicate the same bi-threshold behaviour.
The symbol does not give threshold voltages or hysteresis width. Those values belong to the device datasheet and should be checked against the field signal levels.
readingNotes: Locate the hysteresis mark; it may be centred or next to an input.
Check signal levels against the device thresholds.
drawingChecklist: Draw the hysteresis mark clearly so it is not mistaken for a waveform note.
Reference the device for threshold values.
Keep the input filter components on the same sheet.
entries.distinction: A plain 1 buffer has a single threshold; only the hysteresis mark indicates Schmitt behaviour.

entries.name: IEC Schmitt-trigger inverter (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC inverter with the hysteresis mark, used to clean up slow edges while inverting the signal.
description: This element combines the 1 qualifier, the hysteresis mark and output negation. It inverts the signal while switching at two thresholds, which makes it a common choice for debouncing contacts with an RC network and for building simple relaxation oscillators.

When a Schmitt inverter forms part of an oscillator or delay with external resistors and capacitors, the drawing should keep those components next to the element and note the intended timing. The symbol alone gives no clue that it is part of a timing circuit.
Thresholds, hysteresis width and supply range are device data. Different logic families have markedly different thresholds even though the symbol is identical.
readingNotes: Check for external RC parts that turn the inverter into a timing circuit.
Confirm the output negation as well as the hysteresis mark.
drawingChecklist: Show both the hysteresis mark and the output negation.
Keep associated RC components adjacent.
Note the intended timing if used as an oscillator or debounce.
entries.distinction: The Schmitt buffer has the same hysteresis mark but no output negation.

entries.name: IEC open-collector buffer (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC buffer with an underlined diamond at the output, showing an open-collector or open-drain stage.
description: The underlined diamond inside the outline marks an output that can pull to a low level but needs an external pull-up to produce a high level. TI's public explanation describes this as suitable for a positive-logic wired-AND connection. The 1 qualifier makes the element non-inverting overall.

Open-collector outputs are used for shared alarm lines, level shifting to a higher pull-up voltage, and driving small relays or indicator lamps. The pull-up resistor or load must be shown on the drawing, together with its supply, because the element cannot produce a high level by itself.

entries.name: IEC logic identity element
entries.summary: Element marked = whose output is active only when all inputs stand at the same logic state.
description: The = qualifier defines a logic identity function: the output is active when every input is in the same state, whether all active or all inactive. For two inputs this is the equivalence or exclusive-NOR function, but with three or more inputs it is a distinct agreement check.

Identity elements are useful for voting and agreement logic, such as confirming that three redundant transmitters agree before allowing an action. The drawing should state what happens on disagreement, since the element only reports whether agreement exists.
The symbol does not provide majority selection. If two-out-of-three voting is intended, a different element or a combination of AND and OR elements is needed.
readingNotes: With three or more inputs, read = as all equal, not as majority.
Check what downstream logic does on a disagreement.
drawingChecklist: Use = only where full agreement is intended.
Label redundant inputs with their channel identifiers.
Show the disagreement response on the same sheet.
entries.distinction: A negated =1 element means not exactly one active; it matches identity only for two inputs.

entries.name: IEC even-parity element
entries.summary: Element marked 2k whose output is active when an even number of its inputs are active.
description: The 2k qualifier means the output is active when an even number of inputs, including none, are active. It is the multi-input generalisation of exclusive-NOR and is used in parity generation and checking for data words.

On communication or memory logic drawings the even-parity element may feed a parity bit or compare a received parity bit. The drawing should indicate how many inputs are grouped, often with an input-line grouping or a bus notation, because the function depends on the full set.
The element gives no information about word framing or when the parity result is sampled. Clocking and latching are separate elements.

drawingChecklist: Use 2k rather than =1 or = for parity.

Show where the result is latched or compared.
entries.distinction: The 2k+1 element is its complement and gives odd parity.

entries.name: IEC AND-OR-invert element

AOI structures appear in older TTL-based control boards and in some gate-array documentation. On a drawing they compress several gates into one symbol, so the reader should expand the function mentally as the complement of a sum of products before checking a truth table.
The compound symbol does not show internal timing or whether unused AND inputs are tied. Unused inputs on the physical device must be handled as the datasheet requires.

entries.name: IEC common-output element
entries.summary: Element with a double top line that produces one output depending on all elements of an array above it.
description: TI's public overview of IEEE Std 91 describes the common-output element as having a double line at its top. It sits beneath an array of identical elements and produces a single output that depends on all of them, such as a combined carry or an all-equal flag. It must carry its own general qualifier to say what function it performs.

On data-book style drawings the common-output element saves repeating a gate for every bit. When reading it, look at the qualifier in the element (for example & or ≥1) and remember that its inputs come from each element above as well as any external inputs drawn on its side.
The double line only signals the structural role. Without the qualifier inside, the function is undefined, and the drawing should not be accepted in that state.

entries.name: ANSI three-input AND gate
entries.summary: D-shaped AND outline with three input leads; the output is high only when all three inputs are high.
description: The three-input AND keeps the familiar flat-backed D outline and simply adds a third input lead on the flat side. All three inputs must be at logic 1 in positive logic for the output to be at logic 1. Packages such as triple three-input AND devices provide this function directly.

Drafters use the wider gate rather than cascading two-input gates when the function is a single permissive with three conditions, such as guard closed, pressure healthy and mode selected. A single symbol keeps the logic readable and avoids implying an intermediate signal that does not exist.
The outline does not show whether an unused input is tied high when a three-input part is used for two signals. Unused inputs on the physical device need a defined level shown on the schematic.

description: By De Morgan's theorem, a NAND gate is equivalent to an OR gate whose inputs are inverted. Data books and well-drawn schematics use the OR outline with input bubbles when the inputs are active-low signals, so that the drawing reads as any of these low signals produces a high output.

This form is useful where active-low requests or fault lines are combined. Matching bubbles to active-low nets lets a reader follow the logic without mentally inverting each signal, which is the main reason for choosing this representation.
The symbol represents the same physical part as the conventional NAND outline. It does not mean an OR device and inverters are fitted, and the bill of materials will still list a NAND package.

entries.summary: Inverter triangle with output bubble and an open-circuit mark, needing an external pull-up to produce a high level.

A pull-up resistor or load to a supply completes the circuit.

Open-drain inverters are used to drive indicator LEDs, relay inputs and shared interrupt or alarm lines, and to translate to a higher pull-up voltage within the device rating. The schematic should show the pull-up value and its supply rail next to the gate.
The output state with no pull-up is undefined when the transistor is off. A drawing that omits the pull-up is incomplete even though the gate symbol is correct.

entries.name: ANSI wired-AND connection
entries.summary: Several open-collector outputs joined on one pulled-up line, so any output pulling low makes the line low.
description: A wired-AND connection is formed by joining open-collector or open-drain outputs to a single line with one pull-up. The line is high only when every output is off, so in positive logic the result is the AND of the individual output states. Some schematics draw a small AND outline around the junction to make the implied function visible.

Shared interrupt lines, ready signals and I2C-style buses rely on this arrangement. A drawing should show every output on the net, the single pull-up, and the supply, because adding or removing a driver changes the logic and the pull-up current.
The connection only works with open-circuit outputs. Joining push-pull outputs in the same way causes contention and possible damage, so the output type of each gate must be checked.

A negation circle does not specify how the inversion is implemented. It may be a separate inverter, an internal feature of the device, or a negated contact in a PLC rung.

entries.name: IEC logic negation at output
entries.summary: Circle on an output edge meaning the internal 1 state of the element produces an external 0.
description: Output negation turns AND into NAND, OR into NOR and a buffer into an inverter. The circle sits where the output line meets the outline and states that the internal 1 state produces the external 0 state. As with input negation, a logic convention must be declared to relate this to voltage levels.

Drafters use output negation to avoid drawing separate inverters. When a negated output feeds a negated input on the next element, the two cancel, and reviewers often simplify the drawing by removing both.
The circle carries no information about output drive type or loading. Open-circuit or three-state behaviour needs its own qualifier inside the outline.
readingNotes: Look for double negations between elements that cancel.
Confirm the logic convention declared for the sheet.
drawingChecklist: Place the circle at the outline edge, not along the line.
Declare the logic convention.
Simplify cancelling negations where the hardware allows.
entries.distinction: An active-low output triangle states the level directly and is the data-book alternative.

entries.name: IEC polarity indicator at input (active-low input)
entries.summary: Small triangle on an input lead meaning a low level produces the internal active state.
description: The polarity indicator is a small right-angled triangle drawn on the input line where it meets the outline. It states that the L level produces the internal 1 state. Because it refers directly to levels, it does not need a positive or negative logic declaration, which is why device data books favour it.

On drawings that combine device-level schematics with functional logic, the polarity triangle tells the reader that a pin is active low, such as an enable, chip-select or reset input. In positive logic it means the same as a negation circle.
The triangle does not indicate an internal pull-up or default state for an unconnected input. Those details are device data.
readingNotes: Read the triangle as active when low.
Equivalent to a negation circle only in positive logic.
drawingChecklist: Draw the triangle on the outside of the outline, pointing in the signal direction.
Use it consistently in place of circles on level-based schematics.
Name active-low nets with a consistent suffix or overbar.
entries.distinction: The negation circle is a logic statement that needs a declared convention; the triangle is a level statement.

entries.summary: Triangle on an output lead meaning the internal active state drives the output to a low level.
description: At an output, the polarity indicator triangle means the internal 1 state produces an external L level. It is the level-based counterpart of output negation and is used on device symbols for active-low interrupt, ready or fault outputs.

When an active-low output drives an active-low input, the two triangles show directly that the signal is asserted low throughout, which avoids the double-negation reading needed with circles. This makes signal names with a low-active suffix line up with the graphic.
The triangle does not state the output drive type. An active-low open-drain output also needs the open-circuit qualifier inside the outline.
readingNotes: Read the output as asserted when low.
Check for an open-circuit qualifier as well.
drawingChecklist: Draw the triangle on the output line at the outline edge.
Name the net to show low-active sense.

entries.name: IEC dynamic input (edge-triggered)
entries.summary: Wedge drawn inside the outline at an input, meaning the input acts on a transition rather than a level.
description: The dynamic input indicator is a small wedge inside the outline at the point where the input line enters. It means the input is active only on a transition, normally from external 0 to 1 in positive logic. It is the mark that distinguishes an edge-triggered flip-flop clock from a level-sensitive latch enable.

On sequential logic drawings the reader should look for the wedge at every C input. A missing wedge on a clock input changes the device from edge-triggered to transparent, which changes timing behaviour significantly.

The wedge does not specify setup or hold time, nor maximum clock rate. Those are device timing parameters. Check the active clock edge against the input waveform and the timing data of the actual logic element.
readingNotes: Wedge present: edge-triggered; wedge absent: level-sensitive.
Check for a negation or polarity mark that reverses the active edge.
drawingChecklist: Draw the wedge inside the outline at the clock input.
Show negation outside the outline for falling-edge inputs.
Label the input with its dependency number, for example C1.
entries.distinction: The postponed-output mark relates to pulse-triggered elements whose output changes at the end of the pulse, not at the edge.

entries.name: IEC dynamic input with negation (falling edge)
entries.summary: Clock wedge combined with a negation circle or polarity triangle, so the input acts on a falling edge.
description: Combining the dynamic input wedge with input negation, or with a polarity indicator, means the input is active on the transition from high to low. TI's public overview tabulates how the active transition reads in positive logic, negative logic and polarity notation.

Negative-edge clocking appears in JK flip-flops and some counters, and in designs where two stages are clocked on opposite edges. A reader must check both the wedge and the external mark before deciding which edge the device responds to.

The symbol does not state duty-cycle or minimum pulse width requirements; those come from device timing data. The input waveform must satisfy those limits at the active falling transition, not just reach a valid steady logic level.
readingNotes: Look outside the outline for the circle or triangle as well as inside for the wedge.
Opposite-edge clocking between stages is often deliberate.
drawingChecklist: Draw both the wedge and the external negation mark.
Keep notation consistent with the rest of the sheet.
Annotate the clock net with its active edge if mixed edges are used.
entries.distinction: A wedge without an external mark is rising-edge triggered.

entries.name: IEC postponed output qualifier
entries.summary: Angle mark beside an output showing it changes only when the initiating input returns to its original level.
description: The postponed output qualifier is a small right-angle mark inside the outline next to an output. It indicates that the output changes when the input that initiated the change, typically the C input, returns to its initial external state. It identifies pulse-triggered or master-slave flip-flops and data lock-out types.

This matters for timing analysis. On a pulse-triggered device the data must be stable for the whole time the clock is active, whereas on an edge-triggered device only setup and hold around the edge matter. The mark tells the reader which rule applies.
The qualifier does not distinguish a pulse-triggered element from a data lock-out element; the clock input marking does. A dynamic mark on C with a postponed output indicates the data lock-out form.
readingNotes: Find the mark at each Q output of a flip-flop.
Check the C input for a dynamic mark to identify the data lock-out type.
drawingChecklist: Draw the mark inside the outline at the output.
Show C input marking consistently.
Note data stability requirements for pulse-triggered devices.
entries.distinction: An edge-triggered flip-flop has a dynamic C input and no postponed output mark.

entries.name: IEC open-circuit output, L-type (open collector)
entries.summary: Underlined diamond inside an outline: an open-circuit output that can only drive a low level.
description: The underlined diamond marks an output, such as an NPN open collector or an N-channel open drain, that can supply a relatively low-impedance L level when on and is open when off. An external pull-up is needed. TI's public overview notes this output type supports a positive-logic wired-AND connection.

When a variant with a built-in passive pull-up exists, a further mark inside the diamond distinguishes it. Reviewing the exact qualifier tells the drafter whether an external pull-up must be added to the schematic.
The qualifier does not state the maximum pull-up voltage. Some open-drain outputs tolerate a higher pull-up rail than the device supply and some do not.

Find the external pull-up on the net.
drawingChecklist: Draw the diamond with its underline next to the output.

Record the permitted pull-up voltage.
