entries.name: IEC open-circuit output, H-type (open emitter)
entries.summary: Overlined diamond at an output: an open-emitter or open-source stage that can only drive a high level.
description: The H-type open-circuit output is drawn as a diamond with a line above it. It can supply a relatively low-impedance H level when on and is open when off, so it needs an external pull-down. TI's public overview notes it supports a positive-logic wired-OR connection.

Open-emitter outputs are typical of emitter-coupled logic and some line drivers. On a drawing the pull-down or termination must be shown, often to a negative or termination rail rather than to ground.
The qualifier does not give the termination value or rail. Those come from the logic family's application guidance and the device datasheet.

entries.name: IEC three-state output qualifier
entries.summary: Downward triangle inside an outline marking an output that can enter a high-impedance state.
description: The three-state qualifier is a small triangle pointing downwards, drawn inside the outline next to the output. It says the output has a third, high-impedance state in addition to high and low. The output is controlled by an EN input or by EN dependency.

Wherever this qualifier appears, the reader should find the controlling EN input and confirm that only one driver on the net can be enabled at once. On bus diagrams the qualifier is often shown on only the first element of an array to reduce clutter.
The qualifier does not indicate bus hold or default level when all drivers are off. A floating bus needs pull resistors or bus-keeper circuitry shown separately.
readingNotes: Find the EN input or EN dependency label that controls the output.
In arrays, the qualifier may appear only on the first element.
drawingChecklist: Place the triangle inside the outline next to the output.
Show the enable source.
Show bus defaulting components where needed.
entries.distinction: The open-circuit diamond indicates a stage that is off in one level, not a controlled high-impedance state.

entries.name: IEC hysteresis (bi-threshold) qualifier
entries.summary: Small hysteresis loop mark showing a Schmitt-trigger function or a bi-threshold input.
description: The hysteresis mark, a small loop drawn with two offset steps, appears either as a general qualifier for a Schmitt-trigger element or next to a single input to show that input has two thresholds. TI's public overview lists both uses.

When the mark is next to one input only, the other inputs of the element have normal single thresholds. That matters on devices such as gates with one Schmitt input used to accept a slow external signal.
The mark does not quantify hysteresis. Threshold and hysteresis values must be read from device data and compared with the signal source.
readingNotes: Check whether the mark applies to the whole element or one input.
Compare thresholds with the signal source levels.
drawingChecklist: Draw the mark clearly, not as a waveform sketch.
Place it at the input it applies to where only some inputs have hysteresis.
Reference device thresholds.
entries.distinction: A drawn square-wave inside a G element indicates an astable, not hysteresis.

entries.name: IEC enable input (EN)
entries.summary: Input labelled EN that enables all outputs of the element when at its internal 1 state.
description: An input labelled EN inside the outline enables every external output of the element. At its internal 0 state, open-circuit outputs are off, three-state outputs go to high impedance and other outputs take their internal 0 state. It has no effect on inputs, according to TI's public summary of the notation.

When an enable affects only some outputs, the notation changes to EN dependency with a number, for example EN1 with affected outputs labelled 1. Readers should distinguish a plain EN from ENm because the scope is different.

The label does not show the timing needed between enable and valid output. Enable and disable times are device data. Check the enabled and disabled output conditions in the selected device truth table before connecting a shared bus.
readingNotes: A plain EN affects all outputs; ENm affects only outputs labelled m.
Check for an external polarity mark on the EN input.
drawingChecklist: Write EN inside the outline at the input.
Use ENm where scope is limited.
Show the source of the enable signal.
entries.distinction: A C (control) input permits action of affected inputs; EN acts on outputs.

entries.name: IEC common-control block
entries.summary: Notched block above an array; its inputs apply to every element below unless dependency notation limits them.
description: TI's overview of IEEE Std 91 describes the common-control block as the only distinctively shaped outline used in the IEC system. It sits above an array of elements, and an input to it is an input to every element below unless dependency notation states otherwise. Clocks, clears and enables of multi-bit registers are typically drawn here.

When reading a register or latch symbol, start with the common-control block: it shows which signals act on all bits. The elements below then show only the per-bit data inputs and outputs, which keeps an octal device readable on one sheet.

The block itself does not define a function; the labels and dependency numbers on its inputs do. Without those labels it is not possible to tell whether an input is a clock, an enable or a mode control.
readingNotes: Read the control block first, then the per-bit elements.
Dependency numbers decide which bits each control affects.
drawingChecklist: Draw the notched shape distinct from ordinary elements.
Label each control input with its function and dependency number.
Show only per-bit signals on the elements below.
entries.distinction: The common-output element has a double line and collects outputs below an array.

entries.name: IEC AND dependency (G)
entries.summary: Dependency label Gm: inputs or outputs carrying the number m are ANDed with the affecting G input.
description: In dependency notation, an input labelled G followed by a number is an affecting input. Every input or output labelled with the same number is ANDed with it. When the G input is at its internal 1 state the affected signals act normally; at its internal 0 state they are forced to 0. A bar over the number means the complement of the G input affects them.

G dependency lets a device symbol show gating relationships without drawing extra AND gates. It is common on multiplexers, gated clocks and register symbols in device data books, and a drafter copying such a symbol must keep the numbers intact or the meaning changes.
The label describes logic only. It does not tell you whether the gating causes glitches on a clock line or what setup time applies between G and the affected input.
readingNotes: Match each G number to every input or output carrying that number.
A bar over the affected number means the complement of G applies.
drawingChecklist: Keep G numbers unique within a symbol.
Label every affected terminal with the matching number.
Avoid mixing G numbers with other dependency letters using the same number.
entries.distinction: V (OR) dependency imposes a 1 state when the affecting input is 1; G imposes a 0 state when the affecting input is 0.

entries.name: IEC OR dependency (V)
entries.summary: Dependency label Vm: affected terminals are ORed with the V input, forced to 1 when V is active.
description: V dependency is the OR counterpart of G dependency. When the Vm affecting input is at its internal 1 state, every input or output labelled m is forced to its internal 1 state. When Vm is at 0, the affected signals act normally.

Device symbols use V dependency to show override or force functions, for example an output that can be forced active regardless of the normal logic. Recognising the letter avoids misreading the affected output as purely driven by the main function.
Like all dependency labels, V gives no timing information and does not imply a particular circuit. It is a compact statement of a logical relationship within the symbol.
readingNotes: V forces affected terminals to 1; G forces them to 0.
Look for a bar over the number for complemented action.
drawingChecklist: Label the affecting input with V and a number.
Mark every affected terminal with the same number.
Explain any override behaviour in the sheet notes.
entries.distinction: G dependency is the AND relationship; V is the OR relationship.

entries.name: IEC negate dependency (N)
entries.summary: Dependency label Nm: when the N input is active, affected terminals are complemented.
description: N dependency is the negate or exclusive-OR relationship. When the Nm affecting input is at its internal 1 state, each affected input or output labelled m is complemented. At 0 it has no effect. The result is a controllable inverter folded into the device symbol.

This notation appears on devices with selectable output polarity, such as programmable inverting or non-inverting buffers. Reading the N label tells the drafter that the same pin can produce either sense depending on the control input.
The label does not indicate when the polarity may be changed during operation. That is a matter of device timing and system design.
readingNotes: An active N input inverts every terminal labelled with its number.
Check the state of the N control in each operating mode.
drawingChecklist: Label the polarity control input as Nm.
Mark affected terminals with m.
State the default polarity in the sheet notes.
entries.distinction: Fixed output negation is a circle or triangle; N dependency makes the negation switchable.

entries.name: IEC control dependency (C)
entries.summary: Dependency label Cm on a clock or control input; inputs prefixed with m act only when Cm is active.
description: C dependency identifies a control input, usually a clock, and the inputs it controls. Data inputs labelled 1D, 1J or 1S act only when C1 is at its internal 1 state, or on its active transition if C1 has a dynamic mark. TI's overview notes that synchronous inputs are recognisable by these dependency prefixes.

Reading C dependency correctly is the key to understanding flip-flops, latches, registers and counters drawn in IEC form. Inputs without the prefix, such as a plain R, are asynchronous and act regardless of the clock.

The label does not tell you setup and hold times or clock frequency limits. Those remain device data. Trace each prefixed data input to the numbered control before deciding whether it can change the stored state asynchronously.

Inputs without the prefix are asynchronous overrides.
drawingChecklist: Label clock inputs as Cm.

Mark the clock input dynamic where edge-triggered.
entries.distinction: EN acts on outputs; C dependency acts on inputs.

entries.name: IEC mode dependency (M)
entries.summary: Dependency label Mm used to show operating modes; affected inputs and outputs act only in the selected mode.
description: M dependency is used where a device has several operating modes. When an Mm input is at its internal 1 state, inputs and outputs labelled m have their normal effect; otherwise they are disabled. Mode inputs are often produced from two select lines by binary grouping, giving M0 to M3.

Universal shift registers and up/down counters are typical users. On the symbol, a label such as 1,4D means the input acts as data only in mode 1 and with control 4. Reading these compound labels from left to right gives the order of conditions.
The notation does not define what happens during a mode change. Any restrictions on changing mode while clocking are device-specific.
readingNotes: Decode the mode inputs before reading other labels.
Compound labels list affecting numbers separated by commas.
drawingChecklist: Show the mode-select inputs and their binary grouping.

entries.distinction: A (address) dependency selects among arrays of identical elements; M selects operating modes of one element.

entries.name: IEC interconnection dependency (Z)
entries.summary: Dependency label Zm showing an internal connection from one point of a symbol to every terminal labelled m.
description: Z dependency states that the affecting input or output is internally connected to every input or output labelled with the same number, which then takes its logic state. It lets a symbol show internal wiring without drawing it, for example an internal output that drives several internal inputs.

On device symbols, Z dependency often explains why an output appears to have the same state as an internal signal or why a pin also acts on another function. Drafters reproducing such symbols should keep the labels together.
Z dependency indicates logic state transfer only. It does not imply the connection is externally accessible or measurable.

Z labels describe internal connections, not external wiring.

Mark each connected terminal with m.
Do not use Z labels to stand in for external wiring.

entries.name: IEC address dependency (A)
entries.summary: Dependency label A used on memory symbols to show which word of an array the address inputs select.
description: A dependency is used mainly on memory symbols. Address inputs are grouped, often with the binary grouping symbol, to produce internal affecting inputs A0 to An. Data inputs and outputs labelled A then act only on the selected word, so one symbol can represent an entire array.

Reading a memory symbol, start with the address grouping to see the range, then follow the A-labelled data terminals. TI's public overview shows an array of latches forming a small random-access memory using this method.
The notation does not give access time or organisation details beyond word count and width. Those are in the device data.
readingNotes: Find the address grouping and its range first.
Terminals labelled A act on the selected word only.
drawingChecklist: Show the address bus with its binary grouping.
Label affected data terminals with A.
State word count and width in the outline title.

entries.name: IEC set and reset dependency (S, R)
entries.summary: Dependency labels Sm and Rm: the affected output behaves as if set or reset when the affecting input is active.
description: S and R dependencies specify the internal state of an output when both set and reset conditions could be active together. An Rm input at its internal 1 state makes the affected output react as it would to S=0, R=1; an Sm input does the opposite. At 0 they have no effect.

These labels are used where a storage element must have a defined priority between set and reset. A reader can see from the symbol whether set or reset dominates, which matters in latching alarm and interlock logic.
Plain S and R labels without numbers are the ordinary set and reset inputs of a bistable element. The dependency form only applies when a number follows the letter.
readingNotes: S or R followed by a number is a dependency; without a number it is an ordinary input.
Check which one dominates when both are active.
drawingChecklist: Number dependency inputs explicitly.
Label affected outputs with the matching number.
State set or reset priority in the logic description.
entries.distinction: An ordinary R input resets the element directly; Rm dependency states the reaction of particular outputs.

entries.name: IEC D flip-flop (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC bistable with a dynamic C1 clock and a 1D data input, storing D on the active clock edge.
description: In IEC form the D flip-flop is an unlabelled bistable outline with a clock input labelled C1 carrying the dynamic wedge, and a data input labelled 1D to show it is controlled by C1. Asynchronous set and reset inputs are labelled S and R without a number. The two outputs are Q and its complement shown with a negation or polarity mark.

TI's overview stresses that a D input always sets the storage element to 1 at its internal 1 state and resets it at 0. On sequential drawings this form makes clocking explicit: anything without the 1 prefix acts immediately, regardless of the clock.
The symbol does not state setup, hold or propagation times, and does not define the power-up state unless an I=0 or I=1 qualifier is added.
readingNotes: The wedge on C1 indicates edge triggering.
S and R without numbers are asynchronous.
drawingChecklist: Label the clock C1 with a dynamic mark.
Prefix the data input with 1.
Add I=0 or I=1 where power-up state matters.

entries.name: IEC JK flip-flop (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC bistable with 1J and 1K inputs controlled by a dynamic C1 clock; J=K=1 toggles the state.
description: The IEC JK flip-flop has inputs labelled 1J and 1K, both controlled by C1. On the active clock transition J=1, K=0 sets; J=0, K=1 resets; J=K=1 toggles; and J=K=0 holds. A negation mark outside the C1 input with the wedge indicates a falling-edge device.

JK devices are used in counters and divider chains. On IEC drawings check the clock marking carefully, because rising-edge and falling-edge versions are visually similar and mixing them changes counter sequencing.
The rectangle does not reveal whether the device is edge-triggered or pulse-triggered unless the clock and output marks are read together. A postponed output mark indicates a pulse-triggered type.
readingNotes: Read the clock edge from the wedge and any external negation.
Look for postponed output marks.
drawingChecklist: Label J and K with the C prefix.
Show the active clock edge clearly.
Show asynchronous S and R inputs where present.
entries.distinction: An IEC T flip-flop has a single 1T input; a JK with J and K tied high behaves the same way.

entries.name: IEC SR latch (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Rectangular IEC bistable with S and R inputs that set or reset the stored state immediately.
description: The simplest IEC bistable is a rectangle with inputs labelled S and R and outputs Q and complemented Q. An active S sets the element to 1 and an active R resets it to 0, with no clock involved. Negation or polarity marks show active-low inputs, as on devices built from cross-coupled NAND gates.

SR latches appear in alarm-latching and seal-in logic on control drawings. The key question for a reviewer is what happens when both S and R are active; dependency notation or a note should state whether set or reset dominates.

The symbol does not specify the power-up state. Where it matters, add the I=0 or I=1 qualifier or a note. A separate reset or initialisation circuit is needed when the system requires a defined starting condition.
readingNotes: Check for active-low marks on S and R.
Look for a stated set or reset priority.
drawingChecklist: Label S and R inside the outline.
State the priority when both are active.
Specify the power-up state where relevant.
entries.distinction: A clocked SR flip-flop has 1S and 1R inputs under C1 control; the plain latch has none.

entries.name: IEC transparent D latch (rectangular form)
entries.summary: IEC bistable with a static C1 control and 1D input; the output follows D while C1 is active.
description: The transparent latch is drawn like the D flip-flop but the C1 input has no dynamic wedge. While C1 is at its internal 1 state, the output follows the 1D input; when C1 returns to 0 the last value is held. TI's overview describes this as a level-operated control input.

Latches are used to capture data from a bus or to hold a value for a display or relay driver. In octal devices the common-control block carries C1 and the output enable, with eight per-bit elements below.

Because the output follows the input during the active level, glitches on D during that time pass through. The symbol shows this behaviour only through the absence of the wedge, so check it carefully.

In octal parts, look for C1 in the common-control block.

entries.name: IEC T (toggle) flip-flop
entries.summary: IEC bistable with a 1T toggle input; when T is active, each clock edge changes the stored state.
description: The toggle input T causes the internal state to change to its complement. In IEC form it is labelled 1T when controlled by a C1 clock, or drawn as a single dynamic T input where each transition toggles. A T stage is the basic divide-by-two element in counters and frequency dividers.

Dedicated T flip-flop packages are rare; the function is usually built from a JK with J and K tied high or a D flip-flop with its complemented output fed back. Functional logic drawings, PLC function-block diagrams and FPGA documentation still use the T form because it states the intent clearly.
The symbol does not show how the toggle function is implemented. Where a JK or D device is used, the physical wiring should appear on the detailed schematic.
readingNotes: Read T as change state on each enabled clock.
Check the implementation on the detailed schematic.
drawingChecklist: Label the toggle input as 1T with a C1 clock, or as a dynamic T.

entries.name: IEC pulse-triggered (master-slave) JK flip-flop
entries.summary: JK bistable whose outputs carry postponed marks: they change when the clock pulse ends, not at its start.
description: A pulse-triggered or master-slave JK flip-flop is drawn with a static C1 input and postponed output marks at Q and its complement. The data must be set up before the clock pulse starts and held while C1 is active; the outputs change when C1 returns to its initial level.

Older TTL designs and some relay-logic equivalents use this behaviour. When reviewing, the presence of the postponed mark tells you that J and K must not change during the clock pulse, a stricter rule than for edge-triggered devices.
If the C1 input also carries a dynamic mark, the device is the data lock-out type, which samples on the edge but still postpones the output.
readingNotes: Postponed marks at outputs indicate pulse triggering.
A dynamic C1 together with postponed outputs indicates data lock-out.
drawingChecklist: Draw postponed marks next to both outputs.
Show C1 as static unless data lock-out is intended.
Note data stability requirements.
entries.distinction: The edge-triggered JK flip-flop has a dynamic C1 and no postponed marks.

entries.summary: IEC bistable with 1S and 1R inputs that act only under C1 control, giving a synchronous set-reset function.
description: Adding the C1 prefix to S and R makes them synchronous: they act only when C1 is active or on its active transition. The element therefore combines set-reset storage with clocking, which keeps state changes aligned with the rest of a synchronous system.

Clocked SR elements appear in function-block diagrams for PLCs and in state-machine documentation. On hardware schematics the same function is often implemented with a JK or D flip-flop and gating, so cross-reference the implementation.
The symbol needs a stated rule for 1S and 1R active together. Without S or R dependency or a note, that condition is undefined.

entries.name: IEC non-retriggerable monostable
entries.summary: IEC monostable marked with 1 and a single pulse: a trigger during the output pulse is ignored.
description: The non-retriggerable monostable produces one output pulse of fixed duration when triggered. Further triggers during that pulse have no effect. IEC drawings show the qualifier 1 with a single pulse shape inside the outline, and timing component connections are shown as non-logic inputs.

These elements are used to stretch short events into pulses long enough to be seen by slower logic, or to produce a fixed-width command. The external resistor and capacitor that set the pulse width should be drawn next to the element and the nominal width stated.
Pulse width tolerance depends on the timing components and the device. The symbol shows the behaviour, not the accuracy.
readingNotes: Retriggers during the pulse are ignored.
Find the timing resistor and capacitor connections.
drawingChecklist: Show the single-pulse qualifier.
Draw the timing components and state the nominal width.
Mark trigger input edge sense.

entries.name: IEC retriggerable monostable
entries.summary: IEC monostable showing only the single-pulse qualifier; each new trigger restarts the output pulse.
description: The retriggerable monostable is marked with the single pulse shape without the preceding 1. Each trigger during the output pulse restarts the timing, so the output remains active as long as triggers arrive more often than the set period.

This behaviour is useful for missing-pulse detection and activity monitoring, where the output drops only when a regular signal stops. The drawing should note the expected trigger rate and the timeout chosen.

The symbol does not show whether a clear input truncates the pulse. Check for an R input and its polarity. Include reset behaviour in the timing chart so a missing-pulse indication can be distinguished from an externally forced clear.

entries.name: ANSI cross-coupled NAND latch
entries.summary: Two NAND gates with outputs fed back to each other, forming an SR latch with active-low set and reset.
description: Drawing the latch as two cross-coupled NAND gates shows its construction explicitly. A low on the set input forces Q high; a low on the reset input forces the complement high. With both inputs high the latch holds. Both inputs low drives both outputs high, which is normally treated as invalid.

This drawing form is common in teaching material, switch debounce circuits and older schematics where the latch is built from a quad NAND package. It lets a reviewer see the feedback paths and the pins used.
Because the latch is built from gates, the drawing shows nothing about which state it adopts at power-up. If a defined state is needed, a reset pulse or a pull network must be shown.
readingNotes: Inputs are active low.
Both inputs low gives both outputs high and is usually avoided.
drawingChecklist: Draw the feedback paths clearly without ambiguous crossings.
Mark inputs as active low in the net names.
Show any power-up reset arrangement.
entries.distinction: The cross-coupled NOR latch has active-high inputs.

entries.name: IEC synchronous binary counter (CTRm)
entries.summary: IEC counter marked CTRm, where m is the bit count and the cycle length is 2 to the power m.
description: The general qualifier CTRm identifies a counter with m bits and a cycle length of 2 to the power m. In IEC form the clock appears as C with a + to show counting up, and load, clear and enable inputs use dependency notation such as M1 for load mode and G for count enable. Outputs carry binary weights 1, 2, 4 and 8.

A reader should identify the synchronous and asynchronous inputs from their prefixes, then find the carry output, often labelled CT=15, used to cascade stages. On control drawings counters represent event totals, batch counts or divide-by-n timing.
The symbol does not state maximum count rate or whether the clear is synchronous, except through dependency labels. Read the prefixes carefully.
readingNotes: CTRm gives the bit count; the cycle is 2 to the power m.
CT=15 marks the terminal-count output used for cascading.
drawingChecklist: State the bit count in the qualifier.
Label load, clear and enable with dependency notation.
Show cascade connections between stages.
entries.distinction: CTR DIVm states the cycle length directly and is used for non-binary counters such as decade counters.

entries.name: IEC ripple counter (RCTRm)
entries.summary: IEC counter marked RCTRm: an asynchronous ripple-carry counter with a cycle length of 2 to the power m.

Ripple counters are used where outputs are not decoded together at high speed, such as long frequency dividers or simple timers. Drawing them with RCTR rather than CTR warns a reviewer that decoding several outputs together may produce brief false states.
The symbol does not state the cumulative delay through the stages. That depends on the logic family and the number of bits.

drawingChecklist: Use RCTR for asynchronous counters.

entries.distinction: CTRm counters are synchronous and all outputs change on the same clock edge.

These devices are used in data conversion, sequence generation and bidirectional serial links. Reading the compound labels left to right, mode first then clock, tells you exactly when each input is used.
The symbol does not state which mode is safe to change during clocking. Mode changes are normally made with the clock inactive.

entries.name: IEC multiplexer (MUX)
entries.summary: IEC MUX element whose select inputs, grouped with G dependency, pick which data input reaches the output.
description: The IEC multiplexer carries the MUX qualifier. Select inputs are drawn with a binary grouping bracket producing G0 to Gn, and each data input is labelled with the matching number, so the data input whose number equals the select value is ANDed through to the output. An EN input, often active low, enables the whole element.

Multiplexers on control drawings route one of several signals to a shared output, for example selecting a measurement channel or an operating mode source. The binary grouping makes the select range clear without drawing a decoder.
The symbol does not state the switching time or whether outputs glitch during a select change. Those are device timing considerations.

entries.name: IEC binary decoder (X/Y coder)
entries.summary: IEC coder marked BIN/OCT or similar, converting a binary input code into one active output.
description: IEC coders use the general qualifier X/Y, where X is the input code and Y is the output code. A three-to-eight-line decoder is therefore marked BIN/OCT, with input weights 1, 2 and 4 and outputs numbered 0 to 7. Enable inputs are often combined with an & element in the common-control area.

Decoders select one of several devices, relays or indicator lines from a binary code. A drawing should keep the output numbers so a reviewer can confirm that, for example, input code 5 activates output 5.
The qualifier says nothing about output polarity; polarity triangles at outputs show active-low outputs, which are common on decoder devices.

The symbol does not state whether inputs are latched. If the encoder input is a momentary event, a latch stage is needed before it.

Seven-segment decoders appear on drawings for local numeric displays, counters and older instrument panels. The output stage type matters: many drivers have open-collector outputs intended to sink LED or lamp current, which should be shown with the open-circuit qualifier.

Where the codes are not standard, inputs and outputs carry numbers and a table on the drawing gives the relationship. TI's overview also shows coders embedded in larger symbols to produce affecting inputs for dependency notation.

entries.name: IEC magnitude comparator (COMP)
entries.summary: IEC COMP element comparing two binary words P and Q, with outputs for P>Q, P=Q and P<Q.
description: The IEC magnitude comparator is marked COMP. Its inputs are grouped as word P and word Q with binary weights, and its outputs are labelled P>Q, P=Q and P<Q. Cascading inputs carry the same labels in a separate group so that comparators can be chained for longer words.

Digital comparators appear in set-point logic, address matching and limit checking. A reviewer should confirm the bit order of P and Q, because a swapped weight produces a comparison that is correct only for some values.
The symbol does not indicate whether the comparison is for signed or unsigned numbers. Standard devices compare unsigned binary.

Cascade inputs are needed for words longer than one device.

The symbol does not state whether the device uses ripple or look-ahead carry internally. Speed depends on that and on the word length.

entries.name: IEC arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
entries.summary: IEC element marked ALU, performing arithmetic or logic functions on two words as chosen by mode inputs.
description: The ALU qualifier identifies an element that can perform several arithmetic and logic operations on input words P and Q. Function-select inputs use M dependency or a binary grouping to choose the operation, and outputs include the result, carry and often a P=Q flag. Because the function table is large, the symbol usually refers to a table on the drawing or in the datasheet.

ALU symbols appear in processor and controller block diagrams and in legacy logic boards. On a modern control drawing they mainly document programmable logic or explain how a processor module handles signals.

The ALU qualifier does not list the operations. A function table is essential and should be referenced explicitly. Preserve the mode-select signal names and the carry interpretation when comparing the symbol with that table.

entries.name: IEC first-in first-out memory (FIFO)
entries.summary: IEC element marked FIFO that stores words in arrival order and reads them out in the same order.
description: The FIFO qualifier identifies a first-in first-out memory. There are no address inputs; instead, a write clock stores input words and a read clock delivers them in the same order. Status outputs indicate empty, full and sometimes half-full conditions.

FIFOs buffer data between parts of a system that run at different rates, such as a serial receiver and a processor. On a drawing, the status outputs should be traced to see how the system avoids overflow and underflow.
The symbol does not specify depth or whether read and write clocks can be asynchronous. The organisation and device data provide those details.

entries.name: IEC operational amplifier (rectangular form)
entries.summary: Rectangular IEC-style op-amp drawn as a box with an amplifier triangle and an infinity sign for very high gain.
description: In IEC-style analogue element diagrams an operational amplifier is often drawn as a rectangle containing a small amplifier triangle and an infinity sign, meaning very high open-loop gain. Inverting and non-inverting inputs are marked with minus and plus signs at the input side.

This form appears on European instrumentation and protection relay schematics, where analogue elements share the rectangular style used for logic. The surrounding feedback network defines what the circuit does, so the resistor and capacitor values must be read together with the element.
The rectangular form gives no information about supply rails, offset, bandwidth or output swing. Those are device parameters, and the supply pins are often omitted from functional diagrams.

entries.name: IEC summing amplifier element (Σ)
entries.summary: Analogue element with Σ and several inputs, producing an output proportional to the weighted sum of the inputs.
description: A summing amplifier adds several analogue inputs, each with its own weighting. In IEC-style analogue element diagrams it is drawn as a rectangle with an amplifier mark and the Σ function, with weighting factors written next to each input. The usual circuit realisation is an inverting op-amp with one input resistor per signal.

Summers appear in control loops for combining set-point and feedforward signals, in audio-style mixing of measurements, and in analogue computation. The weighting factors and the sign of the output must be stated because an inverting realisation reverses polarity.
The element does not show the resistor network that sets the weights. For a construction schematic, the op-amp circuit with values should be drawn or referenced.

entries.name: Op-amp voltage follower
entries.summary: Op-amp with its output tied directly to the inverting input, giving unity gain and a low-impedance output.
description: A voltage follower connects the op-amp output straight back to the inverting input and applies the signal to the non-inverting input. The output equals the input, but it is driven from a low impedance, so a high-impedance source can drive a load without being disturbed.

Followers appear as buffers after voltage dividers, references, sensors and sample-and-hold capacitors, and before ADC inputs. On schematics they are easy to recognise by the direct feedback wire with no resistor.
The circuit does not guarantee stability with heavy capacitive loads, and not every op-amp is unity-gain stable. Check the part selection and any isolating resistor at the output.

entries.name: Op-amp comparator with hysteresis
entries.summary: Comparator or op-amp with positive feedback to the plus input, creating two switching thresholds.
description: Adding a resistor from the output to the non-inverting input of a comparator gives positive feedback, so the switching threshold depends on the current output state. The result is hysteresis: the circuit switches at one level on a rising input and a lower level on a falling input, rejecting noise near the threshold.

This circuit is used for level detection from slow analogue signals such as temperature, battery voltage or tank level. The drawing should state both thresholds, or the resistor values and reference from which they are derived.
The circuit symbol does not show the thresholds directly and they depend on output swing, so a part with rail-to-rail or open-collector output changes the calculation.
readingNotes: Feedback to the plus input indicates hysteresis, not gain.
Thresholds depend on output swing.
drawingChecklist: Show the positive feedback resistor and reference.
State both switching thresholds.
Show the output pull-up if the comparator is open collector.
entries.distinction: An op-amp amplifier uses negative feedback to the minus input; this circuit uses positive feedback.

entries.name: IEC subtracter (P-Q)
entries.summary: IEC arithmetic element marked P-Q that subtracts word Q from word P, with borrow handling.
description: The subtracter qualifier is written P minus Q. Inputs are grouped as the P and Q words with binary weights and outputs give the difference, with borrow input and output terminals for cascading. TI's overview lists it with the adder and other arithmetic qualifiers.

Dedicated subtracter devices are uncommon; the function is often provided by an adder with an inverted input word or by an arithmetic logic unit. Functional diagrams and programmable logic documentation still use the P-Q element to state intent clearly.
The symbol does not say whether the result is signed or how negative results are represented. State that in the logic description.
readingNotes: P is the minuend and Q the subtrahend.
Check borrow terminals when cascading.
drawingChecklist: Mark the element P-Q.
Group and weight both words.
Describe the result representation.
entries.distinction: The Σ adder adds P and Q; an ALU may perform either under mode control.

entries.name: IEC look-ahead carry generator (CPG)
entries.summary: IEC element marked CPG that computes carries for several adder stages at once to speed up arithmetic.
description: The CPG qualifier identifies a look-ahead carry generator. It takes carry generate and carry propagate signals from several adder or ALU stages and produces their carry inputs in parallel, avoiding the delay of a rippling carry chain.

On block diagrams of arithmetic sections the CPG sits beside a row of ALUs, with generate and propagate lines going in and carry lines coming out. Recognising it explains why carries do not pass directly from one ALU to the next.

The symbol does not indicate how many stages it serves; count the input groups or refer to the device data. Label the carry input and output ordering explicitly so the arithmetic stages cannot be connected in the wrong significance order.
readingNotes: Generate and propagate lines come from each arithmetic stage.
Carries return to each stage in parallel.
drawingChecklist: Mark the element CPG.
Label generate, propagate and carry lines per stage.
Show the stage count.
entries.distinction: A ripple-carry arrangement chains CO to CI directly with no CPG element.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE phase-angle meter symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-library form of the phase meter, used where a drawing must show where the angle between two measured quantities is read.
description: In IEEE-oriented panel schematics the phase meter appears as a circular instrument fed from both a voltage reference and a current or second voltage input. The reading is the angle between those two inputs, so the symbol only makes sense when both connections are traced back to their instrument transformers and their polarity marks.

The circle and label identify an indicating instrument, not a protection function. It does not tell you the reference convention (leading or lagging positive), the frequency range or whether the meter is analogue or a digital display; those come from the instrument schedule and the vendor data.
readingNotes: Confirm which voltage is the reference and which quantity is compared against it.
Check CT and VT polarity dots, because a reversed input shifts the reading by 180 degrees.
drawingChecklist: Identify the reference voltage input
Show polarity of the compared input
State the scale or angle convention
entries.distinction: A phase-angle meter reads an angle; a power-factor meter reads the cosine of that angle and is scaled lead/lag around unity.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE thermometer symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-library thermometer instrument form for a local or panel temperature reading taken from a sensor input.
description: The thermometer form is an indicating instrument circle whose input is a temperature sensor rather than a power circuit. On control schematics it sits at the end of a thermocouple, RTD or transmitter loop, so the important connections are the sensor wiring and any compensation or lead-resistance arrangement.

The symbol identifies indication only. Alarm and trip set points belong to separate switch or relay contacts, and the measuring range, sensor type and accuracy class must be read from the instrument schedule because the circle carries none of that information.

Look for separate contacts if the instrument also gives alarms.
drawingChecklist: Name the sensor and its location
State the range and units
Reference any alarm or trip contacts
entries.distinction: A thermometer indicates temperature; a temperature switch changes contact state at a set point and may have no display at all.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE ampere-hour meter symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-library ampere-hour meter form for integrating charge in DC circuits such as battery and plating supplies.
description: An ampere-hour meter integrates current over time and is most often drawn in DC battery, charger and electrochemical supply circuits. It is normally fed from a shunt, so the schematic should show the shunt, its millivolt rating and the polarity of the sensing leads alongside the meter.

The symbol does not say whether the register counts charge in one direction only or nets charge and discharge. Battery state-of-charge estimation depends on that setting and on efficiency correction, neither of which is visible from the instrument form.
readingNotes: Find the shunt or sensor that supplies the current signal.
Confirm whether the register is unidirectional or bidirectional.
drawingChecklist: Reference the shunt rating
Show sensing polarity
State register direction
entries.distinction: An ampere-hour meter accumulates charge; an ammeter shows instantaneous current and a kWh meter accumulates energy.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE thermocouple symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-library thermocouple form showing the junction of two dissimilar conductors and their polarity leads.
description: The thermocouple form shows two dissimilar conductors meeting at a measuring junction, with the free ends wired to an instrument or transducer. The library offers left and right handed versions so the junction can face the process side of the drawing, and the two leads must keep their polarity all the way to the cold junction.

The symbol does not identify the thermocouple type (for example K, J or T), the sheath or the extension cable. Those details matter because ordinary copper wiring between the head and the instrument introduces error unless matching extension or compensating cable is used.
readingNotes: Check the thermocouple type in the instrument schedule.
Verify extension cable type and polarity from the head to the input.
drawingChecklist: State thermocouple type
Mark lead polarity
Specify extension or compensating cable
entries.distinction: A thermocouple generates a small voltage from a temperature difference; an RTD changes resistance and needs an excitation current.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE active power indicator symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-library wattmeter form for indicating active power from combined current and voltage inputs.
description: The active power indicator, usually labelled W or kW, needs both current and voltage inputs. On a single-line diagram it is drawn off the CT and VT secondaries of a feeder or generator, and on a schematic its current coils sit in series with the CT circuit while its voltage elements are connected across the VT secondary.

Whether the instrument measures one phase, three-phase three-wire or three-phase four-wire power is not visible from the circle. Element count, direction convention for import and export, and the CT and VT ratios used for scaling all need to be read from the meter data and connection diagram.
readingNotes: Trace both the CT and VT connections to the meter.
Check the number of measuring elements against the system wiring.
drawingChecklist: Show CT and VT ratios
State element configuration
Define positive power direction
entries.distinction: An active power indicator shows instantaneous watts; a recording wattmeter keeps a time record and a kWh meter integrates energy.

entries.name: Reverse-current measuring relay
entries.summary: Measuring relay that operates when current flows in the opposite direction to normal, such as back-feed into a DC source.
description: A reverse-current relay compares the direction of current with a reference and operates when current flows the wrong way. Classic uses are DC generators and battery chargers in parallel, where a failed source would otherwise draw current from the bus, and rectifier feeders where back-feed indicates a fault.

On the schematic the relay box carries a current quantity with a direction qualifier, and its contacts are drawn elsewhere in the trip or alarm circuit. The box does not show the pick-up level or time delay, and in AC systems the equivalent requirement is usually met with a directional power function rather than a simple current-direction element.
readingNotes: Identify which direction is treated as normal for the source.
Find the contacts that trip or disconnect the source.
drawingChecklist: State normal current direction
Give pick-up and delay
Reference the trip contact
entries.distinction: A reverse-current relay responds to current direction; a maximum-current relay responds to magnitude regardless of direction.

entries.name: Percentage-biased differential current relay
entries.summary: Differential relay form whose operating threshold rises in proportion to the through current, set as a relative value.
description: This relay form represents differential protection where the operate quantity is the difference between currents entering and leaving a zone, and the threshold is a percentage of the through current. The bias keeps the relay stable when CT errors grow during heavy external faults or transformer tap changes.

On a drawing the relay box is fed from CT sets at each boundary of the protected zone. The symbol does not show the slope settings, the harmonic restraint used for transformer inrush, or the vector-group and ratio compensation, all of which must be taken from the relay settings record.
readingNotes: Locate every CT set that bounds the protected zone.
Check CT polarity so through current cancels in the relay.
drawingChecklist: Show all zone CTs
Mark CT polarity
Reference slope and restraint settings
entries.distinction: A biased differential relay raises its threshold with through current; a plain differential current relay uses a fixed threshold.

entries.name: Neutral-current measuring relay
entries.summary: Measuring relay fed from a CT in a neutral conductor or star-point connection, responding to neutral current.
description: This relay form is used where a CT is installed in a neutral conductor or in the earthing connection of a transformer or generator star point. Current there indicates earth faults or, in four-wire systems, heavy unbalance and triplen harmonic loading, depending on where the CT sits.

The symbol identifies the measured conductor but not the purpose. A neutral CT in the star-point earth lead gives standby earth-fault protection, while one in the four-wire neutral of a feeder sees load unbalance as well, so settings and grading differ greatly.
readingNotes: Confirm whether the CT is in the neutral conductor or the earthing lead.
Check grading against downstream earth-fault devices.
drawingChecklist: Show neutral CT location
State setting and delay
Reference grading study
entries.distinction: A neutral-current relay measures one neutral path; a residual connection sums the three phase CTs to derive the same quantity.

entries.name: Neutral-unbalance relay between two polyphase systems
aliases: in neutral between two multi-phase systems
entries.summary: Relay form measuring current in a link joining the star points of two polyphase systems, such as split capacitor banks.
description: This form shows a current relay in the conductor that joins the neutral points of two star-connected polyphase systems. A familiar application is the double-star capacitor bank, where a CT in the link between the two star points detects unbalance caused by failed capacitor units.

In a healthy balanced arrangement the link carries little current, so the relay setting is a small fraction of phase current and must allow for natural unbalance. The symbol does not tell you the alarm and trip stages or the compensation for inherent unbalance; those are in the bank protection settings.
readingNotes: Identify the two star points joined by the measured link.
Look for separate alarm and trip stages.
drawingChecklist: Show the interconnecting link and CT
State alarm and trip settings
Note inherent unbalance compensation
entries.distinction: This relay measures the link between two star points; a neutral-current relay measures one neutral path to earth or to the supply.

entries.name: Earth-fault current relay
entries.summary: Measuring relay form that operates on current flowing to earth, fed from a residual connection or core-balance CT.
description: The earth-fault current relay form identifies a relay whose operating quantity is current flowing to earth. It may be fed from a core-balance CT around all live conductors, from the residual connection of three phase CTs, or from a CT in the star-point earth lead, and the source changes its achievable sensitivity.

The relay box shows the quantity with an earth qualifier but not the setting, characteristic or whether it is directional. In resistance-earthed and isolated networks earth-fault current is small and often needs a sensitive or directional element that must be stated separately.
readingNotes: Identify the CT arrangement that supplies the residual current.
Check whether the element is directional or sensitive.
drawingChecklist: Show residual CT source
State setting and characteristic
Reference system earthing method
entries.distinction: An earth-fault current relay measures current to earth; an earth-fault voltage relay measures neutral displacement voltage.

entries.name: Minimum-voltage measuring relay
entries.summary: Measuring relay that operates when voltage falls below a set level while some voltage is still present.
description: The minimum-voltage relay form operates when the measured voltage falls below its setting. It is used for motor undervoltage tripping, load shedding and transfer schemes, where a sustained voltage dip indicates a supply problem rather than a momentary disturbance.

The symbol shows the voltage quantity and the less-than threshold but not the time delay, which phases are monitored or whether operation is blocked on VT fuse failure. Without a blocking input a blown VT fuse can cause an unwanted trip, so the supervision arrangement should be cross-referenced.
readingNotes: Check which phase voltages are monitored.
Look for VT supervision or fuse-failure blocking.
drawingChecklist: State threshold and delay
Show VT source
Reference blocking input
entries.distinction: A minimum-voltage relay responds to a reduced voltage; a loss-of-voltage relay responds to absence of voltage.

entries.name: Maximum-voltage measuring relay
entries.summary: Measuring relay that operates when the monitored voltage rises above its set level.
description: The maximum-voltage relay form operates when voltage exceeds its setting. Typical uses include generator overvoltage after load rejection, capacitor bank protection and inverter connection points, where sustained high voltage can stress insulation or breach grid connection limits.

The box shows a greater-than voltage threshold but not whether the element uses phase-to-phase or phase-to-neutral quantities, the reset ratio or the time delay. Grid-connection settings are usually specified as several stages with different delays, which this single symbol does not reveal.
readingNotes: Identify the voltage connection used by the element.
Check for multiple stages in the settings record.
drawingChecklist: State threshold and delay
Show VT connection
Reference stage settings
entries.distinction: A maximum-voltage relay responds to high voltage magnitude; a residual voltage relay responds to neutral displacement.

entries.name: Earth-fault voltage relay
entries.summary: Relay form that operates on a voltage appearing because of an earth fault, such as between a frame and earth.
description: This relay measures a voltage that appears only when there is an earth fault, for example between exposed metalwork and a reference earth, or across a neutral earthing impedance. It is useful where earth-fault current is limited and a voltage is easier to detect than a current.

The symbol does not say where the voltage is measured. A relay across a neutral earthing resistor and one connected between frame and auxiliary earth electrode have very different settings, so the measurement points must be drawn and labelled.
readingNotes: Trace both measurement connections of the relay.
Check the reference earth used by the relay.
drawingChecklist: Show measurement points
State threshold and delay
Reference earthing arrangement
entries.distinction: An earth-fault voltage relay measures fault-related voltage; a residual voltage relay measures zero-sequence voltage from VT windings.

entries.name: Minimum-impedance measuring relay
entries.summary: Measuring relay that compares voltage with current and operates when the apparent impedance falls below a set value.
description: A minimum-impedance relay divides measured voltage by measured current and operates when the result falls below its setting, indicating a fault close enough to fall inside its reach. It is used as generator and transformer backup protection and is the basic idea behind distance protection.

The relay needs both CT and VT inputs, so the symbol should always be read with both connections. It does not show the characteristic shape on the impedance plane, any directional element, or the loss-of-voltage blocking needed to avoid operation when the VT supply fails.
readingNotes: Confirm both voltage and current inputs are shown.
Check for VT fuse-failure blocking.
drawingChecklist: Show CT and VT inputs
State reach and delay
Reference blocking logic
entries.distinction: A minimum-impedance relay uses voltage and current together; an overcurrent relay uses current alone.

entries.name: Insulation monitoring relay
entries.summary: Relay that continuously checks insulation resistance of an unearthed (IT) system to earth and alarms on a first fault.
description: An insulation monitoring relay is connected between the conductors of an unearthed (IT) system and earth, and injects a measuring signal to determine insulation resistance. It warns when insulation falls below its setting so a first fault can be located before a second fault causes a trip.

The symbol shows the device and its connections but not the measuring method, which matters on systems with drives or large DC components. Only one insulation monitor should normally be active on a galvanically connected system, so the drawing should show any disconnection or interlock between parallel systems.
readingNotes: Check that only one monitor is active on each connected IT system.
Identify alarm outputs and test button wiring.
drawingChecklist: Show system and earth connections
State alarm thresholds
Reference interlock between parallel monitors
entries.distinction: An insulation monitoring relay measures insulation resistance of an unearthed system; a residual current monitor measures leakage current in an earthed system.

entries.name: Indicating instrument general symbol
entries.summary: General circle form for any indicating instrument, with a placeholder replaced by the unit or quantity measured.
description: In IEC-style diagrams an indicating instrument is drawn as a circle, and the asterisk inside is replaced by the unit symbol or quantity, such as V, A, Hz or cos φ. The general form is useful in legends and in early design drawings when the exact instrument is not yet chosen.

Because the placeholder carries all of the meaning, an unfilled general symbol tells the reader only that some reading is shown at that point. The drawing must still state the measuring connection, scaling from instrument transformers and whether the instrument is analogue or part of a digital meter.
readingNotes: Replace the placeholder with the actual unit before issue.
Read the circle together with its measuring connections.
drawingChecklist: Fill in the measured quantity
Show instrument transformer ratios
List the instrument in the schedule
entries.distinction: The circle is the indicating form; recording instruments use a square and integrating instruments use a rectangle with a band.

entries.name: Recording instrument general symbol
entries.summary: General square form for an instrument that keeps a time record of a quantity rather than just displaying it.
description: A recording instrument keeps a record of a measured quantity over time, traditionally on a paper chart and now usually in memory. IEC-style diagrams draw it as a square, with the placeholder replaced by the recorded quantity, so it can be told apart from a simple indicating meter at a glance.

The square does not say how often samples are stored, how long records are retained or how they are retrieved. Those details are what make a recording useful in an investigation, and they belong in the instrument specification rather than on the symbol.
readingNotes: Identify what quantity is recorded and its source.
Check how records are retrieved or exported.
drawingChecklist: Fill in the recorded quantity
State sampling or chart speed
Reference data retrieval method
entries.distinction: A recording instrument stores values against time; an indicating instrument shows only the present value.

entries.name: Integrating instrument general symbol
entries.summary: General rectangle-with-band form for instruments that totalise a quantity over time, such as energy meters.
description: Integrating instruments add up a quantity over time, and IEC-style diagrams draw them as a rectangle with a narrow band across the top. The unit inside, such as kWh, kvarh or Ah, tells the reader what is being totalised, and extra marks in the band can show multi-rate or demand features.

The general symbol does not tell you whether the meter is a billing meter or a check meter, its accuracy class, or the direction of energy that each register records. Those are often contractual requirements and must be stated in the metering schedule.
readingNotes: Read the unit to find the integrated quantity.
Look for marks in the band that add tariff or demand features.
drawingChecklist: State integrated quantity
Give accuracy class
Define register direction
entries.distinction: The integrating form totalises; the indicating circle shows an instantaneous value.

entries.name: Ohmmeter
entries.summary: Indicating instrument for electrical resistance, shown as an instrument circle marked with the ohm sign.
description: An ohmmeter indicates resistance by passing a small current from its own source and measuring the result. On permanent drawings it appears in test equipment, earthing test points and some machine monitoring panels, while on schematics for test procedures it shows where resistance is to be measured.

Because the instrument supplies its own measuring current, it must only be connected to de-energised circuits unless it is specifically designed otherwise. The symbol does not tell you the measuring voltage, range or whether a two-wire or four-wire connection is used.
readingNotes: Confirm the measured circuit is de-energised.
Check for four-wire connection when low resistances are measured.
drawingChecklist: State range
Show test connections
Note isolation requirements
entries.distinction: An ohmmeter measures ordinary resistance at low voltage; an insulation resistance meter applies a high test voltage to measure megohms.

entries.name: Insulation resistance meter
entries.summary: Indicating instrument applying a high DC test voltage to read insulation resistance in megohms.
description: An insulation resistance meter applies a DC test voltage, typically hundreds or thousands of volts, between conductors and earth and reads the leakage as resistance in megohms. On drawings it appears in test procedures and in permanently installed test panels for motors and cables.

The test voltage can damage electronics and leaves charge on capacitive cables, so the drawing should show what must be disconnected and how the circuit is discharged afterwards. The symbol itself does not state the test voltage or the acceptance value.
readingNotes: Identify electronics that must be disconnected before testing.
Check the test voltage suits the insulation rating.
drawingChecklist: State test voltage
Show disconnection points
Reference discharge procedure
entries.distinction: An insulation resistance meter is a periodic test instrument; an insulation monitoring relay checks an unearthed system continuously in service.

entries.name: Galvanometer
entries.summary: Sensitive indicating instrument used to detect very small currents or a balance point in a bridge circuit.
description: A galvanometer is a very sensitive current indicator, often with a centre zero, used to detect small currents rather than measure them to a scale. It is drawn in bridge and comparison circuits, where the operator adjusts a component until the galvanometer reads zero.

On modern drawings the function is often performed by an electronic null detector, but the symbol still marks the balance point. It does not show sensitivity, damping or protection against overload, which matter because the instrument is easily damaged by currents far above its scale.
readingNotes: Identify the two points whose balance is being detected.
Look for protective shunts or switches around the instrument.
drawingChecklist: State sensitivity
Show protective shunt
Identify bridge arms
entries.distinction: A galvanometer detects small or zero current; an ammeter measures current to a calibrated scale.

entries.name: Oscilloscope
entries.summary: Instrument that displays the waveform of a signal against time, drawn with a waveform inside the instrument outline.
description: An oscilloscope displays how a voltage or current changes over time. In drawings it appears in test set-ups, laboratory panels and commissioning procedures, with its probe points shown so readers know exactly where waveforms are to be captured.

The symbol does not show probe type or reference. Connecting an earth-referenced scope ground lead to a live point in a power circuit can short the circuit, so differential probes or isolated channels must be specified in the procedure rather than assumed from the symbol.
readingNotes: Identify the probe reference point for each channel.
Check whether differential probes are required.
drawingChecklist: Mark probe points
State probe type
Note bandwidth if relevant
entries.distinction: An oscilloscope shows a waveform shape; a disturbance recorder stores triggered records for later analysis.

entries.name: Recording voltmeter
entries.summary: Recording instrument that keeps a time record of voltage, drawn as a square marked V.
description: A recording voltmeter stores voltage against time so that sags, swells and slow variations can be reviewed later. On single-line diagrams it is drawn off a VT secondary at a busbar or supply point, and on schematics it is wired across the VT circuit like an indicating voltmeter.

The symbol does not say how fast the recorder samples. A slow recorder logging averages every few minutes cannot show short dips, so the recording interval must be checked against what the record will be used to investigate.

Check the recording interval against the events of interest.
drawingChecklist: Show VT ratio
State recording interval
Reference data retrieval

entries.name: Recording ammeter
entries.summary: Recording instrument that keeps a time record of current, drawn as a square marked A.
description: A recording ammeter logs current against time and is used to study load profiles, motor starting and feeder loading. It is connected in a CT secondary circuit, so like any CT-fed instrument its input forms part of a loop that must never be opened under load.

The record is only as useful as its interval and range. The symbol does not show whether peaks are captured or averaged, and a recorder sized for normal load may clip during starting or fault current.
readingNotes: Treat the input as part of the CT secondary loop.
Check whether peaks or averages are recorded.
drawingChecklist: Show CT ratio
State range and interval
Provide CT shorting point

entries.name: Apparent-energy meter
entries.summary: Integrating meter that totalises apparent energy in kVAh, used where tariffs charge on kVA rather than kW.
description: An apparent-energy meter totalises volt-amperes over time. Some network tariffs and demand charges are based on kVA, so this register appears on supply-point single-line diagrams beside the kWh and kvarh registers of the revenue meter.

Apparent energy can be calculated in more than one way when harmonics or unbalance are present, for example arithmetically from each phase or vectorially from total watts and vars. The symbol does not say which method is used, and two meters with different methods can disagree.

drawingChecklist: State calculation method

entries.summary: Energy meter with separate registers for energy flowing in each direction, as used at generation and solar connection points.

entries.name: Energy meter with pulse transmitter
entries.summary: Energy meter that sends a pulse output proportional to energy for remote counting, totalising or building management.
description: This form shows an energy meter with a transmitting output, normally a pulse contact where each pulse represents a fixed amount of energy. The output feeds a remote counter, a summation meter, a PLC or a building management system, so the meter symbol is linked to a separate signal circuit.

The pulse weight, such as watt-hours per pulse, and the pulse width are essential for the receiver. The symbol does not show them, and a mismatch between pulse weight and receiver scaling produces errors that are easy to miss.

Trace the pulse output to its receiving device.

Show output contact wiring
Reference receiving input scaling

entries.name: Energy meter repeater
entries.summary: Remote register that counts pulses from a transmitting energy meter and repeats its reading at another location.
description: An energy meter repeater has no measuring inputs of its own. It counts pulses from a transmitting meter and displays the resulting energy at a control room or tenant panel, so on the drawing it connects only to a signal circuit rather than to CTs and VTs.

Because it counts pulses, the repeater can drift from the master meter if pulses are lost or the supply is interrupted. The symbol does not show whether it has non-volatile memory or how it is reconciled with the master, which matters if the repeater is used for billing.

entries.name: Prepayment energy meter
entries.summary: Energy meter with credit control that disconnects supply through an integral switch when credit is used up.
description: A prepayment meter combines an energy register with a credit system and a supply switch. When credit is exhausted the switch opens the supply, so on the schematic the meter includes or controls a load switch in the main circuit as well as its measuring element.

The integral switch is a disconnection device rather than protection. The symbol does not show emergency credit arrangements or which circuits are supplied through the switch, and essential loads may need to be wired so they are not interrupted.

Check that protection is provided separately.

entries.name: Volt-squared-hour meter
entries.summary: Integrating meter that totalises the square of voltage over time, used to assess voltage-dependent losses and stress.
description: A volt-squared-hour meter integrates the square of voltage over time. Quantities such as iron losses in transformers and the stress on some insulation vary roughly with voltage squared, so the register gives a measure of exposure that a simple time-at-voltage record would not.

It is uncommon on modern drawings and is often provided as a calculated register inside a multifunction meter. The symbol does not tell you the reference voltage or whether the value is per phase or combined, so the meter documentation is needed to use the reading.
readingNotes: Check whether the value is per phase or combined.
Confirm whether this is a separate meter or a calculated register.

entries.name: Summation energy meter
entries.summary: Integrating device that adds energy from several meters or circuits to give one total register.
description: A summation meter totalises energy from more than one circuit. It may count pulses from several transmitting meters or, in older schemes, be fed by a summation CT, and it appears where several incomers or feeders must be billed or monitored as one supply.

Every input must use the same direction convention and consistent pulse weights, or the total is wrong. The symbol shows the summing function but not the inputs, so each source meter should be listed with its weighting.

entries.name: Maximum-demand indicator
entries.summary: Indicating instrument with a resettable pointer or register showing the highest averaged current or power reached.
description: A maximum-demand indicator shows the highest averaged load reached since it was last reset. Thermal demand ammeters with a drag pointer were common on switchboard feeders and transformer secondaries, and they help assess loading without a full recording instrument.

Thermal types respond with a time constant rather than a fixed interval, so their readings are not directly comparable with tariff demand meters. The symbol does not show the response time or reset method, both of which affect how the reading is used.

entries.name: Phase-sequence indicator
entries.summary: Instrument that shows whether three-phase supply rotation is positive or reversed before motors are run or sources paralleled.
description: A phase-sequence indicator connects to all three phases and shows whether rotation is L1-L2-L3 or reversed. It is used when commissioning motors, generators and supply changes, because wrong rotation reverses motors and prevents correct paralleling.

The instrument gives a check at one moment and does not protect anything on its own. If permanent protection against reversed rotation is needed, a phase-sequence monitoring relay with contacts must be shown instead of, or as well as, the indicator.
readingNotes: Confirm all three phases are connected in the stated order.
Check whether a protective relay is also required.

entries.name: Voltage presence indicating system
entries.summary: Capacitively coupled indicator on MV switchgear that shows whether each phase of a cable or busbar is energised.
description: Voltage presence indicating systems are built into medium-voltage switchgear and ring main units. A capacitive divider in the bushing or insulator feeds a low-voltage indicator for each phase, and test sockets allow phase comparison before connecting cables or closing onto another source.

An indicator showing no voltage is not proof that the circuit is dead. Safe isolation still requires the approved test method and earthing procedure, and the symbol does not show the indicator's thresholds or whether it is self-testing.

entries.name: Double voltmeter
entries.summary: Instrument with two voltage movements in one case, showing running and incoming voltage side by side for synchronising.
description: A double voltmeter contains two voltage measuring elements, usually reading the running busbar and the incoming generator or feeder. Mounted on a synchronising panel next to the double frequency meter and synchroscope, it lets the operator match voltages before closing.

The two inputs must come from VTs with equivalent ratios and the same phase pair, otherwise the comparison is misleading. The symbol does not show the switching that selects which incoming source is connected to the instrument.

Check the synchronising selector that switches the inputs.

entries.name: Double frequency meter
entries.summary: Instrument with two frequency elements showing running and incoming frequency together on a synchronising panel.
description: A double frequency meter shows the frequency of the running system and the incoming machine on one instrument. During manual synchronising the operator adjusts the incoming governor until the two readings match closely, then uses the synchroscope for final phase alignment.

The meter shows frequency only and gives no information on phase angle. Closing with matched frequencies but a large phase difference can still cause a severe disturbance, so it must always be read with the synchroscope or check-synchronising relay.

entries.summary: Digital panel meter that measures voltage, current, power, energy and power factor from one set of CT and VT inputs.
description: A multifunction power meter replaces separate ammeters, voltmeters, wattmeters and energy meters with one digital device. On single-line diagrams it is drawn as one block at a feeder or incomer with its CT and VT connections, and on schematics its terminals show current inputs, voltage inputs, auxiliary supply and communications.

Listing the meter once hides how many quantities it provides. The drawing or schedule should state which values are used for billing, monitoring or control, and which communication protocol carries them, because those uses carry different accuracy requirements.

Check which values are sent over communications.

entries.name: Power quality analyser
entries.summary: Instrument that measures and logs harmonics, flicker, dips, swells and unbalance at a point of the network.
description: A power quality analyser measures disturbances as well as ordinary quantities: harmonics, flicker, voltage dips and swells, unbalance and transients. It is installed at supply points and sensitive loads to show whether supply quality meets the agreed limits, and it keeps event logs for investigation.

Measurement methods for power quality are standardised so that different instruments give comparable results, and the class of measurement matters when results are used in disputes. The symbol does not show that class, the VT and CT bandwidth or the logging settings.

entries.name: Disturbance recorder
entries.summary: Recorder that captures analogue waveforms and binary signals before and after a trigger for fault analysis.
description: A disturbance recorder captures sampled current and voltage waveforms together with breaker and protection contact states when a trigger occurs. Pre-fault and post-fault data let engineers check how protection performed, so the recorder is drawn with its analogue inputs from CTs and VTs and its binary inputs from trip and position contacts.

Many protection relays now include this function, so a separate recorder symbol usually indicates a dedicated substation-wide unit. The symbol does not show trigger conditions, sample rate or record length, and records are commonly exchanged in a standard file format that should be named in the specification.
readingNotes: Trace analogue inputs to their CTs and VTs.
List binary inputs and their sources.
drawingChecklist: List analogue channels
List binary channels
State trigger and record length
entries.distinction: A disturbance recorder stores high-rate waveforms around an event; a sequence-of-events recorder stores timestamped contact changes only.

entries.name: Sequence-of-events recorder
entries.summary: Recorder that timestamps changes of state on many binary inputs so the order of operations can be reconstructed.
description: A sequence-of-events recorder monitors breaker auxiliary contacts, protection trip outputs, alarms and other binary signals, and stores each change with an accurate timestamp. After an incident the list shows which device operated first, which is often impossible to tell from alarms alone.

Timestamp resolution and time synchronisation are what make the record useful. The symbol does not show the time source, such as a GPS clock, or the debounce settings on each input, and without synchronisation records from different devices cannot be merged reliably.

Check which contacts are wired as inputs.
drawingChecklist: List monitored inputs
Show time source
State resolution and debounce

entries.name: Phasor measurement unit
entries.summary: Device that measures voltage and current phasors with precise time stamps so angles can be compared across a network.
description: A phasor measurement unit samples voltages and currents and calculates magnitude and phase angle referenced to an absolute time source, normally GPS. Data from many PMUs can then be compared to see angle differences across a network, oscillations and islanding.

On a single-line diagram the PMU is drawn with its CT and VT inputs and a time input. The symbol does not show reporting rate, the communications path to a data concentrator or the measurement class, which together determine whether the data suits protection, control or monitoring.

entries.summary: Measuring transducer that converts CT and VT inputs into a DC signal proportional to active power for SCADA or control.
description: An active-power transducer takes current and voltage inputs and produces a DC current or voltage signal proportional to watts, often bipolar so that export and import give opposite signs. It is used where a governor, load controller or older SCADA needs an analogue power signal.

The output range, including how negative power is represented, must match the receiving input. The symbol shows the conversion but not the element configuration, response time or the scaling between rated power and output signal.
