entries.name: Voltage measuring transducer
entries.summary: Transducer that converts a VT secondary or direct voltage into an isolated analogue signal for remote measurement.
description: A voltage measuring transducer converts a voltage into a standard analogue signal such as 4-20 mA, with galvanic isolation between input and output. It is fed from a VT secondary or, at low voltage, directly from the busbar through fuses, and it supplies a PLC, SCADA or regulator input.

The symbol does not show whether the output follows RMS or average value, or the live zero of the output range. If the transducer is self-powered from the measured voltage, its output fails when the voltage collapses, which matters when it is used to detect loss of supply.

entries.name: Multi-core current transformer
entries.summary: CT with several independent magnetic cores on one primary, each with its own secondary for metering or protection.
description: A multi-core CT has one primary passing through two or more separate cores, each with its own secondary winding. Typical MV and HV CTs have one metering core and one or more protection cores, so the single-line diagram shows each core as its own ring on the primary with its ratio and class beside it.

Separate cores mean a fault-saturated protection core does not disturb the metering core, and each can have a different accuracy class. The symbol shows how many cores exist but not which relay or meter each feeds, so every core needs its own designation and cross-reference.
readingNotes: Count the cores and read each ratio and class separately.
Follow each secondary to its own relay or meter.

State ratio and class per core

entries.name: Summation current transformer
entries.summary: Auxiliary CT with several primary windings that adds the secondary currents of other CTs into one output.
description: A summation CT has several primary windings, each fed from the secondary of a main CT, and one secondary winding that carries their sum. It lets one meter or relay see the total current of several feeders, or in some relay designs combines three phase currents into a single weighted quantity.

All main CTs feeding a summation CT must have the same ratio, and their polarity must be consistent, otherwise currents cancel instead of adding. The symbol shows the summing arrangement but the burden it adds to each main CT has to be checked separately.

Verify polarity of each primary winding.

entries.name: Interposing current transformer
entries.summary: Auxiliary CT inserted in a CT secondary circuit to correct ratio, phase shift or provide isolation for a relay.
description: An interposing CT sits between a main CT and a relay or meter. It corrects ratio mismatch, provides phase-shift compensation for transformer differential schemes, or isolates circuits, and it was standard in electromechanical differential protection before relays could compensate internally.

The interposing CT adds burden to the main CT and can introduce its own errors at high fault current. The symbol shows its presence, but its ratio, connection (star or delta) and taps must be shown beside it because they decide whether the differential scheme balances.

entries.name: Rogowski coil current sensor
entries.summary: Air-cored coil around a conductor whose output voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current.
description: A Rogowski coil is wound on a non-magnetic former and placed around the conductor. Its output voltage is proportional to the rate of change of current, so an integrator in the relay or meter reconstructs the current waveform. With no iron core it does not saturate, which suits high fault currents and wide measuring ranges.

The output is a low-level voltage, not a current, so it must go to an input designed for it and cannot be wired into a conventional 1 A or 5 A CT circuit. The symbol does not show the sensor's coefficient, cable length limits or the matching relay input, all of which affect accuracy.
readingNotes: Confirm the receiving input is designed for Rogowski sensors.
Do not apply CT shorting practice to this low-level voltage output.

Reference matching input
Respect cable length limit

entries.name: Wound-primary current transformer
entries.summary: CT with a primary winding of several turns, used for low primary currents where a bar primary gives too little accuracy.
description: A wound-primary CT has a primary winding of more than one turn rather than a single bar or conductor through a window. This is needed at low primary currents, where a single turn would not produce enough magnetising ampere-turns for accurate metering, and it is common in MV metering units.

The wound primary has a lower short-time withstand than a bar primary, so its thermal and dynamic ratings need checking against the fault level. The symbol shows the winding but not those ratings, which belong in the CT schedule.

description: A bushing CT is a toroidal core and secondary slipped over the bushing of a power transformer, generator or dead-tank circuit breaker. The bushing conductor is the primary, and several CTs may be stacked on one bushing for differential, overcurrent and metering duties.

Bushing CTs are often multi-ratio, with taps on the secondary, and only the selected tap should be wired to the relay. The symbol shows the location at the bushing, so the reader must check which side of the breaker or transformer the CT sits on to understand the protection zone overlap.

Both windings share the same core, so their combined burden must stay within the VT's thermal rating. The symbol shows the two windings but not the class of each or the secondary protection, which must be stated for each circuit.

entries.name: Voltage transformer set with broken-delta residual winding
entries.summary: Three single-phase VTs whose residual windings are connected in broken delta to produce the zero-sequence voltage.
description: In this arrangement three single-phase earthed VTs each carry a residual winding, and the three residual windings are connected in series as a broken delta. In a healthy balanced system the voltage across the open corner is near zero, and during an earth fault it rises towards three times the zero-sequence voltage, which feeds residual voltage and directional earth-fault elements.

A damping resistor is often connected across the broken delta to suppress ferroresonance in isolated or resonant-earthed networks. The symbol does not show that resistor or the earthing of the VT primaries, both of which need explicit detail on the schematic.
readingNotes: Check the primaries are earthed star so zero sequence can be measured.

entries.name: Open-delta voltage transformer connection
entries.summary: Two phase-to-phase VTs connected in V to provide all three line voltages without a neutral reference.
description: The open-delta or V-V connection uses two double-pole VTs connected between phases, sharing one phase as a common point. It gives all three line-to-line secondary voltages at lower cost than three VTs and is common in MV metering and switchgear where neutral voltages are not needed.

Because there is no neutral reference, phase-to-neutral voltages and zero-sequence voltage cannot be measured. Earth-fault directional elements or meters needing phase-to-neutral inputs therefore cannot be fed from this connection, which the reader must check against the relay requirements.

entries.name: Resistive voltage divider sensor
entries.summary: Low-power voltage sensor using a resistive divider to give a small voltage signal proportional to primary voltage.
description: A resistive voltage divider sensor is a low-power instrument transformer in which a high-value resistor chain steps the primary voltage down to a small signal. It has no iron core, so it does not cause ferroresonance, and one sensor can cover a wide range of primary voltages.

The output is a low-energy signal that must go to an input designed for it, and the cable between sensor and relay is part of the measurement. The symbol does not show the division ratio, correction factors or connector type, which must match the relay configuration.
readingNotes: Confirm the relay input is configured for the sensor ratio.
Keep the supplied sensor cable unless the manufacturer allows changes.
drawingChecklist: State division ratio
Reference correction factors
Show connector and cable
entries.distinction: A resistive divider sensor gives a low-level signal; a conventional VT gives a standard secondary voltage capable of supplying burden.

entries.name: Low-power current transformer
entries.summary: Small iron-core CT with an integral shunt that delivers a low-level voltage signal instead of a standard secondary current.
description: A low-power CT uses a small magnetic core and an integral burden resistor, so its output is a low-level voltage proportional to primary current. It suits digital relays and compact switchgear, and a single LPCT can often replace several conventional CT ratios.

Because the burden is built in, the output must not be shorted or loaded like a conventional CT, and it cannot feed electromechanical relays or ordinary meters. The symbol shows the sensor but the reader must confirm the relay input type and the sensor's rated output.
readingNotes: Check the receiving input is an LPCT input.
Do not short the output as for a conventional CT.
drawingChecklist: State rated output
Reference relay input type
Show sensor cable
entries.distinction: An LPCT has an iron core with integral burden; a Rogowski coil has no iron core and gives a di/dt output.

entries.name: Optical current sensor
entries.summary: Current sensor using light in an optical fibre around the conductor, whose polarisation changes with the magnetic field.
description: An optical current sensor measures current from the rotation of polarised light in a fibre wound around the conductor, a magneto-optic effect proportional to the enclosed magnetic field. It is used in HV and DC applications where conventional CTs are bulky or where saturation and insulation are concerns.

The sensor head connects through fibre to an electronics unit, which usually outputs digital sampled values to protection and metering devices. The symbol does not show the electronics unit, its supply or the data interface, all of which must be drawn for the measurement chain to be complete.
readingNotes: Find the electronics unit that converts the optical signal.
Check the data interface to protection devices.
drawingChecklist: Show sensor head and electronics
Reference output interface
State auxiliary supply
entries.distinction: An optical current sensor uses light in fibre; a conventional CT uses magnetic induction in a winding.

entries.name: Numerical protection relay (IED)
entries.summary: Single relay block on an SLD that lists the protection functions it provides, with CT, VT and trip connections.
description: A numerical protection relay, or IED, combines many protection, control and measuring functions in one device. Single-line diagrams draw it as a block connected to its CTs, VTs and breaker trip coil, with the enabled functions listed inside or beside it using IEC function symbols or ANSI device numbers.

Listing a function on the block shows it is enabled, not how it is set. The block does not show settings, logic between functions, or communications, so it must be read with the settings file and the protection logic diagram.

Trace CT, VT and trip connections to the block.

entries.name: Trip-circuit supervision relay
entries.summary: Relay that passes a small current through the trip circuit to check continuity and alarms if the circuit is broken.
description: A trip-circuit supervision relay monitors the wiring, auxiliary contacts and trip coil of a circuit breaker by passing a current too small to trip it. If the trip circuit is broken or its supply fails, the relay drops out and raises an alarm, so a failed trip path is found before a fault needs it.

Schemes differ in whether they supervise the circuit with the breaker open and closed, which needs resistors or connections across the breaker auxiliary contacts. The symbol shows the relay but the reader must check which states are actually covered.
readingNotes: Check supervision covers both breaker positions.
Verify the supervision current cannot operate the trip coil.
drawingChecklist: Show connections across trip contacts
State supervised breaker states
Reference alarm output
entries.distinction: Trip-circuit supervision monitors trip path continuity; a lockout relay latches after a trip.

entries.name: Buchholz relay
entries.summary: Gas-and-oil actuated relay in the pipe to the conservator, giving alarm on gas build-up and trip on oil surge.
description: A Buchholz relay is fitted in the pipe between an oil-filled transformer tank and its conservator. Slow gas accumulation from minor internal faults operates an alarm float, while a rapid surge of oil from a serious internal fault operates a trip element, so the schematic shows two separate contacts.

On single-line diagrams it may appear only as a label on the transformer, while the control schematic shows its alarm and trip contacts wired to annunciation and the transformer trip relay. The symbol does not show the gas sampling procedure or the test arrangement used during maintenance.
readingNotes: Identify separate alarm and trip contacts.
Follow the trip contact to the transformer lockout or trip relay.
drawingChecklist: Show alarm contact
Show trip contact
Reference transformer trip relay
entries.distinction: A Buchholz relay detects gas and oil movement; a sudden pressure relay responds to rapid tank pressure rise.

entries.name: Winding temperature indicator
entries.summary: Transformer indicator that adds a CT-heated thermal image to top-oil temperature to estimate winding hot-spot temperature.
description: A winding temperature indicator estimates transformer winding hot-spot temperature, which cannot easily be measured directly. A sensor in the top-oil pocket is heated by a small element fed from a CT on the load current, so the reading rises with both oil temperature and load, and its contacts control fans and give alarm and trip.

The schematic should show the CT feeding the heater, the calibration resistor and each contact stage. The symbol does not show the thermal gradient setting, which must be adjusted to the transformer heat-run data for the reading to be meaningful.
readingNotes: Trace the CT circuit feeding the thermal image heater.
Identify contact stages for cooling, alarm and trip.
drawingChecklist: Show heater CT
List contact stages
Reference gradient setting

entries.name: Thermistor motor protection relay
entries.summary: Relay that monitors PTC thermistors embedded in motor windings and trips when their resistance rises at the rated temperature.
description: A thermistor protection relay is connected to a chain of PTC thermistors built into a motor's windings. When the windings reach the thermistors' rated response temperature, their resistance rises sharply and the relay opens its contact in the motor control circuit, protecting against overheating that a current-based overload cannot detect.

Typical causes it catches are blocked ventilation, high ambient temperature and frequent starting. The symbol does not show whether the relay detects a short-circuited sensor loop, whether it latches, or how it is reset, which affect safety where automatic restart is possible.
readingNotes: Follow the sensor loop to the motor terminal box.
Check reset type and short-circuit detection.
drawingChecklist: Show sensor loop terminals
State reset type
Reference motor control trip contact
entries.distinction: A thermistor relay measures winding temperature directly; a thermal overload relay models heating from current.

entries.name: Arc-flash point light sensor
entries.summary: Light sensor in a switchgear compartment that detects the flash of an internal arc and signals an arc-flash relay.
description: A point light sensor is mounted inside a switchgear compartment, such as a breaker or cable compartment, and detects the intense light of an internal arc. It is wired or fibre-connected to an arc-flash relay that usually also checks for overcurrent before tripping, so light alone from an external source does not cause a trip.

The drawing should show which compartment each sensor watches, because the trip zone depends on it. The symbol does not show sensitivity, field of view or the self-supervision used to detect a disconnected sensor.
readingNotes: Identify the compartment each sensor covers.
Check whether trip needs light plus overcurrent.
drawingChecklist: Locate each sensor by compartment
Show connection to the arc relay
State trip logic
entries.distinction: A point sensor covers one compartment; a fibre loop sensor covers a long area such as a busbar run.

entries.name: Arc-flash fibre loop sensor
entries.summary: Bare optical fibre routed through switchgear that picks up arc light anywhere along its length.
description: A fibre loop sensor is an unjacketed optical fibre routed through busbar chambers or along switchgear lines. Light from an arc anywhere along its length enters the fibre and reaches the arc-flash relay, so one loop can cover a large area that would need many point sensors.

Because the whole length is sensitive, a loop identifies the zone but not the exact compartment, and the trip zone therefore follows the routing. Loop length affects sensitivity, and the symbol does not show routing, length or the loop-check function, which should be recorded on the layout and schematic.
readingNotes: Read the routing drawing to see which compartments the loop crosses.
Check that the trip zone matches the loop coverage.
drawingChecklist: Show loop routing
State loop length
Reference relay channel
entries.distinction: A fibre loop covers a long area without locating the arc precisely; a point sensor watches one compartment.

entries.name: Residual current monitor
entries.summary: Device with a toroid that measures residual current and gives a warning or signal without interrupting the circuit itself.
description: A residual current monitor measures residual current with a summation toroid around the circuit conductors and signals when it exceeds a threshold. It is used where an unexpected trip would be unacceptable but rising leakage still needs attention, for example in data centres and process plant.

An RCM does not disconnect the circuit by itself, so it is not a substitute for an RCD where automatic disconnection is required. The symbol shows the toroid and monitor, but the reader must find out whether its output drives an alarm only or a separate switching device.
readingNotes: Check whether the output alarms or trips another device.
Confirm that all live conductors, including neutral, pass through the toroid.
drawingChecklist: Show toroid and conductors
State threshold
Reference alarm or trip output
entries.distinction: An RCM signals residual current; an RCD measures it and also disconnects the circuit.

facts.value: Signal or alarm, no integral disconnection

entries.name: Definite-time delay qualifier for measuring relays
entries.summary: Qualifier added to a measuring relay symbol to show that operation follows a fixed time delay after pick-up.
description: This qualifier is added inside or beside a measuring relay box to show that the relay operates a fixed time after its measured quantity crosses the threshold. Combined with a quantity such as I> or U<, it tells the reader the element is definite-time rather than instantaneous or inverse-time.

The qualifier states the type of delay, not its value. The delay setting itself must appear in the settings table, and an element shown without any time qualifier should not automatically be assumed to be instantaneous unless the legend says so.
readingNotes: Read the qualifier together with the quantity and threshold sign.
Take the actual delay value from the settings record.
drawingChecklist: Pair with quantity and threshold
State delay setting
Confirm legend convention
entries.distinction: A definite-time qualifier gives a fixed delay; an inverse-time qualifier gives a delay that shortens as the quantity increases.

entries.name: Inverse-time characteristic qualifier
entries.summary: Qualifier showing that a measuring relay's operating time falls as the measured quantity rises above its setting.
description: The inverse-time qualifier marks a measuring element whose operating time depends on how far the measured quantity exceeds the setting: the larger the overcurrent, the faster the trip. On drawings it appears with overcurrent and earth-fault elements that are graded against fuses and downstream relays.

The qualifier does not name the curve. Standard inverse, very inverse and extremely inverse curves grade very differently, and the curve type, time multiplier and pick-up current must be taken from the protection settings.

Read with the grading study for the feeder.

description: A directional qualifier is an arrow added to a measuring relay symbol, showing that the element responds only when the measured quantity flows in the indicated direction. On single-line diagrams the arrow usually points away from or towards the busbar, which tells the reader which faults the element is meant to see.

The arrow depends on correct CT and VT polarity to mean anything in practice. The symbol does not show the characteristic angle or the polarising quantity, so the drawing direction must be confirmed against the relay settings and commissioning tests.

entries.name: Relay test block
entries.summary: Multi-pole test facility between CT, VT and trip wiring and a relay, allowing safe isolation and test injection.
description: A relay test block sits in the secondary wiring between CTs, VTs, trip outputs and a protection relay. Inserting a test plug or opening the block isolates the relay from the plant, automatically shorts CT circuits before they are opened and isolates trip outputs, so the relay can be tested with secondary injection while the primary circuit stays in service.

The schematic should show the order in which poles break and make, because CT shorting must occur before CT circuits open. The symbol alone does not show that sequence, so the terminal arrangement of each pole needs to be drawn or referenced to the manufacturer data.

Confirm trip outputs are isolated when the block is opened.
drawingChecklist: Number each pole
Show CT shorting arrangement
Show trip isolation poles

entries.summary: Plug inserted into a test block or switch to connect test equipment to the relay side while isolating the plant side.
description: A test plug fits into a test block or test switch and brings each pole out to test leads. Depending on its design it can connect test equipment to the relay side only, or link plant and relay sides through an ammeter for in-service current measurement.

Different plug types for the same block do different things, so the procedure must name the plug variant. The symbol shows the plug's poles but not its internal links, and using the wrong plug can open a live CT circuit or leave a trip output connected.

entries.summary: Panel test switch for CT circuits that shorts the CT side before opening the relay side, with a test jack between.
description: Panel-mounted test switches used in North American practice often combine a knife switch with a shorting contact for each CT circuit. Opening the switch first shorts the CT secondary and then isolates the relay or meter, so a test set can be connected without exposing the CT to an open circuit.

Current test switches are usually grouped with potential test switches and trip-isolating switches on one assembly. The symbol shows a single pole, and the full assembly arrangement, including which poles are current and which are potential, must be read from the panel wiring diagram.

entries.name: Potential test switch
entries.summary: Panel test switch that opens a VT secondary circuit to a relay or meter so test voltages can be applied safely.
description: A potential test switch is a knife switch in a VT secondary circuit that isolates a relay or meter from the VT so test voltages can be injected. Unlike a current switch it has no shorting contact, because a VT secondary must never be shorted.

When the switch is open, protection that relies on the voltage may be disabled or may see loss of voltage. The symbol does not show that consequence, so the test procedure should list the functions affected and whether any trip outputs must also be isolated.

entries.name: Synchronising lamps
entries.summary: Set of lamps connected between incoming and running phases that brighten and dim with the phase difference during synchronising.
description: Synchronising lamps are connected between corresponding phases of the running system and the incoming machine. As the phase difference changes the lamps brighten and dim, and in the dark-lamp method the breaker is closed when they are dark, showing the voltages are in phase.

Lamps cannot show small residual voltage differences reliably, since a lamp can look dark with a significant voltage across it. They are therefore a backup or visual aid, and the drawing should show a synchroscope or check-synchronising relay for the actual permission to close.

entries.summary: Device on an MV cable or overhead feeder that shows whether fault current has passed its location, to speed fault finding.
description: A fault passage indicator senses current at a point on a medium-voltage feeder and shows, with a flag or LED, when fault current has passed. Operators follow the indicators along a feeder to find the faulted section between the last operated indicator and the first unoperated one.

Indicators may sense phase faults, earth faults or both, and many can signal remotely to SCADA. The symbol does not show the sensing method, reset method or thresholds, which must suit the network earthing and feeder load to avoid false or missed indications.

entries.name: Surge arrester counter
entries.summary: Counter in a surge arrester's earth lead that registers discharges and often shows leakage current.
description: A surge counter is installed in the earth connection of a surge arrester, which must therefore be mounted on an insulating base. It increments each time the arrester discharges a significant surge, and many models include a milliammeter for leakage current, which helps assess arrester condition.

On single-line diagrams the counter is drawn between the arrester and earth. The symbol does not tell you the counting threshold or whether leakage reading is total or resistive, and the insulating base must be shown so the counter is not bypassed.

entries.name: Partial discharge sensor
entries.summary: Sensor on switchgear, cables or transformers that picks up signals from partial discharge for insulation condition monitoring.
description: Partial discharge sensors detect small electrical discharges inside insulation before it fails. Common types include transient earth voltage sensors on metal-clad switchgear, UHF antennas in gas-insulated equipment and high-frequency CTs on cable earth straps, each feeding a monitoring unit that records and trends the activity.

The symbol shows the sensor location but not its type or frequency range, and results from different sensor types are not directly comparable. Monitoring is used for maintenance decisions rather than protection, so the sensor output normally goes to alarms or a condition monitoring system rather than a trip circuit.

entries.name: Fixed-speed wind turbine generator (Type 1)
entries.summary: A wind turbine whose squirrel-cage induction generator connects to the network directly, running at nearly constant speed.
description: This symbol marks a Type 1 wind turbine: a rotor-driven squirrel-cage induction generator whose stator connects to the collector network through a soft starter and a step-up transformer, with no power converter in the main path. Speed varies only by the generator slip, typically one or two per cent, so the turbine is described as fixed-speed.

On a single-line diagram it is usually drawn as a blade or rotor glyph coupled to a generator circle marked for an induction machine, followed by the soft starter, switched capacitor steps for reactive power and the pad-mount or nacelle transformer. Older wind farms and small community turbines are the main places it still appears.

The symbol does not state the reactive demand of the generator, the capacitor step sizes or how the turbine behaves during voltage dips. Those values come from the turbine data sheet and the grid connection study, because an induction generator draws magnetising current from the network rather than supplying it.
readingNotes: Look for shunt capacitor steps beside the generator; they supply the reactive power the induction machine absorbs.
A soft starter or thyristor bypass shown in series is for connection inrush only, not for speed control.
drawingChecklist: State generator rating, voltage and slip range.
Show soft starter and capacitor compensation steps.
Reference the turbine step-up transformer and collector feeder.
entries.distinction: A Type 1 turbine has no converter in the power path; a Type 3 or Type 4 turbine shows a converter that sets speed and reactive output.

entries.name: Variable-slip wind turbine generator (Type 2)
entries.summary: A wind turbine using a wound-rotor induction generator with controlled external rotor resistance to widen the slip range.
description: A Type 2 wind turbine uses a wound-rotor induction generator whose rotor circuit is connected to a variable resistance, usually switched by power electronics mounted on the rotor. Raising the rotor resistance lets the slip increase to around ten per cent, which softens torque peaks from gusts while the stator stays connected directly to the network.

Drawings show the generator circle with rotor slip-ring or rotor-winding marks and a resistor element with a variable arrow attached to the rotor side. The stator side follows the same path as a Type 1 machine: soft starter, capacitor compensation and step-up transformer.

Energy dissipated in the rotor resistance is lost as heat, so the symbol says nothing about efficiency or about any capability to deliver reactive power. Fault ride-through behaviour and resistor ratings must be read from the turbine model data.
readingNotes: The variable resistor on the rotor side is a slip control element, not a braking resistor or a load.
Stator-side compensation capacitors are still normally present.
drawingChecklist: State rotor resistance control range.
Show stator connection and compensation.
Reference turbine model data for dynamic studies.
entries.distinction: A Type 2 turbine dissipates rotor energy in resistance; a doubly-fed generator returns rotor power to the network through a converter.

entries.name: Doubly-fed induction generator
entries.summary: A wound-rotor induction generator with the stator on the network and the rotor fed through a back-to-back converter sized for slip power.
description: A doubly-fed induction generator has its stator connected directly to the turbine transformer while the rotor windings, reached through slip rings, connect to a back-to-back AC/DC/AC converter. The converter injects rotor currents at slip frequency, allowing variable speed of roughly plus or minus thirty per cent around synchronous speed and independent control of active and reactive power.

On a single-line diagram the generator circle shows two connections: the stator branch to the main breaker and the rotor branch to a pair of converter blocks joined by a DC link. A crowbar or DC chopper is often shown on the rotor converter for fault protection, and a line filter or reactor sits on the grid-side converter.

Because the converter only carries slip power, typically a quarter to a third of the turbine rating, the symbol does not imply full decoupling from the network. Short-circuit contribution, crowbar operation and ride-through capability depend on control settings that the diagram does not show.
readingNotes: Follow both the stator and rotor paths; they usually join again at the turbine transformer low-voltage side.
Identify the crowbar or chopper, since it changes fault behaviour.
drawingChecklist: State stator rating and rotor converter rating separately.
Show crowbar, chopper and line filter if fitted.
Reference grid-code ride-through data.
entries.distinction: A DFIG converter handles only rotor slip power; a full-converter turbine passes all generator output through the converter.

facts.label: Converter rating
facts.value: Typically about 25 to 35 per cent of turbine rating

entries.name: Full-converter wind turbine generator (Type 4)
entries.summary: A wind turbine whose entire generator output passes through a full-rated back-to-back converter before reaching the network.
description: In a Type 4 turbine the generator, commonly a permanent-magnet or wound-field synchronous machine and sometimes an induction machine, is fully decoupled from the network by a back-to-back converter rated for the whole turbine output. The machine-side converter rectifies variable-frequency generator output to a DC link and the grid-side converter produces network-frequency AC.

Single-line drawings show the generator circle, a machine-side converter block, a DC link with chopper or brake resistor, a grid-side converter block and the line filter before the step-up transformer. Some drawings collapse this to a generator and a single converter symbol labelled with the conversion direction.

The network sees a converter, not a rotating machine, so fault current is limited to the converter capability and reactive output is a control function. The symbol does not tell you whether the converter is grid-following or grid-forming, which must be checked in the plant control description.
readingNotes: Treat the turbine short-circuit contribution as converter-limited.
A DC chopper resistor in the link absorbs energy during network faults; it is not a load.
drawingChecklist: State generator type and full converter rating.
Show DC link chopper and line filter.
Reference converter control mode and ride-through data.
entries.distinction: A Type 4 turbine routes all power through the converter; a DFIG routes only rotor slip power through it.

entries.name: Three-phase induction generator
entries.summary: A squirrel-cage asynchronous machine driven above synchronous speed so that it delivers power into a three-phase network.
description: An induction generator is an asynchronous machine driven slightly faster than synchronous speed by a turbine or engine. It exports active power but needs reactive power from the network or from capacitors to establish its magnetic field, so it cannot normally hold voltage and frequency on its own.

The symbol is a machine circle with G, a three-phase AC mark and often the letters ASG or a squirrel-cage indication to separate it from a synchronous generator. It is found in small hydro, older wind turbines and some biogas or heat recovery sets connected in parallel with a stronger supply.

The symbol does not tell you whether the machine can run isolated with self-excitation capacitors, or what happens to its output when the network trips. Islanded operation and reverse power or loss-of-mains protection have to be read from the protection and control drawings.
readingNotes: Look for excitation capacitors near the machine terminals.
Check loss-of-mains protection, since the machine may self-excite on capacitors if islanded.
drawingChecklist: State rating, voltage and rated slip.
Show capacitor compensation and its switching.
Reference loss-of-mains protection.
entries.distinction: An induction generator draws its magnetising current from the network; a synchronous generator has its own field and can regulate voltage.

entries.name: Single-phase synchronous generator
entries.summary: A synchronous alternator delivering a single-phase output, common on small portable and standby generating sets.
description: This symbol identifies a synchronous generator with a single-phase output, usually two terminals or a split winding giving 120/240 V. Small standby and portable sets, and some hybrid off-grid systems, use this type because their loads are single-phase.

The generator circle carries G with a single-phase AC mark. Where a centre-tapped or split winding is used, two output leads plus a neutral are drawn, and a bonding link between neutral and earth may be shown at the set or at the main switchboard.

The symbol does not tell you the voltage regulation method, whether the winding is reconnectable or where the neutral is bonded. Those are critical for safe earthing, so they need explicit notes on the drawing.
readingNotes: Count output conductors to tell a plain two-wire output from a split-phase winding.
Locate the neutral-earth bond; it should exist in one place only.
drawingChecklist: State voltage, frequency and kVA.
Show neutral bonding location.
Reference the transfer arrangement to the installation.
entries.distinction: A single-phase generator has one output phase; a three-phase synchronous generator has three phase outputs and often a star neutral.

facts.value: Neutral bond location must be shown

entries.name: Synchronous generator with brushless exciter
entries.summary: A synchronous alternator shown with its exciter machine and rotating rectifier, as used on most generating sets.
description: Most modern generating sets use a brushless excitation system: a small exciter generator on the same shaft feeds a rotating diode rectifier, which supplies DC to the main field without slip rings. The automatic voltage regulator controls the exciter field, and some sets add a permanent-magnet pilot exciter to power the regulator independently of the output voltage.

Schematics draw the main generator circle, a smaller exciter circle on the same shaft line and a rectifier bridge between them, with the regulator connected to the exciter field. Single-line diagrams often reduce this to the main machine with a note, so the expanded form usually appears on the generator control schematic.

The symbol does not give the regulator type, the excitation support during short circuits, or whether a pilot exciter is fitted. Those determine whether the set can sustain fault current long enough for downstream protection to operate.
readingNotes: The rotating rectifier is shown inside the shaft boundary; it is not an external rectifier.
A permanent-magnet pilot exciter indicates excitation support independent of terminal voltage.
drawingChecklist: Identify regulator type and sensing connections.
State pilot exciter presence.
Reference fault-current support data.
entries.distinction: This form shows the excitation chain explicitly; the plain synchronous generator symbol shows only the main machine.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE permanent-magnet synchronous generator symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-oriented library form of a three-phase synchronous generator with permanent-magnet excitation, with reading notes.
description: This entry covers the permanent-magnet synchronous generator as it appears in an IEEE-oriented drawing library. The machine has a magnet rotor and no field winding, so output voltage rises with speed and cannot be trimmed by an excitation regulator; voltage control is done by the converter or by the load.

Within IEEE-style one-line and schematic drawings the machine is a circle with the generator letter and a magnet indication, with three output leads. The block identifier quoted here is a vendor library name and only meaningful inside that library. This is a convention-specific lookup; the geometry is independently drawn and is not a certified reproduction of the standard graphic.
readingNotes: Expect a converter or rectifier immediately downstream; a permanent-magnet machine rarely connects directly to a fixed-frequency bus.
Read the vendor block name only within the library it belongs to.
drawingChecklist: State rated speed and voltage at that speed.
Show the converter or rectifier interface.
Cross-reference the counterpart IEC-style entry where both conventions are used.
entries.distinction: A permanent-magnet generator has no field winding to regulate; a wound-field synchronous generator has an exciter and regulator.

entries.name: ANSI/IEEE compound-excited DC generator symbol
entries.summary: IEEE-oriented library form of a DC generator with both series and shunt field windings, for drawing lookup.
description: A compound-excited DC generator combines a shunt field across the armature with a series field carrying load current. Depending on whether the series field aids or opposes the shunt field, terminal voltage can stay nearly flat, rise or fall with load. Such machines survive in legacy battery charging, traction and test installations.

IEEE-style schematics draw the armature circle with brushes, the series field as a winding in the armature lead and the shunt field as a separate winding across the terminals. This entry is a convention-specific lookup based on a publisher's IEEE-labelled preview; the geometry here is independently drawn and is not a certified reproduction of the standard graphic.
readingNotes: Identify whether the shunt field is connected across the armature only (short shunt) or across the series field as well (long shunt).
The vendor block identifier is a library name, not a standard number.
drawingChecklist: State field connection: short or long shunt, cumulative or differential.
Show field rheostat if fitted.
Cross-reference the IEC-style counterpart entry.
entries.distinction: A compound generator has both series and shunt fields; a plain DC generator symbol does not specify the field arrangement.

entries.name: Diesel generator set
entries.summary: A compression-ignition engine coupled to an alternator, shown as a source on microgrid and standby power single-line diagrams.
description: A diesel generator set combines a diesel engine, an alternator, a controller and usually a generator breaker into one package. On a microgrid single-line diagram it is the dispatchable source that sets voltage and frequency when the utility is absent, or that supports the battery during long periods of low renewable output.

It is commonly drawn as a generator circle with an engine box or the letters DG or D beside the mechanical coupling, followed by the generator breaker and its protection relay. Ratings are often written as prime, continuous or standby, because the same set can carry different loads under each duty definition.

The symbol does not tell you minimum loading limits, fuel autonomy or the governor and regulator settings needed to share load with other sources. Light loading of diesel engines causes wet stacking, so microgrid controls often maintain a minimum genset load that the diagram does not show.
readingNotes: Check whether the rating shown is standby, prime or continuous.
Follow the controller connections to see whether the set can parallel with other sources.
drawingChecklist: State kVA, kW, power factor and duty rating.
Show generator breaker and neutral earthing.
Reference controller and fuel system drawings.
entries.distinction: A diesel set uses compression ignition and liquid fuel; a gas engine set uses spark ignition and gaseous fuel with different load-acceptance behaviour.

entries.name: Gas engine generator set
entries.summary: A spark-ignited reciprocating engine on natural gas, biogas or LPG driving an alternator, shown as a generating source.
description: A gas engine generator set uses a spark-ignited reciprocating engine running on natural gas, biogas, landfill gas or LPG. These sets are common in combined heat and power plants, prime power microgrids and sites with a reliable gas supply, and they are often run continuously rather than only as backup.

Single-line diagrams draw the alternator circle with an engine block marked G or GAS, the generator breaker, and sometimes heat recovery references. When several sets run in parallel, a common synchronising bus and a load-sharing controller appear alongside.

Gas engines usually accept large load steps less readily than diesel engines, which affects how a microgrid sequences load after a blackout. The symbol does not express block-load acceptance, gas pressure requirements or emissions limits.
readingNotes: Check the load-step limits in the controller documents before assuming the set can pick up a whole bus at once.
Heat recovery or CHP notes indicate continuous running.
drawingChecklist: State fuel type and rating basis.
Show breaker and synchronising arrangement.
Reference load acceptance and start sequence.
entries.distinction: A gas engine set uses spark ignition and gaseous fuel; a gas turbine generator uses a continuous-combustion turbine.

entries.name: Gas turbine generator
entries.summary: A combustion gas turbine coupled to a synchronous generator, often through a gearbox, shown as a generating unit.
description: A gas turbine generator uses a continuous-combustion turbine to drive a synchronous generator, often through a reduction gearbox for smaller industrial machines. Units range from microturbines of tens of kilowatts with high-speed alternators and inverters, up to large industrial turbines feeding a medium-voltage bus.

The drawing usually shows a turbine glyph, a trapezoid widening in the direction of flow, joined by a shaft line to the generator circle. A generator step-up transformer, generator breaker and neutral earthing equipment follow on the single-line diagram.

Microturbines with high-speed alternators produce high-frequency output that must pass through a rectifier and inverter, so check whether a converter sits between the machine and the bus. The symbol does not state fuel, start method or ambient derating.
readingNotes: A trapezoid on the shaft line indicates the turbine; a gearbox may be drawn as a small box between turbine and generator.
Look for a converter stage on microturbine packages.
drawingChecklist: State ISO rating and site derating.
Show gearbox, generator breaker and earthing.
Reference start system and black-start capability.
entries.distinction: A gas turbine is a continuous-combustion rotating prime mover; a gas engine is reciprocating.

entries.name: Hydro turbine generator
entries.summary: A water turbine driving a generator, used for mini and micro hydro sources within microgrids and remote supplies.
description: A hydro turbine generator converts water flow and head into electrical power through a Pelton, Francis, Kaplan or crossflow turbine driving a synchronous or induction generator. In microgrids, small hydro is valuable because it is dispatchable within the limits of the water available and supplies real rotating inertia.

Drawings show a turbine element on the shaft line to the generator circle, sometimes with a governor or a dump-load controller attached. Very small run-of-river units often regulate frequency by diverting surplus power to a ballast load rather than adjusting water flow, so the dump load may appear beside the generator.

The symbol does not state head, flow, runaway speed or whether the unit can operate isolated. Penstock and water-hammer constraints limit how quickly load can change, which is not visible on the electrical drawing.
readingNotes: A ballast or dump load beside a small hydro set indicates electronic load control instead of a mechanical governor.
Check whether the generator is synchronous or induction.
drawingChecklist: State turbine type, head and flow.
Show governor or load controller.
Reference generator type and protection.
entries.distinction: A hydro unit is driven by water; its control differs from a thermal genset because load changes are limited by penstock dynamics.

entries.name: Fuel cell
entries.summary: An electrochemical source that converts hydrogen or another fuel directly into DC electricity, usually followed by a converter.
description: A fuel cell produces DC electricity from an electrochemical reaction between a fuel, usually hydrogen, and oxygen from air. Unlike a battery it does not store its reactants; it runs as long as fuel is supplied. Stack voltage falls noticeably with load current, so a DC/DC converter or inverter almost always follows it.

Drawings show the cell or stack as a rectangle with plates, or as a cell symbol labelled FC, with positive and negative DC leads. Balance-of-plant items such as the air blower, humidifier and coolant pump are auxiliary loads and normally appear on a separate auxiliary supply drawing.

The symbol does not state whether the stack can follow fast load changes. Most fuel cell systems pair with a battery or supercapacitor to cover transients, and the fuel supply, purge and safety interlocks belong on the process drawings.
readingNotes: Expect a converter and often a battery buffer next to the stack.
Separate stack output from auxiliary consumption when reading ratings.
drawingChecklist: State stack voltage range and current.
Show converter and buffer storage.
Reference fuel supply and safety interlocks.
entries.distinction: A fuel cell converts supplied fuel continuously; a battery stores a fixed charge and must be recharged.

entries.name: Hydrogen electrolyser
entries.summary: A DC load that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, supplied through a rectifier as a controllable sink in a microgrid.
description: An electrolyser uses DC current to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. In microgrids and renewable hubs it acts as a large controllable load that can absorb surplus solar or wind generation, with the hydrogen stored for later use in a fuel cell or sold off site.

On a single-line diagram the electrolyser stack appears as a DC load fed from a transformer-rectifier or an active front-end rectifier. Large units show the rectifier transformer, harmonic filtering and a DC busbar to the stack; smaller units may be drawn as a single block labelled with the stack rating.

Thyristor rectifiers for large electrolysers draw significant harmonic current and reactive power, so filters or compensators may be needed. The symbol does not state ramp rate, minimum load or the gas plant constraints that limit how flexibly the electrolyser can follow generation.
readingNotes: Read the rectifier type to judge harmonic and reactive impact.
Treat the stack as DC load; its rating is often given in MW of DC input.
drawingChecklist: State stack DC rating and ramp limits.
Show rectifier, transformer and filters.
Reference minimum load and process interlocks.
entries.distinction: An electrolyser consumes electricity to make hydrogen; a fuel cell consumes hydrogen to make electricity.

entries.name: Flywheel energy storage
entries.summary: A rotating mass coupled to a motor-generator and converter that stores energy kinetically for short, high-power bursts.
description: Flywheel energy storage holds energy in a rotating mass, usually in a vacuum enclosure with magnetic or low-loss bearings. A motor-generator accelerates the rotor to charge and decelerates it to discharge, and a bidirectional converter links the variable-frequency machine to a DC bus or AC network.

Single-line diagrams show a machine circle with a flywheel mass or disc symbol on the shaft and a converter block to the bus. Flywheels appear in rotary and some static UPS systems as a battery substitute, and in microgrids for frequency regulation and ride-through of short disturbances.

Stored energy is usually small, from seconds to a few minutes at rated power, so the symbol does not imply long backup time. Standby losses, minimum speed and the energy actually usable between maximum and minimum speed must be read from the data sheet.
readingNotes: Read discharge time at rated power rather than total stored energy.
A converter is needed because machine frequency changes with speed.
drawingChecklist: State power rating and ride-through time.
Show converter and bus connection.
Reference standby loss and containment data.
entries.distinction: A flywheel stores kinetic energy for seconds to minutes; a battery stores chemical energy for much longer durations.

entries.name: Supercapacitor bank
entries.summary: A series-parallel array of double-layer capacitor cells storing energy for very fast, short-duration power delivery.
description: A supercapacitor bank uses electric double-layer capacitor cells, each rated at only a few volts, connected in series strings to reach a useful DC voltage. It can charge and discharge at very high current for hundreds of thousands of cycles, but stores far less energy than a battery of similar size.

Drawings use a polarised capacitor symbol repeated or annotated with the series and parallel cell count, together with a balancing circuit and a DC/DC converter. In microgrids the bank smooths fast power fluctuations, supports converter DC links or covers the gap before a generator starts.

Supercapacitor voltage falls linearly as energy is drawn out, so usable energy depends on the converter minimum voltage. The symbol does not show cell balancing, temperature limits or the converter range needed to extract the stored energy.
readingNotes: Check the series cell count and the balancing method.
Usable energy depends on the voltage window, not the full rated voltage.
drawingChecklist: State rated voltage, capacitance and string arrangement.
Show balancing and the DC/DC converter.
Reference minimum operating voltage.
entries.distinction: A supercapacitor bank delivers short high-power bursts; a battery bank delivers lower power for much longer.

entries.name: Single battery cell
entries.summary: One electrochemical cell drawn as a single long plate and short plate pair, marking cell-level voltage and polarity.
description: The single cell symbol is one long line for the positive plate and one shorter, often thicker, line for the negative plate. It represents one electrochemical cell, for example a 2 V lead-acid cell or a nominal 3.2 V lithium iron phosphate cell, and is the building block from which battery symbols are composed.

It appears on schematics where cell-level detail matters, such as cell monitoring connections, a backup cell on a controller board or a pilot cell for temperature and voltage measurement in a stationary battery. On power single-line diagrams the multi-cell battery symbol is normally used instead.

The symbol shows polarity but not chemistry, capacity or nominal voltage, all of which must be labelled. Drawing one cell does not mean the battery has one cell; check whether the drawing uses a single cell glyph as shorthand for a whole battery.
readingNotes: The longer plate is positive.
Confirm whether the glyph is a true single cell or a simplified battery.
drawingChecklist: State chemistry and nominal cell voltage.
Mark polarity.
Reference monitoring connections if any.
entries.distinction: A single cell is one plate pair; the battery symbol repeats plate pairs or adds a dashed line between them to show several cells.

entries.name: Battery string
entries.summary: A series connection of cells or modules reaching the system DC voltage, often with its own fuse or breaker and monitoring.
description: A battery string is a group of cells or modules connected in series to reach the operating DC voltage of an inverter, UPS or DC system. Several strings may run in parallel to increase capacity, and each string normally has its own protective device and disconnect so that one string can be isolated without shutting down the others.

Drawings show the battery symbol with the cell or module count annotated, a dashed line indicating omitted cells, and the string fuse or breaker at the positive and sometimes negative terminal. String current sensors and the battery management connections are often drawn at the same point.

The symbol does not state how strings share current or what happens when one string has a weak cell. Parallel strings of different ages or states of health share current unevenly, which the drawing alone cannot reveal.
readingNotes: Read the annotated number of cells or modules in series.
Each parallel string should have its own isolation and protection.
drawingChecklist: State cells or modules in series and nominal string voltage.
Show string fuse or breaker and disconnect.
Reference string current measurement.
entries.distinction: A string is one series chain; a battery bank or rack may contain several strings in parallel.

entries.name: Battery rack
entries.summary: A rack of series-connected battery modules with its own switchgear and battery management unit, forming one DC source.
description: In stationary lithium-ion systems a battery rack holds modules connected in series to form one string, together with a rack-level switchgear box containing contactors, fuses, precharge circuit and the rack battery management unit. Racks are then paralleled onto a DC bus feeding the power conversion system.

Single-line diagrams draw each rack as a battery symbol within a boundary box that also contains the rack contactors and fuse, with the management unit shown as a small block linked by a communication line. Large systems may show one typical rack and note the number of racks in parallel.

The rack boundary on an electrical drawing does not describe mechanical arrangement, fire separation or cooling. It also does not state whether racks of different capacities can be mixed, which the battery manufacturer must confirm.
readingNotes: One typical rack is often drawn with a multiplier note for the rest.
Rack contactors are opened by the management system, not by the inverter.
drawingChecklist: State modules per rack and rack voltage.
Show rack contactors, fuses and precharge.
Reference number of racks in parallel.
entries.distinction: A rack is the packaged string with switchgear and management; a plain battery string symbol shows only the series cells.

entries.name: Battery energy storage system
entries.summary: A complete battery plant block combining batteries, power conversion and controls, shown as one source or sink on an SLD.
description: A battery energy storage system is the full plant: battery racks, a bidirectional power conversion system, transformers, auxiliary supplies and a plant controller. On higher-level single-line diagrams it is shown as one block with a battery mark and a converter mark, connecting to the network through a breaker and often a step-up transformer.

The block is labelled with both power and energy ratings, for example MW and MWh, since the two together define how long the system can deliver rated output. More detailed drawings break the block down into racks, the conversion system and auxiliaries.

The symbol does not show usable energy after depth-of-discharge limits, degradation over life, or whether the converter is grid-forming. These figures, plus the auxiliary load which can be significant for cooling, come from the performance specification.
readingNotes: Always read both the power and energy ratings.
Check whether the block includes its own step-up transformer.
drawingChecklist: State MW, MWh and point of connection voltage.
Show breaker, transformer and auxiliary supply.
Reference converter control mode.
entries.distinction: A BESS block is the complete plant; a battery symbol is only the electrochemical store.

entries.name: Centre-tapped battery bank
entries.summary: A battery bank with a mid-point connection that provides positive and negative rails about a common centre point.
description: A centre-tapped battery bank brings out a connection at the middle of the series chain, giving positive and negative rails referred to that point. It is used in some UPS rectifier-inverter designs, three-level converters and telecom or substation DC systems that need a symmetric supply or a defined midpoint for earth-fault detection.

Drawings show the battery symbol split into two halves with a lead taken from the junction, often labelled N, M or 0 V. The midpoint may be earthed, earthed through a resistance or left floating with an insulation monitor, and the drawing should state which.

The symbol does not show how the two halves are kept balanced. Unequal loading on the two rails discharges one half faster, and the midpoint earthing method changes how an earth fault on either rail behaves.
readingNotes: Identify how the midpoint is earthed or monitored.
Check whether loads draw from one half only.
drawingChecklist: State voltage of each half and total.
Show midpoint earthing or monitoring.
Reference balancing and fault detection.
entries.distinction: A centre-tapped bank has a usable midpoint; an ordinary battery string presents only positive and negative terminals.

entries.name: Battery power conversion system
entries.summary: The bidirectional inverter stage of a battery plant that charges and discharges the DC battery from the AC network.
description: The power conversion system is the bidirectional converter that sits between the battery DC bus and the AC network in a storage plant. It charges the battery by rectifying AC and discharges it by inverting DC, under the direction of a plant controller that sets active and reactive power or operates in a grid-forming mode.

Drawings show a converter box with both AC and DC marks and a bidirectional energy-flow arrow, a DC breaker or switch on the battery side, and an AC breaker, filter and often a medium-voltage skid transformer on the network side. Several PCS units may share one transformer.

The symbol does not tell you whether the unit can black-start a dead bus, how much overload it can supply or how it limits fault current. Those features drive protection settings and must be read from the converter specification.
readingNotes: Look for the bidirectional energy-flow qualifier to confirm charge and discharge capability.
Check the transformer and filter on the AC side.
drawingChecklist: State kW, kVA and DC voltage window.
Show DC and AC switching and filters.
Reference control modes and black-start capability.
entries.distinction: A PCS is a utility or commercial storage converter; an inverter-charger is a smaller low-voltage unit with an integral AC transfer relay.

facts.label: Ratings
facts.value: kW, kVA and DC voltage window

facts.label: Network side
facts.value: Filter and often a skid transformer

entries.name: Float and boost battery charger
entries.summary: A rectifier charger that holds a stationary battery at float voltage and can apply a higher boost or equalise voltage.
description: A float and boost charger is the rectifier that maintains a stationary battery, typically for switchgear tripping supplies, telecom or a microgrid DC bus. In float mode it supplies the standing DC load and a small trickle current, while boost or equalise mode raises the voltage to recharge the battery quickly after a discharge or to equalise lead-acid cells.

Drawings show a rectifier block with an AC input breaker, DC output to the battery and the DC distribution board, and often a blocking diode or dropping diode chain to keep load voltage within limits during boost. Alarm contacts for charger failure, earth fault and low voltage are drawn on the control schematic.

The symbol does not state the current limit, whether the charger alone can carry the full load without the battery, or temperature compensation of float voltage. These matter for sizing and for battery life, so they must be in the specification.
readingNotes: Look for voltage-dropping diodes that protect loads during boost charging.
Check whether two chargers share one battery for redundancy.
drawingChecklist: State float and boost voltages and current rating.
Show AC supply, battery and load connections.
Reference alarms and temperature compensation.
entries.distinction: A station charger is a power rectifier supplying load and battery; a battery charger controller is an integrated circuit inside smaller equipment.

facts.label: Typical alarms
facts.value: Charger fail, earth fault, low voltage

entries.name: Thyristor phase-controlled rectifier
entries.summary: An AC-to-DC converter using thyristors fired at a controlled angle to set its DC output voltage.
description: A phase-controlled rectifier uses thyristors instead of diodes, so the firing angle sets the average DC output voltage. Six-pulse bridges are widely used for large battery chargers, electrolysers, DC drives and older UPS rectifiers because they are robust and simple to control.

On single-line diagrams it appears as the rectifier box with AC and DC marks plus a thyristor or control qualifier, or as a bridge of thyristor symbols on detailed schematics. A rectifier transformer, line reactor and harmonic filter are often drawn upstream.

Reducing the output voltage by delaying firing also lowers the input power factor, and the converter draws characteristic harmonics at 5th, 7th, 11th and 13th orders. The symbol does not show these effects, which must be assessed with the network harmonic study.
readingNotes: A thyristor mark inside or beside the rectifier block distinguishes it from a diode rectifier.
Expect harmonic filtering or a phase-shifting transformer on large units.
drawingChecklist: State pulse number and DC rating.
Show rectifier transformer and line reactor.
Reference harmonic study and filter design.
entries.distinction: A phase-controlled rectifier sets voltage by firing angle; an active front-end rectifier uses switched transistors and can run near unity power factor.

facts.label: Characteristic harmonics
facts.value: 6k plus or minus 1 for a six-pulse bridge

entries.name: Twelve-pulse rectifier
entries.summary: Two six-pulse bridges fed from star and delta transformer windings 30 degrees apart, cancelling the lowest harmonics.
description: A twelve-pulse rectifier feeds two six-pulse bridges from transformer secondaries displaced by 30 electrical degrees, usually one star and one delta winding. The two bridge outputs are combined in series or in parallel with an interphase reactor, and the 5th and 7th harmonic currents cancel on the primary side.

The single-line diagram shows a three-winding rectifier transformer with star and delta secondaries, each feeding a rectifier block, and the two DC outputs joining. It is used for large UPS rectifiers, electrolysers, traction substations and some drive front ends.

Cancellation only works when the two bridges share load equally and the supply is balanced. The symbol does not show residual 11th and 13th harmonics or the effect of transformer impedance mismatch, so a harmonic study is still required.
readingNotes: Look for a three-winding transformer with star and delta secondaries.
Check whether the bridges are connected in series or parallel on the DC side.
drawingChecklist: State transformer vector groups and phase shift.
Show both bridges and DC connection.
Reference expected harmonic spectrum.
entries.distinction: A twelve-pulse rectifier uses two phase-shifted bridges; a six-pulse rectifier uses one bridge and has larger 5th and 7th harmonics.

entries.name: Grid-forming inverter
entries.summary: An inverter controlled as a voltage source that sets its own voltage and frequency, able to energise and hold up an island.
description: A grid-forming inverter controls its output as a voltage source behind an impedance, setting voltage magnitude and frequency itself rather than measuring and following them. This lets it start a dead microgrid, share load with other sources through droop or virtual synchronous machine control, and respond instantly to load steps.

Single-line diagrams use the inverter symbol, a box with DC and AC marks, with a GFM label, a voltage-source note or a sine source mark to show the control mode. On microgrid drawings at least one grid-forming source must be available whenever the system is islanded.

Hardware alone does not decide grid-forming behaviour; many converters can switch modes in software. The symbol does not show current limits during faults, which are usually far lower than a synchronous machine, so protection based on fault current needs checking.
readingNotes: Look for GFM or voltage-source notes; the box itself is the same as any inverter.
Confirm that a grid-forming source is present in every islanded operating case.
drawingChecklist: State control mode and droop settings.
Show island and grid-connected switching.
Reference fault current capability.
entries.distinction: A grid-forming inverter sets voltage and frequency; a grid-following inverter injects current synchronised to a voltage that something else provides.

facts.label: Islanding role
facts.value: Can energise and hold an island

entries.name: Grid-following inverter
entries.summary: An inverter that tracks an existing network voltage with a phase-locked loop and injects controlled current into it.
description: A grid-following inverter measures the network voltage, locks to it with a phase-locked loop and injects a controlled current. Most rooftop and utility-scale solar inverters work this way. They need a stable voltage from the grid, a synchronous machine or a grid-forming inverter to operate, and they disconnect when that reference is lost.

Drawings use the standard inverter symbol with a GFL note or a current-source annotation. Anti-islanding protection, often shown as a protection relay or a function list, is associated with this type so that it does not energise a dead network.

In weak networks with high converter penetration, grid-following control can become unstable, so system strength studies are needed. The symbol does not show the phase-locked loop settings or the reactive power mode.
readingNotes: Check that a forming source exists if the inverter is expected to run in an island.
Anti-islanding settings are often listed as protection functions next to the inverter.
drawingChecklist: State reactive power mode and ride-through settings.
Show anti-islanding protection.
Reference system strength assessment.
entries.distinction: A grid-following inverter needs an external voltage reference; a grid-forming inverter provides that reference.

entries.name: Hybrid inverter
entries.summary: A single inverter with PV, battery and AC ports, combining MPPT charging, battery inversion and backup output.
description: A hybrid inverter combines a solar maximum power point tracker, a bidirectional battery converter and an AC inverter in one unit. It typically has three port types: PV DC input, battery DC terminals and an AC grid connection, with many models adding a separate backup or essential load output that stays energised during a network outage.

Single-line diagrams show one inverter block with multiple DC inputs and one or two AC outputs, and the internal DC bus is sometimes drawn as a dashed line. The essential load board, isolators for each port and the grid connection point should all be shown.

The symbol does not state how fast the backup output transfers, whether the battery can be charged from the grid, or what export limit applies. Those depend on the settings and on network operator rules, not on the block itself.
readingNotes: Identify every DC and AC port and its isolator.
Separate the backup output circuits from normal circuits.
drawingChecklist: State PV, battery and AC ratings.
Show backup load board and isolators.
Reference export limit and transfer behaviour.
entries.distinction: A hybrid inverter includes PV and battery ports in one unit; an inverter-charger usually has a battery port only and relies on separate solar chargers.

facts.label: Ports
facts.value: PV, battery, grid, often backup AC

entries.name: Bidirectional inverter-charger
entries.summary: A battery converter that charges from an AC source and inverts back to AC, with an internal transfer relay for the load.
description: An inverter-charger contains one bidirectional power stage between a battery and an AC output, together with an internal transfer relay connecting the AC input to the output when a valid source is present. With the source available it passes power through and charges the battery; without it, it opens the relay and inverts from the battery.

Drawings show a converter box with DC and AC marks, a bidirectional arrow, an AC input from the grid or generator and an AC output to the load. The transfer relay may be drawn inside the boundary as a changeover contact, and some units have a second output that drops during battery operation.

The symbol does not show the internal neutral-earth relay many units use when inverting, which matters for earthing and residual current device operation. Power assist settings, which let the inverter add battery power to a limited generator supply, are also invisible on the drawing.
readingNotes: Look for the internal transfer relay and any neutral-earth relay.
Check whether a second output is shed on battery operation.
drawingChecklist: State inverter VA, charger current and battery voltage.
Show AC input, outputs and earthing arrangement.
Reference input current limit settings.
entries.distinction: An inverter-charger has an internal transfer relay and charger; a plain DC-to-AC inverter only converts battery power to AC.

entries.name: PV string inverter
entries.summary: A solar inverter connecting a small number of PV strings directly, each group tracked by its own MPPT input.
description: A string inverter connects one or a few PV strings directly to its DC inputs, usually with two or more independent maximum power point trackers. In commercial and utility plants many string inverters are spread across the array and their AC outputs are collected at an AC combiner board.

Single-line diagrams show the inverter box with several DC inputs, each labelled by MPPT and string count, plus a DC isolator and sometimes string fuses inside the inverter. The AC side shows the output breaker and the combiner or distribution board.

The symbol does not tell you whether strings on the same tracker share orientation, which affects yield, nor whether the inverter has integrated arc fault detection. The string configuration schedule carries that detail.
readingNotes: Count MPPT inputs and the strings on each.
Check for DC isolators on each input.
drawingChecklist: State number of MPPTs and strings per MPPT.
Show DC isolation and AC protection.
Reference string configuration schedule.
entries.distinction: A string inverter serves a few strings near the array; a central inverter collects many combined strings at one large unit.

facts.value: A few kW to a few hundred kW

entries.name: PV central inverter
entries.summary: A large solar inverter fed from DC combiner boxes, usually paired with its own medium-voltage transformer.
description: A central inverter converts the combined output of many PV strings at a single location. Strings are first paralleled in DC combiner boxes, which feed DC recombiners and then the inverter. Ratings run from several hundred kilowatts to several megawatts, and the inverter usually sits in a skid with a medium-voltage step-up transformer and switchgear.

Single-line diagrams show the DC combiner network converging on one inverter block, the inverter output to a low-voltage winding of the skid transformer, and the medium-voltage ring main unit. Dual inverters sharing one three-winding transformer are also common.

A central inverter fault takes a large part of the plant offline, and the DC cabling distances are long. The symbol does not show DC earthing arrangement or insulation monitoring, which differ between plants and must be stated separately.
readingNotes: Trace DC combiner and recombiner levels back to the strings.
Check whether two inverters share one transformer.
drawingChecklist: State inverter rating and DC voltage range.
Show combiner hierarchy and skid transformer.
Reference DC earthing and insulation monitoring.
entries.distinction: A central inverter collects many combined strings; a string inverter connects a few strings directly.

facts.label: Typical rating
facts.value: Hundreds of kW to several MW

entries.name: PV microinverter
entries.summary: A small inverter attached to one or two PV modules, converting to AC at the module and paralleling on an AC trunk cable.
description: A microinverter converts the output of one, two or four PV modules to AC right at the array. Each unit has its own maximum power point tracker, so shading on one module does not drag down the rest, and the array wiring carries AC at network voltage instead of high-voltage DC.

Drawings show a small inverter block attached to each module symbol, with AC outputs daisy-chained along a trunk cable to an AC isolator and a dedicated circuit breaker in the switchboard. The number of units per branch circuit is limited by the trunk cable and breaker rating and should be noted.
The symbol does not state the gateway or communication method, nor how many microinverters a branch can carry. Ambient temperature on the roof also affects output, which is not shown on the drawing.
readingNotes: Count units per AC branch against the trunk cable rating.
There is no high-voltage DC string; the DC side ends at each module.
drawingChecklist: State units per branch and branch breaker rating.
Show AC isolator and trunk cable.
Reference monitoring gateway.
entries.distinction: A microinverter converts at module level to AC; a power optimiser stays on the DC side and still needs a string inverter.

entries.name: Bidirectional DC-to-DC converter
entries.summary: A DC/DC stage that can pass power in either direction, linking a battery or supercapacitor to a DC bus.
description: A bidirectional DC/DC converter moves power in either direction between two DC voltage levels. In microgrids and DC-coupled solar plants it connects a battery or supercapacitor to a common DC bus, charging the store from surplus and discharging it when the bus voltage falls.

The drawing is the DC/DC converter box with DC marks on both sides and a bidirectional arrow, or a double-headed arrow along the box. Detailed schematics may show a half-bridge buck-boost or dual-active-bridge topology inside.

The symbol does not state whether the two sides are galvanically isolated, the current limits in each direction, or the control mode, which may regulate bus voltage or battery current. These must come from the converter data.
readingNotes: Check the arrow direction marks for confirmation that power flows both ways.
Isolation is not implied unless stated or a transformer is shown.
drawingChecklist: State voltage ranges and power in each direction.
Show isolation if present.
Reference control mode.
entries.distinction: A bidirectional converter transfers power both ways; a standard DC/DC converter passes power from input to output only.
